articles.title: Pressure builds in Spain to deny US extradition request for leftwing donor
articles.summary:
Key government meeting this month will consider US bid to try James ‘Fergie’ Chambers over alleged support for Hamas

Attorneys for James “Fergie” Chambers, the US citizen and wealthy donor…

blocks.text: Attorneys for James “Fergie” Chambers, the US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects worldwide who is currently imprisoned in Madrid and sought in extradition, have submitted a brief ahead of a decisive government meeting on the case.
Meanwhile, Chambers’ partner, the actor and activist Stella Schnabel, met last week with multiple members of the Spanish parliament to assert his innocence.

The legal team’s arguments include that the US government has failed to identify specific acts of violence or damages personally attributable to Chambers and instead is seeking to criminalize acts linked to political protest.
They also assert that at least one figure of US law underpinning the request – “conspiracy to commit riot” – has no equivalent in Spanish law, which would also help render the extradition invalid.
It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas.

Chambers’ defense has submitted its brief to the government ahead of a meeting by Spain’s council of ministers expected to take place on 22 September. The council can decide whether or not to allow the US extradition request to proceed, based in part on an evaluation of supporting materials the Trump administration supplied to the government on 26 August.
Under Spanish law, at this “administrative” stage, the 22-member council has the power to deny the request, before it reaches a “judicial” stage.

The US government’s case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m that he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to support the Palestinian group Hamas. The exact details of the indictment against Chambers remain sealed.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators gather at Puerta del Sol in Madrid during a rally demanding the release of the US activist Fergie Chambers and opposing his extradition to the US on 5 September 2026 Photograph: Richard Zubelzu/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Chambers’ team say he has been supporting humanitarian aid and other projects. The 41–year-old self-described anti–imperialist’s defense is also asserting that the Trump administration’s additional charges of “international money laundering” don’t hold up because, as heir to one of the richest families in the US, he obtained his personal wealth through legal means. Chambers’ donations have gone to about 100 projects in 20 countries for several years – including the Sameer Project, in Gaza.

“It would set an alarming precedent in all of Europe if Spain allowed the Trump administration to criminalize offering vital humanitarian aid to the Palestinian people and defending their rights,” said Baltasar Garzón, the acclaimed human rights lawyer and a member of Chambers’ legal team.
“That’s what Fergie has financed: humanitarian aid and support for people in a situation of great need,” said Garzón. “That’s not terrorism, according to Spanish and European legal standards.”

Meanwhile, Schnabel has met with members of Sumar and Podemos – progressive political movements vital to the coalition government of the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – and has written a one-page letter to Sánchez asking him to make “the only morally acceptable decision”, that of denying extradition. Sánchez forms part of the council of ministers.
Schnabel has not escaped scrutiny since her partner was detained on 10 July in Ibiza. On a recent trip to New York, the FBI pulled her aside at JFK airport and confiscated her phone, she said.

Support for Chambers in the lead-up to the 20 September meeting has come from Ione Bellara, leader of Podemos, who opened the party’s quarterly meeting last Saturday with a statement opposing the extradition request, saying that Chambers was “on the right side of history” with his financial support of Palestinians in Gaza.

Similarly, Sumar, the leftwing coalition that governs jointly with Sánchez’s Socialist party, filed a statement in Spain’s congress earlier this week urging the government to deny the petition, “given that the goal of the extradition request … is to criminalize, persecute or punish [Chambers] due to his political opinions, his public activity or his participation in political movements – in this case, in support of the Palestinian people”.

Irene Montero, member of Podemos and Spanish representative to the European parliament, told the Guardian that “Our laws don’t contemplate the actions he is accused of … [and] we can’t become a subject of the United States.”
Activists have held rallies in recent days in at least six cities across Spain in support of Chambers, with plans for more.

Other shows of support from farther afield have included a petition delivered to the Spanish government signed by actors, academics, activists and others, including Richard Gere, Greta Thunberg and Angela Davis. In Tunisia, supporters of the Club Africain football team displayed banners and T-shirts at a recent match that read, “Free Fergie”. In Portugal, at Festa do Avante, one of that country’s largest cultural festivals, fans held up a banner saying: “Free Fergie – supporting Palestine isn’t a crime.”

Schnabel told the Guardian last month that the $7.5m went to support Club Africain. Hamed Mbarek, one of the club’s supporters and an organizer of fans at last Saturday’s match, said Club Africain was “pro-Palestine” and that Chambers and the club had “synchronicity”.

Chambers’ money comes from a mid-2023 settlement with his family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications, in which he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m. Members of his family severed contact with him at the time.

His views and donations have been extensively profiled in US media. He was interviewed on a TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group now proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”.

Chambers’ public comments on Israel and Gaza have also brought controversy. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/ There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/ No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/ It’s simply genocide/ Like it has been.”
He has also been a staunch critic of the US, telling a reporter in 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.”

Irene Zugasti helped organize rallies earlier this week and last weekend in support of Chambers in Madrid, Barcelona and several other Spanish cities. She sees the case as bigger than whether he is extradited or not. “If they go after Fergie, they’ll go after anyone … It’s a test – to see until what point European governments feel pressure from the United States.”

articles.title: Russians on the Goethe-Institut: 'Hostage to politics'
articles.summary: Canceled language exams, disrupted plans to study in Germany, and the disappearance of an important cultural link: DW users shared how the closure of Germany's Goethe-Institut in Russia affects their…

image.caption: The Goethe-Institut in Moscow is one of three branches of Germany’s cultural center that'll have to closeImage: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Germany's Goethe-Institut is set toclose all Russian branches by Sunday, amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany.

The Russian Foreign Ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempteddrone attackat Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House, and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens.

"All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Goethe-Institut Secretary General Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."

blocks.caption: The library of the Goethe-Institut's Moscow branch won't be accessible anymore after September 13 eitherImage: Timur Gusarov/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.
'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams

Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.
Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.

"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.
DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.
"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig

It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.
Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard

The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.

"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.
"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.
"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.

Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.
'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'
Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.

"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."

blocks.caption: Leipzig/Halle airport in Germany was the target of an attempted drone attack in August 2026Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.

"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.
Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected.

"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.
Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship
Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.
"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.

A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.
President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."
According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

articles.title: Iran war reshapes Brics ties but also exposes divisions
articles.summary: Brics members agree they need a new global order but it's harder to answer what should replace it and how to get there.

blocks.text: This weekend, some of the most powerful people in the world gathered in Delhi around a vast circular table.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that together, the leaders next to him should increasingly become "rule-shapers", not "rule-takers".

Among those listening were members of the Brics group, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa.
These are hardly natural allies. They have histories of border disputes and even military confrontations.

India and China engaged in a deadly clash along their disputed border in 2020. Iran and the UAE have been on opposing ends of the war in the Middle East, with Tehran launching missiles and drones at its fellow Brics member as the conflict sent shockwaves across global economies.

The fact that India was able to gather these leaders together in person is a feat in and of itself and testament to its diplomatic reach. The weekend also provided a platform for countries to reassess their relationships in light of the Iran war.
But agreeing on what a new global order should look like and achieving clear, tangible outcomes was a much harder task, and that tension ran through this weekend's summit.
The summit succeeded in delivering a joint declaration when divisions among members have rarely been so glaring.

Twice earlier this year, meetings between Brics ministers had failed to produce a joint statement. This time a consensus was reached, but by side-stepping issues that members sharply disagree on, with few solutions.
The "New Delhi Declaration" was adopted on the first day of the summit. But what is striking is what it doesn't say.
On the war in the Middle East, the declaration urges "maximum restraint". It also condemns "attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities" but assigns no blame.

It reiterates support for a two-state solution, opposes forced displacement of Palestinians or actions that could "legitimise or prolong occupation", framing it carefully around existing UN resolutions.
It makes no mention at all of Russia's war in Ukraine, a departure from previous Brics declarations.
There is similar caution on trade. It lists concerns over "indiscriminate rising tariffs" and condemns unilateral sanctions but stops short of naming the US, and is likely to avoid Washington's ire.

items: Trump shadow looms large over Brics as Modi hosts Putin and Xi in Delhi

blocks.text: Several Brics members would have been loath to draw President Donald Trump's anger, as he has previously called the group's proposals, including potentially linking central-bank digital currencies for cross-border trade, "anti-American".
"Not mentioning any country by name, even as they condemned the conflict in the Middle East, bears the hallmark of India," says Praveen Donthi, senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.

"I was pleasantly surprised that there was a strong reference to tariffs, because India could have wanted to be less direct about it, but perhaps this was a chance to convey their displeasure," he added.
In the wake of Trump's trade threats and the shock of the war in the Middle East, reshaping the global order has become a vital need for many member economies.
What the summit did provide is a platform for meetings that seemed hard to imagine just a few months ago.
Iran's Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince sat down for talks together - the highest-level face-to-face meeting known between the two countries since the war began.
This weekend offered Tehran a chance to show that it does not stand alone amid the US and Israel's military attacks and economic pressure.

As Iran tries to withstand US sanctions, Washington's "Operation Economic Outcast" and a naval blockade on its ports, Pezeshkian pressed for deeper economic ties with Brics members, including Malaysia, India and Ethiopia.

As for China, this was President Xi's first visit to Delhi in seven years. There has been deep mistrust between China and India since the 2020 border dispute, but those tensions have eased. There is also a large trade imbalance, with a deficit tilting heavily in China's favour.
There was a cordial handshake between Xi and Modi, not the latter's signature hug. Xi also stayed for less than 24 hours, skipping the gala dinner hosted by Modi on Saturday night.

But the weekend was still a big moment for two countries with such a difficult relationship. According to official readouts, the two leaders agreed to strengthen business ties and transport links and address barriers to trade.

Trigunayat believes this is part of a gradual warming of relations in recent years, and that there is a will on both sides to work together. But whether it will produce substantial progress remains to be seen.
"I always say we have to trust, but verify first," he says.

articles.title: Voting under way in Sweden with far-right eyeing first role in government
articles.summary:
Party with neo-Nazi roots is in line for key ministerial positions if rightwing bloc wins the election

Voting is under way in Sweden in a high-stakes election that could lead to the…

blocks.text: Voting is under way in Sweden in a high-stakes election that could lead to the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) entering government for the first time.

It comes after an unusually heated and polarised campaign punctuated by personal attacks between leaders, accusations of misinformation and Maga-inspired ads. Polls suggest an extremely tight race, with one showing just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs.
Polling stations across the country opened at 8am local time (07.00 BST). A record 3.6 million voters took part in early voting.

Early indications of results will come at 8pm when the first exit polls are released, followed by a forecast from the broadcaster SVT an hour later. The first preliminary vote count is expected between 10.30 and 11pm. Whatever the result, coalition talks are expected to take weeks if not months.

The right-leaning bloc, made up of what are known as the Tidö parties, has been in power for four years. It is formed of the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals with a supporting role for SD, Sweden’s second biggest party.
The opposition left-leaning bloc is formed of Sweden’s biggest party, the Social Democrats, the Centre party, the Green party and the Left party.

blocks.caption: The leader of the Social Democrats, Magdalena Andersson, casts her vote in Stockholm. Photograph: Stefan Jerrevang/EPA

blocks.text: The rightwing coalition broke a long-standing taboo in 2022 by going into partnership with SD, which has neo-Nazi roots.
SD has attempted to make itself more palatable to the mainstream by toning down its overtly racist rhetoric, while arguing that immigration is responsible for Sweden’s crime problems.

After four years in a supporting role for the Moderates-run coalition government, however, during which it has shifted much of the Swedish establishment to the right, SD’s approach to the election has been more brazen. If the right-leaning coalition win, the party has been promised a prominent role in the government, including key ministerial positions.

SD’s campaign slogan of “make Sweden Sweden again” was reminiscent of Donald Trump’s “make America great again”. Their controversial ads on buses – with messages including: “Do you miss Mogadishu? The repatriation grant will help you get home” – were taken down after drivers refused to work in vehicles displaying them.
after newsletter promotion
The party leader, Jimmie Åkesson, was accused of sexism after asking the Social Democrats’ leader, Magdalena Andersson, why she was so angry during a TV debate.

Another leading SD figure, Gustav Gellerbrant, came under national scrutiny after an investigation by the publication Expo connected his partner to Russian state actors and the spread of Russian propaganda. His partner, who is Russian, works as a civil servant for SD in parliament. Gellerbrant said in response that it was “isolated information” intended to raise suspicion about her Russian origins and has since gone on leave.
Andersson, who voted on Sunday morning in the Stockholm suburb of Nacka, said the campaign had been “a tale of two sides”.

“There have been a lot of lies and bickering, but at the same time there are so many sensible people out there across the country,” she told SVT. “The focus is on winning and setting a new direction for Sweden.”

Abba’s Benny Andersson showed his support for Social Democrats’ leader by performing a reworked version of Mamma Mia to supporters at the the party’s headquarters, replacing the words “Mamma Mia” with “Magdalena”.

The prime minister and leader of the Moderates, Ulf Kristersson, has put considerable focus in the final days of campaigning on the penalty discount applied to criminals convicted of various offences. He accused Andersson of not standing up for female rape victims. In response, she accused him of weaponising men’s violence against women.

Voters say the most important election issues are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy. But much of the election debate has been focused on personal finance, said Radio Sweden’s senior political correspondent, Fredrik Furtenbach. “The parties have tried to outdo each other with promises of more money. It has been a sort of auction.”

articles.title: Revered sports journalist Recah Trinidad dies at 83
articles.summary: Recah Trinidad dies 'peacefully in his sleep,' two years after the death of his sports journalist son Chino

blocks.text: ICON. Filipino sports journalist Recah Trinidad.
Manolo Chino Trinidad Facebook page
Recah Trinidad dies 'peacefully in his sleep,' two years after the death of his sports journalist son Chino
MANILA, Philippines – Veteran sports journalist and columnist Ricardo “Recah” Trinidad died on Sunday, September 13. He was 83.
His death was announced by his daughter-in-law Nice, who said Trinidad passed away at around 6 am.

“After suffering a heart attack in June, dad bravely fought for the past few months and finally found his rest. He passed peacefully in his sleep, free from pain and suffering,” wrote Nice on Facebook.

One of the most revered sports journalists of his time, Trinidad wrote for multiple publications, including Daily Express, Tempo, and Malaya, and covered some of the most prestigious sporting events, including the Olympics, Asian Games, and the iconic Thrilla in Manila in 1975, where Muhammad Ali beat Joe Frazier.
He was also an award-winning writer, with his poem Rule Acrobat from Planet F winning second prize for poetry in the 1978 Palanca Awards.

Trinidad passed his passion for sports on to his son Manolo, most commonly known as Chino, who also became a sports journalist, and served as a commissioner of the Philippine Basketball League, and was one of the founding members of the Samahang Basketbol ng Pilipinas.

blocks.caption: FAMILY. Recah Trinidad with son Chino and wife Maria Fe during the 1994 Asian Games in Hiroshima, Japan.

blocks.text: “Ka Recah” passed away two years after Chino died of a heart attack in 2024.
“I find comfort knowing that dad is now reunited with his beloved eldest son, kuya Chino Trinidad,” wrote Nice.
Trinidad was also known for his Bare Eye column in the Philippine Daily Inquirer, which he started in 1986 and continued writing until his final piece in 2020.
A published author as well, Trinidad wrote the book Pacific Storm, which captured the rise of Filipino boxing icon Manny Pacquiao.

In 2023, Trinidad received the Lifetime Award in Sports Journalism from the Philippine Sportswriters Association alongside many of his peers, including the late Eddie Alinea, Percy Della, Jun Engracia, Ding Marcelo, and Al Mendoza.
Trinidad is survived by his wife, Maria Fe; his sons, Paolo and Baste; daughters-in-law Nice and Babs; and six grandchildren.
“Rest peacefully, dad, No more pain. You are home. Thank you for being our dad, I love you. We love you! and We will miss you forever,” said Nice.
The public viewing for Trinidad’s remains will start on Wednesday, September 16, before his cremation on Saturday, September 19. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Albertans to vote on opting out of federal programs — while keeping cash
articles.summary: When referendum day arrives in Alberta on Oct. 19, the focus won’t just be on separation and immigration. One of four constitutional questions will ask voters if they support a push to amend the…

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith arrives ahead of the First Ministers' Meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney in Charlottetown on July 23. (Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary

When referendum day arrives in Alberta on Oct. 19, the focus won’t just be on separation and immigration. One of four constitutional questions will ask voters if they support a push to amend the Constitution so Alberta can opt out of federal programs, while keeping the cash.
It’s 1 of 4 constitutional questions on October ballot, but ‘yes’ vote alone can’t change this
When referendum day arrives in Alberta on Oct. 19, the focus won’t just be on separation and immigration.
Albertans will also be presented with four constitutional questions that range from abolishing the Senate to whether Alberta should appoint the judges who sit on the province’s higher courts.
Third on the list will be a question tied to federal programs like pharmacare. The federal government provides funding to provinces for these programs, sometimes with conditions attached.
The Alberta government wants that to change.
As part of the referendum, voters will be asked if they support a government push to try to amend the Constitution.

The stated goal? To allow provinces to opt out of federal programs “that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services” without losing any associated federal funding for use in social programs.
“What Alberta is gunning for here is an attempt to limit what we call the constitutional spending power,” said Geoffrey Sigalet, director of the UBC Research Group for Constitutional Law.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: Power of the purse
By constitutional spending power, Sigalet is referring to Ottawa’s ability to transfer money to provinces and attach conditions to it.
Today, provinces can decline federal funding if they don’t agree with the conditions attached.
But if agreements between provinces and the federal government aren’t reached, that can also mean leaving money on the table, which can be politically unpopular.
“Different constitutional scholars take different perspectives on this,” Sigalet said.
“Some will be more in favour of centralizing this kind of thing. … My own sense is that Alberta has a point here.”
In Sigalet’s view, setting conditions on federal funding sent to other levels of government can look a lot like policymaking in another's jurisdiction.
He noted that some scholars have argued that the spending power is unconstitutional, and others have said it could be open to future litigation.
David Schneiderman, a law professor at the University of Toronto, argued the federal government only oversteps, constitutionally speaking, when it “imposes" programs.
“When it attaches conditions to spending in an area of provincial jurisdiction, a province can simply refuse to accept federal money,” Schneiderman wrote in an email.

“Note that there has not been any serious constitutional challenge to the exercise of the modern federal spending power. Provinces prefer to accept the money — and then erode conditions, as in the case of healthcare.”
This isn’t the first time the federal government’s spending power has been debated.
Not a new debate

The Meech Lake Accord in the 1980s was a failed attempt to amend the Canadian Constitution. One of the proposed amendments was allowing provinces to opt out with "reasonable compensation" of national shared-cost federal programs — with a notable condition.
“Under the language of Meech Lake, it was still a little limiting,” Sigalet said.
Under Meech, provinces could opt out if they established a program compatible with national objectives.
Alberta’s referendum doesn’t mention such a condition. Voters will simply be asked whether they endorse Alberta pursuing a constitutional change.
That change, as the province sees it, would allow provinces to opt out of federal programs “without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs.”
But as for then setting up a comparable program?
“We won’t make assumptions about the outcome or what decisions should follow until Albertans have had their say,” wrote Kyle Warner, a spokesperson for the province, in an email.
Schneiderman sees an issue.
“Alberta could negotiate with the feds. It is hard to see any federal government agreeing to something short of the Meech formulation,” he said.
Much like the other constitutional questions on the ballot this October, a “yes” vote doesn’t mean immediate change.
Developing an opt-out rule, in whatever form it might take, would require the support of Parliament, as well as at least seven provinces representing at least half of Canada’s population.
Impact on federal programs
All of this might sound familiar to Albertans.
For instance, take Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s statement in 2024 that the province would pull out of the Canadian Dental Care Plan by 2026.

There are, of course, less than four months to go in the calendar year, and Alberta has yet to exit that plan. A spokesperson for the provincial government said officials continue to work with Ottawa to ensure the province “receives its fair share” of federal funding to further expand its coverage.

items: Why Alberta's government wants out of the federal dental care plan — and who it could impact
Alberta wants to opt out of national pharmacare program

blocks.text: Fiona Clement, director of the Centre for Health Policy at the University of Calgary's Cumming School of Medicine, said that in her view, the federal government is in charge of a funding method, not a way to deliver the program.
“I would hope if we were standing something up in Alberta on its own, we would also be attracted to concepts like universality and comprehensiveness,” Clement said.

“On a general stand, I think many of the things that are done by the federal government, you are stronger together … there’s a lot of these processes that make a lot of sense to do at the national, federal level.”
The debate around how this money is spent has been going on for decades.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will have the opportunity to weigh in on whether they feel the current arrangement is working, or whether they think Alberta should fight to try to take control of those dollars — no strings attached.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Joel is a reporter/editor with CBC Calgary. In fall 2021, he spent time with CBC's bureau in Lethbridge. He was previously the editor of the Airdrie City View and Rocky View Weekly newspapers. He hails from Swift Current, Sask. Reach him by email at joel.dryden@cbc.ca

articles.title: Croatia: 'Monster' fire triggers evacuation on Brac island
articles.summary: A rapidly spreading wildfire threatened homes and tourist accommodations on the Croatian island of Brac, with firefighters battling the blaze overnight.

image.caption: The fire spread through remote parts of the island before threatening populated coastal areasImage: Ivo Cagalj/Pixsell/IMAGO

blocks.text: Nearly 700 people were evacuated amid a wildfire on the Adriatic island of Brac, Croatian media outlets reported on Sunday, following a tense night which saw hundreds of firefighters defending homes and tourist accommodations from the approaching blaze.
The situation was especially dramatic near the small town of Milna on the island's western coast.
"Last night was a disaster. It was simply impossible," Milna Mayor Frane Lozic told Net.hr news outlet. "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly."

blocks.caption: Over 220 firefighters and 69 vehicles fought the blaze overnightImage: Ivo Cagalj/Pixsell/IMAGO

blocks.text: The fire was first reported on Thursday, but firefighting efforts were complicated by inaccessible terrain.
Even so, Lozic said that the authorities believed they had the situation in hand by Saturday.
"We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9 p.m. and out of nowhere, there is a monster," he said.
No deaths reported in blaze
Tourist ships joined the rescue efforts overnight, with many tourists spending the night at the beach, waiting to be evacuated.

No deaths were reported due to the blaze. However, one 76-year-old Croatian woman was hospitalized in critical condition, according to Index.hr news portal. The woman is believed to have fallen off a ship during the evacuation process. A 27-year-old man required medical aid for smoke inhalation and was then released.
Authorities estimated some 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) were affected by the fire, according to a report by the AFP news agency.
Officials confirmed some buildings were damaged, but said it was too early for a full damage assessment.
Firefighting planes active on the scene

As of Sunday morning, Croatian authorities said there were no more "open fires" but added teams were still in the field to prevent reignition. Four specialized firefighting planes are also operating in the area.

blocks.caption: The blaze on the island of Brac was visible from Croatia's second city, SplitImage: Zvonimir Barisin/Pixsell/IMAGO

blocks.text: Two government ministers and the head of Croatia's national firefighting service are set to attend a high-level meeting on Brac this afternoon with local officials and leaders of the local firefighting teams, after which they are expected to provide more information about the blaze.

articles.title: George Osborne calls for UK to rejoin EU customs union and boost trade
articles.summary:
Ex-Tory chancellor says economy has ‘fallen off a cliff’ since Brexit but rejoining union could be ‘quite simple’

Former chancellor George Osborne said Britain’s economy has “fallen off a…

blocks.text: Former chancellor George Osborne said Britain’s economy has “fallen off a cliff” since Brexit and that rejoining the European Union’s customs union would be the fastest route to recovery.
Osborne, who resigned as chancellor after being part of David Cameron’s cabinet at the time of the referendum, said it was important to rebuild links with the EU.
“Brexit has been a mess,” he told The Independent. “Britain has basically gone off a cliff. It has had a huge impact on the British economy. It is clearly poorer than it would otherwise be.”
Acknowledging that rejoining the EU would be difficult a decade on from the Brexit referendum, Osborne said closer ties with Europe can boost the economy.
“I would rejoin the customs union,” he said. “It’s a quite simple thing to do. That was never part of the Brexit debate. No one knew we were leaving it and it has had a devastating impact on trade.
“The reason we weren’t supposed to be in the customs union – according to the Brexiteers – was these great trade deals we were going to strike with America. That all looks pretty fanciful now.
“People now realise you can’t look at Britain’s growth problem without beginning to think, ‘How can we revive trade with the continent, how can we get investment?’
after newsletter promotion

“If I was Andy Burnham, I don’t see why you wouldn’t rejoin the customs union. It’s a pretty straightforward decision because unlike (rejoining) the single market it does not require you to accept the free movement of people – which is a pretty complicated issue to sell to people in Britain at the moment.”

articles.title: Vanuatu ferry capsize leaves one dead, 30 missing
articles.summary: Rescue efforts have been slow after a South Pacific inter-island ferry sank in bad weather on Friday. An investigation has already begun into negligence on the part of the operator.

image.caption: The MV Matui sank Friday after leaving Santo Island, it never arrived at its destination, Ambae Island, some 96 kilometers to the eastImage: Chris McCall/AFP

blocks.text: At least one person has died and another 30 remain missing after an inter-island ferry in Vanuatu sank in poor weather on Friday.
The South Pacific archipelagic island nation with a population of just under 350,000 is located about 1,750 kilometers (1,900 miles) east of Australia.
The vessel went down in very heavy seas somewhere between the islands of Santo and Ambae, according to authorities.
The MV Matui, operated by the Tui Shipping Agency, set sail Friday from Santo with more than 40 passengers and crew but never arrived in Ambae.
Prime Minister Jotham Napat's office on Sunday morning said that one body had been recovered, 15 passengers had been "accounted for alive" and "over 30 people are missing at sea."
Napat's office took charge of the search and rescue effort on Sunday afternoon after the prime minister expressed frustration over being unable to reach senior officials.

In a statement, Napat's office said, "Search and rescue operations are continuing," adding that the search "in open waters is being eased off whilst efforts ‌move ​toward a search along the southeast coast, where currents may have carried survivors."

"To the survivors, we pray for your strength and recovery. To ⁠the ​families of those missing and those we ​have lost, please know that the nation stands with you in this time of grief," ​the statement continued.
Napat's office also announced that an investigation into the incident had already been launched amid suspicion of negligence on the part of operator Tui.
"This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded," it said, "and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel."
Local frustration at lack of urgency from authorities

Reports of how the rescue effort began are hazy, with Vanuatu parliamentary representative Matai Seremaiah — who took part in the search — telling New Zealand public broadcaster RNZ that a crew member had swam ashore and "alerted us that the ship had capsized."
French news agency AFP cited a hotel owner on Santo who told reporters an employee of his had pulled a survivor in a life vest to shore on Saturday afternoon and authorities were immediately alerted.
It is unclear if these accounts refer to the same survivor.
"He looked like he had been in the bathtub for 25 hours — he was wrinkled up and white. He was cold," said hotel owner Ashley Beveridge.
"There was no rescue started until this guy got washed up on our beach — lucky he got washed up in an inhabited area," he added.

Beveridge told AFP that locals had expressed great frustration at the lack of urgency shown by authorities, with private citizens mobilizing cargo ships and a plane on Saturday afternoon to search for survivors on their own.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Center (MRCC) in Noumea, New Caledonia, has said it is now assisting in the search effort.
A French Armed Forces aircraft from New Caledonia was also deployed on Sunday morning.
The MRCC said that 12 people had been located Sunday morning.
Local media reported that survivors were being treated at Northern Provincial hospital on Santo Island.

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] I knew you were waiting for Martin Romualdez’s mug shot
articles.summary: …and Sara Duterte in handcuffs

blocks.text: …and Sara Duterte in handcuffs

items: Rappler chose not to publish Martin Romualdez's mugshot taken in a hospital to adhere to ethical reporting standards, emphasizing the presumption of innocence and avoiding sensationalism.
The outlet fact-checked an AI-generated image of Vice President Sara Duterte in handcuffs, clarifying that she was never actually handcuffed and providing context to her legal challenges.
Rappler aims to balance public interest in accountability with the rights of suspects, maintaining a commitment to ethical journalism while navigating pressures from government officials.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Rappler didn’t publish former House speaker Martin Romualdez’s mugshot taken while he was lying in a hospital bed.
Rappler fact-checked a lawyer who initially circulated an image of Vice President Sara Duterte in handcuffs without disclosing that it was AI-generated.
And some of you might have been disappointed in our decision in the first case, and thought we were too grim about the second one.
I understand — “understand” being an understatement if you’ve read our commentary or watched our talk shows or followed our investigative reports.

When the national budget is supposedly plundered by way of anomalous flood control projects, or when the country’s second highest official lets out ear-piercing expletives against the President and admits to thoughts of beheading him, you are reasonably outraged (and horrified).
We are outraged (and horrified).

So why didn’t we indulge the public, who must be desperate for big, presumably untouchable, people to be made to account; who felt like seeing one official’s mugshots or another in handcuffs served some degree of swift justice?

Because we have to provide an anchor amid the waves of emotion. Journalists must presume a suspect’s innocence, avoid sensationalism, and apply standards of ethical reporting equally and consistently for every person. Publishing images that could be humiliating runs counter to those three standards I just mentioned.

We established that the police did their job of serving Romualdez the warrant by showing their photo getting his fingerprints. We cropped and blurred some parts of the photo provided by the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group. We zoomed in on just the booking process, and excluded as much as possible the medical tubes and blood pressure-cum-heartbeat monitor attached to him.

After that photo, I reminded the news desk that, consistent with our policy, we would not use the other one — of Romualdez lying in bed, a tag bearing his name and alleged crime placed atop his haggard body.
We would have followed the same standards if Sara Duterte were indeed handcuffed. No photos if the purpose was to just show a degrading spectacle.
By adhering to these editorial standards, the intention was to ensure that the focus was on the facts of the case, our rigorous and insightful reporting, and our excellent explainers.

In Romualdez’s case, we raised questions about the necessity of a hospital arrest. We laid out the inside story and the timeline that made the circumstances leading to the hospitalization — on the day the anti-graft court issued the arrest warrant — invite suspicion.

In Duterte’s case — to be clear, she was never handcuffed — we gave context to the grave threats cases and walked our audience through what to expect moving forward, and whether or not this could affect her ongoing impeachment trial. We placed her claims of untrustworthy courts and police side by side with contradicting statements she had made in the past.

We acknowledge that government officials occupy a unique position of trust. So when they are accused of violating that, the public needs to see confirmation that law enforcers process them the way they do ordinary suspects. Thus, our use of Romualdez’s finger-printing photo but not the mugshot.

With regard to handcuffs, in some newsrooms overseas, publishing photos of officials in handcuffs are now considered appropriate under certain conditions: when they are arrested on the spot in a public place (as opposed to them submitting themselves to the cops and courts), they are accused of serious abuse of power, and there is a disclaimer that the accused is not yet convicted.

We are watching these trends and will always review our standards — to serve justice and the public, not to protect politicians. (As the newsroom evolves, and some ethical guidelines are further refined, we may have missed updating or purging past contents. We would appreciate you bringing this to our attention via feedback@rappler.com.)

For now, we do our best to show state action while we also uphold the suspect’s rights and adhere to due process. We also avoid giving a platform to the drama the accused officials may have wanted to stage.

More importantly, when we take a deep breath amid the uproar, we — the press and the people — do not become like the monsters in high places we condemn and abhor. Challenging as it may be, we can only make progress as a society if we pursue justice and accountability without moral savagery.

P.S.: We draw the line, however, when an accused official weaponizes the concepts of due process, presumption of innocence, and sub judice to gag the press and prevent free public discourse on legitimate issues.

While I started writing this newsletter Friday morning, September 11, the law firm representing Martin Romualdez wrote to Rappler, seeking to stop our Rappler+ briefing on our series of investigations into multi-million-dollar properties linked to Romualdez. We went ahead with the members-exclusive program at 3 pm on Friday.

The event will not be livestreamed nor uploaded for the broader public. If you miss it, you can still become a Rappler+ member and gain access to our archives and future exclusive reports and events. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [OPINION] 2026 BARMM parliamentary elections under the shadow of resurgent extremism
articles.summary: The rising incidence of violence is not isolated, but part of a persistent pattern that poses an imminent threat to the legitimacy of the peace process and the democratic transition it promises

blocks.text: On Monday, September 14, nearly 2.4 million voters across the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will cast their ballots in the region’s first parliamentary elections, a milestone that represents the culmination of decades of armed struggle and peace negotiations.

The election, originally scheduled for May 2022 but postponed four times due to legal, technical, and political complications, marks the transition from an appointed transitional authority to a democratically elected government.
It is a cornerstone of the political track under the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB), signed by the Philippine government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) in 2014.
Yet as Bangsamoro communities prepare for this historic moment, the region finds itself gripped by a signaling resurgence of violent extremism.
Recent data from Conflict Climate Action shows a troubling picture: violent incidents linked to extremist groups have nearly doubled, rising 91% to 44 cases in 2025 from 23 a year earlier.
These are not isolated encounters. They are part of a persistent pattern that poses an imminent threat to the legitimacy of the peace process and the democratic transition it promises.

The evidence of resurgent extremism is stark and multifaceted. In 2026 alone, military operations in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao have killed 10 members of Dawlah Islamiyah-Maute, the ISIS-affiliated group responsible for the 2017 Marawi siege and numerous attacks since. These operations follow similar deadly encounters in Lanao del Norte in 2024 and 2025, demonstrating a persistent and adaptive threat.

However, the military claims extremist groups have been largely neutralized, while large-scale attacks like the Marawi Siege have been prevented; sporadic but organized violence continues to plague the region.

This escalation must be seen within a longer trajectory. The 2017 Marawi siege, carried out by the ISIS-affiliated Maute group, was the longest urban conflict in the Philippines, devastating the city and displacing more than 350,000 individuals. Nine years later, post-reconstruction remains a predicament for internally displaced people who continue to live with insecurities in transitory shelters with no definitive timeline for their return. Another indication of the threat came in December 2023, when an explosion during a Catholic Mass at Mindanao State University-Marawi killed four people and injured 42. Authorities identified DI-Maute as the primary suspect.

These encounters make clear that they continue to pose an active threat across the Mindanao region as they adapt their tactics, using online channels to recruit local Moros, while remaining operationally and ideologically linked to the foreign-led Islamic State. This digital dimension of extremism makes the threat more diffuse and harder to counter through traditional military means.

The extremist threat in Bangsamoro is not purely domestic. Even after the Marawi Siege, more than 100 foreign terrorist fighters continued traveling to the Philippines to sustain conflicts across Mindanao, as the region is seen as a hub for transnational extremist networks. This is not new. Since the Al Qaeda days, the Philippines has been regarded as a “terrorism academy” in Asia, where its archipelagic setting, porous maritime borders, and historical militant groups provide a conducive environment for training activities. The ease of movement across the island chain and weak coastal surveillance have long made it easier for foreign fighters to embed themselves within local extremist groups.
The resurgence of extremism coincides with the first Bangsamoro election and threatens to undermine it.

Security preparations have been extensive: a gun ban took effect on July 16, 2026, and will last until September 29, 2026. By August 24, at least 15 people had been arrested for violating the ban, while 20 firearms had been seized. More than 24,000 security checkpoints have been established across the region, with approximately 30,000 security personnel deployed to ensure peaceful elections.

Despite these measures, election-related violence has already occurred. On August 14, a convoy carrying interim BARMM Chief Minister Macacua was fired upon by unidentified assailants in Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, as he returned from assuming leadership of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party. While no injuries were recorded, the attack on such a high-profile figure underscores the volatile security environment.

The COMELEC has identified 105 municipalities and three cities for checkpoint implementation to enforce the gun ban. The concentration of security concerns in these areas reflects the persistent influence of armed groups and political dynasties that have historically used violence to influence electoral outcomes.

The resurgence of extremism cannot be understood in isolation from the broader fragility of the Bangsamoro peace process. The creation of the BARMM through the CAB was intended to address historical injustices against the Bangsamoro people and provide a political solution to decades of armed conflict.
Yet after eight years, the accord faces compounding threats that erode its implementation and legitimacy.

The normalization process — the critical component of the peace agreement that includes decommissioning of MILF combatants, transformation of camps, and the delivery of socioeconomic packages — remains in a state of suspension. In July 2025, the MILF Central Committee resolved to halt the decommissioning of its remaining 14,000 combatants and 2,450 weapons, citing the government’s failure to deliver “substantially on its socioeconomic commitments”.

This deadlock in normalization has profound implications for the election and the region’s future. Combatants who remain armed and without viable livelihoods represent a pool of potential recruits for extremist groups that offer alternative narratives of resistance and identity (Crisis Group, 2026). The MILF’s inability to deliver on its promises to its own fighters undermines its credibility and creates openings for more radical actors to fill the void.

Political divisions within the MILF have further complicated the landscape. The United Bangsamoro Justice Party, led by MILF senior leaders, now competes against the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, which draws support from former MILF commanders and established regional politicians. This intra-MILF competition has transformed the movement’s internal dynamics and potentially weakened its ability to present a unified front against extremist threats.

Extremist groups do not merely exploit failures in the peace process; they arise from structural gaps that it has yet to address. While political and socio-economic reforms continue, stability remains uneven after seven years of transition. Poverty rates are dropping, yet the region still has the country’s highest illiteracy rate, and development remains sluggish. Factionalism and dynastic politics remain embedded in political life in the region. The clan feuds across the region, conflicts that have claimed lives and forced families from their homes.

These horizontal conflicts create environments where extremist groups can thrive, offering protection, identity, and purpose to youth who see no future within existing political structures. The Marawi rehabilitation process exemplifies these structural challenges. Nine years after the siege, post-reconstruction remains a predicament for internally displaced persons who continue to live with insecurities in transitory shelters with no definitive timeline for return.

The efforts to prevent violent extremism in Mindanao became a government priority after the Marawi siege. Yet, these programs remain insufficient in scale, with poor interagency coordination, duplication, and uneven evaluation. Hard security measures sometimes backfire due to overly broad definitions of extremism, risk securitizing communities, and narrow civic space, blurring the line between protection and surveillance.

The convergence of the first Bangsamoro election with the resurgence of extremism creates a critical juncture for the region. The election represents more than a political transition; it is a test of whether the peace process can deliver tangible improvements in governance, security, and livelihoods. If the election proceeds peacefully and results in a government perceived as legitimate and effective, it could strengthen the peace process and undercut extremist narratives. Conversely, if the election is marred by violence, fraud, or perceived illegitimacy, it could validate extremist claims that democratic politics cannot address Bangsamoro grievances.

The challenge now is mitigating escalating threats that could lead to another bold extremist attack, not merely another humanitarian crisis, but a terminal blow to the peace process’s legitimacy. Authorities must recognize that counterterrorism alone is insufficient and often counterproductive; military operations without a peace dividend risk producing othering that sustains extremism.

In this volatile context, the central government, MILF, and other stakeholders must act decisively and in coordination. This means returning to comprehensive agreement commitments, accelerating normalization with a clear timeline, the election proceeds without further delay, and fast-tracking the socio-economic package for reintegration to restore political and moral legitimacy. The MILF must consolidate and recalibrate its forces and resist relapse to armed struggle.

The extremism in Mindanao is not merely a symptom of peace process failures; it is an alternative that feeds on them. If authorities continue framing the situation as “under control” through hard security while disregarding these signals, and MILF leaders remain consumed by frictions, these groups will only expand and grow more relevant, waiting for the next wind to fan them into flame.

The September 14 election is not just a vote; it is a referendum on whether peace through political inclusion can prevail over violence through extremist exclusion. The future of Bangsamoro hangs in the balance. – Rappler.com

Reemar B Alonsagay is Faculty Member at the Political Studies Department of Mindanao State University Main Campus. He holds a Masters in Applied Conflict Transformation Studies from the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies in Cambodia.

articles.title: Indonesia rescuers search for 130 people after ferry sinks
articles.summary: The ship was carrying over 240 people in the Java Sea when it ran into bad weather. Officials say six people have died and 130 are still missing.

image.caption: The Virgo Transport 8 ferry ran into bad weather in Indonesia while sailing from Java to BorneoImage: Infuz/AFP

blocks.text: An Indonesian passenger ship carrying 243 people sank in the Java Sea on Sunday after it was hit by bad weather, local authorities said.
Officials said six people had died, while 107 were brought to safety and some 130 passengers were still missing.

"We have carried out efforts to search for victims to the fullest extent. There were passengers who ... had already been successfully evacuated by the units at the scene," I Putu Sudayana, head of the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office, told reporters.
The Virgo Transport 8 was traveling from Indonesia's second-largest city of Surabaya to Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province on Borneo island.

It departed on Saturday at 10:13 a.m. local time (0330 UTC), but the ship's operator lost contact with the vessel early Sunday amid bad weather. It was scheduled to arrive in Banjarmasin at about 2 p.m. local time on (0700 UTC) Sunday.

blocks.caption: Over 100 people have been rescued during ongoing search and rescue operationsImage: Infuz/AFP

blocks.text: Search operation underway
Search and rescue teams launched an operation after the operator alerted authorities. Ships and a helicopter were deployed to the vessel's last known location.
"The ship's operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather," Sudayana said in an earlier video briefing.
The ship's last known position was in the Java Sea, roughly 148 kilometers (92 miles) from a pier in Banjarmasin, according to the Associated Press.

Sudayana added that authorities were mobilizing all available personnel and equipment given the large number of people aboard. The agency was coordinating with maritime authorities while closely monitoring weather conditions in the area, he said.

Indonesia, a nation of roughly 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries for transportation, with sea travel often cheaper and more accessible than flying. But safety enforcement across the country's maritime sector has been inconsistent, contributing to a comparatively high rate of accidents.

articles.title: Ace Barbers: Mans Carpio could provide 'vital information' in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: Lawyer Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, could provide “vital information” if he is called as a witness in the impeachment trial of his wife, House Impeachment Adviser Robert…

blocks.text: Published September 13, 2026 5:20pm

Lawyer Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, could provide “vital information” if he is called as a witness in the impeachment trial of his wife, House impeachment adviser Robert “Ace” Barbers said Sunday.
Barbers said Carpio could provide information relevant to the prosecution’s allegations because spouses are considered co-owners of their assets under the law.
“In my view, this could provide vital information to support our allegations, because under the law, spouses are considered co-owners of their assets and money,” Barbers told Super Radyo dzBB.

"Whatever assets Carpio has, the same are owned by Vice President Sara Duterte. Carpio cannot invoke the right against self-incrimination, so he may be called to testify. I believe this could provide additional information to support the allegations,” he added.

The Senate impeachment court will discuss Article 2 of Duterte’s impeachment complaint, which accuses her of amassing unexplained wealth and failing to disclose all her properties and interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), allegedly constituting a culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust.
Barbers said the prosecution has substantial evidence to present regarding Duterte’s SALN.
"That’s why we are saying that the next article will be more exciting because the prosecution will present a lot of evidence that will not match what she declared in her SALN,” he said.

The three witnesses are retired Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang, Ombudsman Records Division Officer-in-Charge Atty. Karen Batu, and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Company Registration and Monitoring Department Director Atty. Gerardo del Rosario.
"The testimonies of our witnesses are important because they would authenticate what happened in the financial records of our Vice President,” Barbers said.
“Generally, Cabotaje-Tang’s statement will discuss the provisions on integrity and public accountability among public servants,” he added.

Earlier this week, the Office of the City Prosecutor in Quezon City recommended the dismissal of the complaint filed by Carpio against several House members and government officials over the disclosure of his and the Vice President’s bank transaction records.
In a 23-page resolution, the QC Prosecutor’s Office said the acts of the respondents were done in relation to their offices and were “not inherently immoral.”

“The issuance of a subpoena for the production of AMLC reports, the manifestations made during the impeachment proceedings against the Vice-President of the Republic of the Philippines, and the compliance with the subpoena—these acts were done by the respondents, public officers with Salary Grade 28 and higher, in relation to their office,” the resolution read.
“By no stretch of the imagination could we rule that these acts of the respondents were done in their private capacity,” it added.— MCG, GMA News

State-run IRNA news agency quoted the Qeshm governor as blaming a "terrorist enemy." He also said the person killed was among the cargo vessel's 10-member crew, and that authorities had not yet identified the projectile.
There was no immediate statement by the U.S. military, which previously has struck Iranian-flagged vessels

An Iranian commercial vessel was struck early Sunday off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with one person killed and four wounded, Iranian state media said, a day before Tehran seeks to brief regional countries on its contested efforts to manage shipping traffic there.

items: Iraq scrambles to address fallout from alleged militia attack on Saudi oil pipeline
Houthis seize strategic island, Saudis close pipeline as fighting escalates

blocks.text: Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations monitor reported a vessel was hit by a projectile while transiting the strait, with no details.

There was no immediate statement by the U.S. military, which previously has struck Iranian-flagged vessels as it keeps up a blockade of Iranian ports — while facing a new threat in recent days from Iranian ballistic missiles launched at its warships.
Qeshm Island, located about 22 kilometres from the port city of Bandar Abbas, is key to Iran asserting control over traffic through the strait.
Sunday's strike came as tensions continue around the waterway that was seen as an international one before the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28.
The U.S. threatens Iran with ‘economic D-Day’ | About That

Global prices of oil, natural gas and related products have been sent higher, and now Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen are pressuring a key shipping alternative, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. While the Houthis say they are targeting only neighbouring Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government, markets are wary.
Iran on Saturday said foreign ministers from regional countries will meet to discuss efforts by Iran and Oman, located on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz, to manage shipping on it.
Already, however, Bahrain has said it will not attend, and it was not clear what other nations would be there.

Iran has said reaching an agreement with Oman on the strait doesn't mean it will open for shipping. "The waterway would be opened up on the condition that the U.S. will terminate its blockade," Iran's president told broadcaster India Today TV on Saturday.

Commercial ship traffic remains low on the strait as attacks continue. Iran has expressed interest in having ships pay fees for transit. It has also said traffic into the Persian Gulf would pass through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass partly through Iranian waters and partly through Oman's.

articles.title: Dramatic insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley
articles.summary: A recent spate of stark warnings about the dangers of AI has been met with scepticism by executives and investors.

blocks.text: Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs.
This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon.
Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity.
They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything".

Coxon is by no means the first AI insider to publicly sound the alarm. There have been a string of high-profile resignations from both Anthropic and OpenAI in recent years over apparent safety concerns, and some current Anthropic employees even echoed Coxon's post.
"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," a team lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, posted on X.

While Coxon said explicitly in his posts that his warnings were "not marketing", some executives and investors in Silicon Valley have reacted with scepticism to a recent flurry of insiders sounding the alarm.

Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings, and some in the tech sector have suggested the latest stark comments about the dangers of AI may be designed to generate hype by signalling the power of these products.
Anthropic's boss, Dario Amodei, has come under fire for saying AI technology could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and will "test who we are as a species".
One conference speaker, Grindr CEO George Arison, told the BBC he believed this week's comments from Coxon and others were indicative of an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic".
He called them "dangerous" and said they had prompted him to instruct some engineers at the LGBTQ+ dating app to stop using Anthropic's technology.
"It is irresponsible for us as stewards of our shareholders' money to be relying on a business that does what this company does, in terms of its public statements," he said.

"Maybe they actually believe it," Arison said. "Or you could argue they're saying it because it's a great way to gin up more investor support, because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"
Anthropic was valued at $965bn (£713bn) in its most recent fundraising round earlier this year.
The BBC has asked Anthropic for a response to the statements.
In an essay posted early on Saturday, Amodei called for a slowing of AI model development and global regulation - and said the risks associated with AI were "serious".
Nvidia boss Jensen Huang also discussed Coxon's comments before a crowd at the conference, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue.
Huang has previously said the notion that AI "is going to be the end of humanity" is "complete nonsense".

And while he may have a business interest in an AI boom - Nvidia builds chips that power AI systems - his comments reflect a growing backlash in Silicon Valley to the existential warnings from current and former staffers.
Some critics have even accused Anthropic of fearmongering in hopes that it will trigger a regulatory push that could shut out competition and leave it and OpenAI with a duopoly in the sector.
Brad Gerstner, who is the head of the investment firm Altimeter Capital, posted pictures of Huang from the conference and accused Coxon of "ridiculous hyperbole".

On Friday, the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, weighed in. Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it would acquire last week, was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year prompting an outcry over AI safety.

"Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," he wrote on X. "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."

Both Gerstner and Delangue were more circumspect on Saturday after Amodei's proposal was posted, with Gerstner calling the idea "an important step forward" in balancing competing considerations like speed and safety.
Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions proposed by Amodei.

Federal legislation co-sponsored this month by left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, known as the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, would impose a temporary pause in advanced AI development.

"There is a good chance that human beings will lose control over AI," Sanders told the BBC's Newsnight programme on Thursday. "And what happens then, nobody knows. But could it be catastrophic? Yes, it could."
"When scientists tell you there is a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he added.

If an industry-wide government crackdown comes, however, it is likely to be led by legislators and not the Trump administration which largely supports a policy of unfettered AI development. It has framed this as necessary to ensure the US does not cede dominance to China.

Speaking to reporters this week, President Donald Trump was asked if he had any concerns about AI leading to human extinction. "No, I don't have any," he said. "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now."

But the president's relationship with Anthropic has been turbulent. After the company refused to allow the US military to use its AI models, the White House described it as "a radical left, woke company" and designated it a supply chain risk, a move that a federal judge has ruled was illegal.
David Sacks, Trump's AI czar in the early days of his administration, has also levelled repeated attacks at Anthropic.

OpenAI has not endured the same level of scrutiny from the White House. When releasing a new model called Astra last week, OpenAI President Greg Brockman described his firm's relationship with the Trump administration as "a very good partnership".
The company did not respond to a BBC inquiry seeking comment.
At the conference in San Francisco this week, the pursuit of fortunes seemed to mostly trump any mounting existential concerns or fears over potential government restrictions on AI.
OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn, has previously announced plans to allow people to buy shares in its firm by listing on the stock market.

However, its chief executive Sam Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year, calling it an "ill-advised moment" to do so "given everything happening with safety" in an interview with Fortune magazine.
He suggested 2027 would be more likely.
Meanwhile, one investor said he was looking forward to Anthropic's forthcoming S-1, a document a company must file with securities regulators in order to sell shares.
His main question about the company was simple: is the firm profitable?
When asked on Thursday if he fears the world may be coming to an end, Sid Sheth - CEO of the chip company d-Matrix which inked a deal with Nvidia at the conference that day - did not mince his words.
"No," he said.
