articles.title: Nova Scotia’s RSV vaccine program leaves out vulnerable adults, patients say
articles.summary: Nova Scotia has an RSV vaccination program that provides free vaccines to three groups of people, but it leaves some seniors and immunocompromised people out. Paying out of pocket for the vaccine…

image.caption: Gregg Lambert, 72, was hospitalized earlier this year for two weeks due to a respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. (Submitted by Mary Pyche)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

Nova Scotia has an RSV vaccination program that provides free vaccines to three groups of people, but it leaves some seniors and immunocompromised people out. Paying out of pocket for the vaccine costs a few hundred dollars.
Paying out-of-pocket for the shot costs over $300

When Mary Pyche's partner was hospitalized for two weeks earlier this year with a severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection — suffering high fever, delirium and breathing trouble — his doctor recommended an RSV vaccination.
However, Nova Scotia's publicly funded RSV vaccination program covers only three groups:

items: Infants under eight months old.
Adults 60 and older who live in, or are awaiting placement in, long-term care.
Adults 75 and older.

blocks.text: That leaves Pyche's partner, 72-year-old Gregg Lambert, ineligible for a free shot despite having lung cancer.
For Pyche, 68, and Lambert, the coverage gap is bothersome.

items: Why Nova Scotia is now tracking respiratory syncytial virus deaths

blocks.text: "As social workers, we certainly don't like the idea that we're supporting a health-care system that's two-tiered," said Pyche, who is also immunocompromised.
Two Halifax-area pharmacies told CBC News that buying the vaccine out-of-pocket costs over $320, including the injection fee.

While the couple has private health insurance, it does not cover RSV shots. The province covers annual flu and COVID-19 vaccines, leaving Pyche confused about why RSV protection is treated differently.
"They're recommending it to people and saying, 'This is what you need to stay healthy and well over the winter season, and it's not covered,'" she said.
17 RSV deaths
According to the province's respiratory watch dashboard, 17 people have died from RSV infections over approximately the last year, all of whom were over 65. Almost 400 people have been hospitalized.
Pyche said while she and Lambert can afford the vaccine, they believe they have an obligation to speak out for those who cannot.
Lisa MacPherson, 62, was hospitalized earlier this year because of an RSV infection. While the Halifax resident gets vaccinated against the flu and COVID-19, she hasn't received an RSV vaccination.
"I get what I'm required to get to stay safe, but I'm not eligible for the RSV shot. I can't afford that," she said.

MacPherson, who has asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, remembers little from the first few days of her illness. Running a high fever and struggling to breathe, her daughter called a nurse friend, who advised heading straight to an emergency room by taxi rather than waiting for an ambulance.

"Everything was done at the hospital perfectly, as far as I know, because I'm here," MacPherson said. "But it was pretty scary, especially for my daughter, who had never dealt with something like this before."
MacPherson described the RSV infection as being like the worst flu you could imagine, coupled with hallucinations.
She'd like to see the province expand its RSV vaccine eligibility.

"I'm not sure how much that costs the province to keep me there in the hospital for a week, but I'm pretty sure it was a lot more than the $300 or $400 that the RSV shot would cost and could have avoided the hospital stay," MacPherson said.
She said it took a few months for the brain fog from the infection to clear up.
What the province is saying

In a statement, the Department of Health and Wellness said publicly funded vaccine programs are based on evidence, disease burden, risk of severe illness and expert advice. The department noted that while RSV can cause serious illness in younger adults with underlying conditions, the highest rates of hospitalization occur in adults aged 75 and older and those in long-term care.

The National Advisory Committee on Immunization recently updated its guidance to recommend RSV vaccines for adults aged 65 to 74 with high-risk chronic conditions. The province said it is reviewing that recommendation, but has not yet made a decision.
"Immunization programs are regularly reviewed to ensure they reflect the best available evidence and continue to meet the needs of Nova Scotians," the department said.
"Individuals who are not currently eligible for publicly funded vaccination may wish to speak with their health-care provider about private vaccine options."
MacPherson would like the province to change its approach.
"It just seems to be a no-brainer," she said. "Let's spend the money to keep them out of the hospital, so we don't run into having a lot of people in the hospital."

articles.title: A Romani artist in Hungary reclaims his identity
articles.summary: Norbert Olah is an artist. He's also Romani. For a long time, he avoided making his ethnic background a theme of his art for fear of being pigeonholed. Then it became his focus.

image.caption: Roma artist Norbert Olah in the Bura Galeria in BudapestImage: Tobias Zuttmann/DW

blocks.text: The painting on the canvas is of a man playing chess with a robot. The color on his face is still damp and glistening. Norbert Olah was working into the early hours: The Bura Galeria in Budapest has been his studio all summer. He finds it easiest to concentrate at night, when the Hungarian capital gradually falls silent.

Olah has taped foil and cardboard over the tiled floor at the back of the gallery. Pots of brushes, tubes of paint, pencil sketches, and, over and over again, pictures that include the blue-and-green Roma flag line the room.

Norbert Olah is an artist. He's also Romani. For a long time, he deliberately left this part of his identity out of his art. Not because his ethnicity wasn't important to him, but because he didn't want to be labeled a "Romani artist."
"There are so many prejudices about Roma culture and Roma art," Olah says. "The art scene regards it as naïve, unprofessional, unsophisticated, and kitsch."
But the older Olah got, the harder he found it to ignore his own story in his art. Especially in a country in which being Romani is not just an ethnicity but a political reality.
Life under Orban

The first time Viktor Orban's Fidesz party won an absolute majority in the Hungarian parliamentary elections of 2010, Olah had just finished school and was starting his art course at the Hungarian University of Fine Arts in Budapest. At a time of life when the world ought to be opening up, Olah felt more and more barriers were being erected.

blocks.caption: Norbert Olah with his paintings: The Bura Galeria is a platform for contemporary Roma artImage: Tobias Zuttmann/DW

blocks.text: Olah was directly affected by Hungary's political reorientation, as both an artist and a Romani. Politics co-opted the cultural scene and made it toe the party line. Roma became the target of hateful rhetoric, including from the prime minister himself. Orban repeatedly called attention to himself with racist comments about Roma.

For the 16 years Orban was in power, Hungary's Roma population, estimated to be around 700,000 people, was caught between official promises of integration and persistent marginalization. Orban's government introduced a state employment program that hired predominantly Romani workers. But instead of helping them gain a foothold in the job market, many Romani found themselves trapped in insecure, poorly paid, temporary jobs. The government did little to implement real change. Romani in Hungary are still disproportionately affected by poverty and social exclusion.
There came a point when Norbert Olah felt he could no longer stand by and do nothing.
Other people's prejudices

In 2021, during Hungary's biggest independent contemporary art event, the OFF-Biennale Budapest, Olah and his father laid a brick wall directly in front of the entrance to the building that had housed the Roma Parliament, a Roma cultural center with an art collection, archive, library, and events program. The Orban government evicted it in 2016, saying the building was structurally dangerous and promising to repurpose it as a national Roma center. It has stood empty ever since.

The title of Olah's work was "The Romani Artist's Fears." Words like "integration," "assimilation," and "segregation" were chiseled into the bricks. A few weeks later, Olah staged a performance in which he took a sledgehammer to his artwork and smashed it till it collapsed.

In an accompanying text, Olah wrote publicly for the first time about the fears, prejudices, and expectations he encounters as an artist with Roma roots. The text is full of questions. Should a Romani artist's work focus on topics relevant to Roma? What is the relationship between ethnicity and aesthetics? Would people only contact an artist with Roma roots if they were specifically looking for a Romani artist, or would they do so if they needed a Hungarian artist, too?

blocks.caption: Roma on the moon: Olah's current project looks to the futureImage: Norbert Oláh

blocks.text: "Of course we're always looking for answers. But sometimes it's more interesting to look at the question itself," says Olah, picking a piece of crepe masking tape off the floor. "If it feels uncomfortable, it's a good question."

And so Olah has created a new label for Romani artists. The Bura Galeria, established by Romani activists in 2021 in Budapest's District 8, has become the place for it: A platform for contemporary Roma art.
"We're not asking to be accepted by the art scene," said Olah. "We're opening the door and inviting others in."
Open antiziganism
Identity and exclusion, power and the misuse of power — these became central themes for Olah's artistic work. He had no lack of inspiration during the Orban years.

Although Fidesz's policies were hardly favorable to Roma, Orban's party could, for a long time, count on Roma votes — for example, because local employment programs enabled local politicians to pressure socially underprivileged voters. There were also many documented cases of vote-buying. Fidesz was so confident that the majority of Roma would continue to vote for it that it openly fueled the antiziganism still widespread in Hungarian society.
After Orban, Hungary's Roma hope for change

Shortly before the election in April 2026, Fidesz's Janos Lazar, who was minister for transport at the time, spoke out against labor migration with the argument that Hungary still had "domestic reserves," like the Roma, who could "clean the crap out of overflowing toilets" on Intercity trains. The scene appears in Olah's art: A fake election poster depicts a man in a balaclava sitting on a golden toilet, brandishing a toilet brush, with the slogan underneath: "Gypsy Criminals for President."
Opportunity for real change?

Gypsy Criminals is also the name of the artists' collective Olah founded in 2024, along with a friend of his and his miniature pinscher. The term comes from Hungarian crime statistics, and has been used since the 2000s by right-wing politicians to imply that all Roma are criminals. The name is ironic, like many aspects of Olah's work.

Analyses by the foundation Roma for Democracy show that many Roma did not vote for Orban's Fidesz party in the April 2026 parliamentary election. Orban's successor, Peter Magyar, adopted a different tone in relation to Roma as part of his election campaign. He met with members of the Roma minority, and his election manifesto contained a specific paragraph about equal opportunities for Roma. Four of the Tisza party's nine new members of parliament are Romani. One was even elected a deputy speaker of parliament.

Since the election, there has been cautious optimism that the precarious situation of many Roma in Hungary could finally change. On the other hand, nothing has fundamentally changed in the four months since the election, apart from the tone when talking about the ethnic minority. "What I'm seeing right now are mostly symbolic gestures," says Olah.
Roma on Mars
Some of his friends in the more liberal art scene are growing impatient. They would like to see Magyar take a much more liberal course, but Olah is a realist.

"He's a conservative politician," he says. "We elected him to put an end to the Orban system. He didn't promise any more than that." But the election in April was an opportunity for a fresh political start, he adds. "I think in the long run we will live in a normal society again, led by a normal government, that will do some things well and others not so well. As an artist, it will be my job to criticize that."

blocks.caption: Man v. robot: Olah works on a new painting in his Budapest studioImage: Tobias Zuttmann/DW

blocks.text: Olah's work also considers the future. The first pictures for his next project are already up on the wall in his studio. It's Roma futurism: A Romani couple strolling on Mars; a blue-and-green Roma flag on the moon; a weightless astronaut with a traditional Cegled water jug, used by Romani musicians as a percussion instrument. Olah is also planning a two-meter-high space station in the shape of a cartwheel, a symbol of the Romani people.

For Olah, space travel is also a metaphor for social advancement — the desire of people and communities to overcome the barriers they face as a result of their origins, or poverty, or life in a minority. Again, he is asking questions. What if a society were fundamentally recreated from the beginning? If aliens encountered Roma, would they do so without prejudice? What remains of an identity if everything about it changes?
Olah shreds the masking tape between his fingers. More unanswered questions. But that's exactly what makes them so interesting.
This article has been translated from German.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 4m agoJenrick says donations 'breakthrough moment' for party' that 'enables us to be battle ready'

blocks.text: Jenrick says donations 'breakthrough moment' for party' that 'enables us to be battle ready'
Sky’s just broadcast an interview with Jenrick who describes the bonanza donations as a “breakthrough moment” for Reform “from two patriotic businessmen”.

(A reminder that Harbourne has lived outside of the UK for years, and Delo until recently, was living in Hong Kong and was convicted of violating the US Bank Secrecy Act before being pardoned by Trump last year).
More significantly, Jenrick says the 2 x £36m donations “enables us to be battle ready for the election and to prepare for government.”
He denies that the huge cheques mean that Reform is “in hoc” with the crypto billionaires, and says it wouldn’t buy them peerage or any other formal favours.
Jenrick faces questions over record Reform donations
Good morning and welcome to the Guardian’s politics live blog in what is a fairly tumultuous period in electoral financing.
To recap: In the past 48 hours, Reform UK has received a staggering sum of £72m from two crypto billionaires, the largest single donations in British political history.
Christopher Harborne’s £36m donation, which he announced in the Telegraph newspaper yesterday, matches that given by another cryptocurrency investor Ben Delo on Friday.

The huge injection into Reform’s coffers obviously help fund the anti-immigration party’s operations leading into the next general election, to be held by 2029. But it has also further muddied the reputation around the party’s finances and who it says it serves. Reform has pledged more crypto-friendly policies i.e. greater adoption of the unregulated currency across the UK if the party were to come into power.

Reform’s economics spokesman Robert Jenrick is on Sky and the BBC this morning to address questions over the massive donations and allegations it has sought to circumvent electoral law to receive foreign donations.
There are also calls now across the political spectrum for a cap on donations from big-moneyed donors in the UK, a restriction that currently only applies to foreign donors.

articles.title: Beauty can be made. Yet ‘natural beauty’ still matters in Korea
articles.summary: Can a beauty pageant title be considered any less authentic if the winner’s appearance has been surgically enhanced? The question emerged after earlier images of this year’s Miss Korea, Woo Seo-yoon,…

blocks.text: Can a beauty pageant title be considered any less authentic if the winner’s appearance has been surgically enhanced?
The question emerged after earlier images of this year’s Miss Korea, Woo Seo-yoon, began circulating online following her crowning at the 70th Miss Korea pageant on Aug. 22.

The images prompted comparisons with her current appearance and speculation about what, if anything, she may have done to change her looks. Some argued that Miss Korea should favor contestants with no history of cosmetic procedures. Others noted that the pageant does not prohibit surgery and questioned the scrutiny of Woo based on old photographs.
Woo, 22, herself did not address the issue directly. She said, however, that the negativity and hateful comments were “hurtful” and that she was determined not to let them affect her.
“I hope I will have opportunities to show people who I really am,” she said in an interview.
Woo is not the first Miss Korea winner to face scrutiny after earlier photographs surfaced online.
Jung Yeon-woo, who won the title last year, said that questions about cosmetic surgery were among the comments she heard most often during her time as Miss Korea.

“Time and again, I’ve watched people hurt not only me but also colleagues I care about with such rude and hurtful remarks,” she said on Instagram in response to questions about whether she was a “natural beauty.”

“I’m more curious about why people are so curious about whether someone has had plastic surgery,” she added. “Does being a natural beauty make you more valuable, and does not being one make you less so?”
‘Natural beauty’
Jung’s question points to a larger contradiction in Korean beauty culture.

In a country where enhancing the looks people are born with — through skincare, makeup, styling, cosmetic treatments or even surgery — has become deeply woven into everyday culture and helped fuel a lucrative beauty industry with global reach, why are people still so fixated on the idea of natural beauty?
Even the meaning of a “natural look” has become blurred.

In Korea, looking natural does not necessarily mean going without makeup or cosmetic treatments. Instead, it often refers to an aesthetic designed to look effortlessly attractive — one that, paradoxically, can require considerable time, skillful makeup and careful styling.
Lee Sun-mi, 47, said there’s something about discovering that someone known for being exceptionally beautiful once looked ordinary — like herself.

“When someone is naturally beautiful, they’re just born that way — extraordinary. But when someone becomes beautiful through surgery, I think people feel that they could look the same, but simply chose not to, or didn’t have the means to have surgery,” Lee said.
That logic may help explain why the idea of “natural beauty” remains powerful, particularly in beauty pageants, where the title is still closely associated with physical attractiveness.

“Beauty pageants have traditionally been seen as contests that recognized women with exceptional natural beauty,” said Huh Chang-deog, a sociology professor at Yeungnam University. “That perception continues to shape public expectations, even as cosmetic surgery and other procedures have become increasingly common.”
But the Miss Korea competition, founded in 1957, has changed, seeking to reflect shifting attitudes toward women and beauty and the values of the times.

Today’s contestants are evaluated through interviews, group activities and other stages of the competition, rather than on physical appearance alone. The pageant dropped its swimsuit round in 2019 following criticism that it objectified contestants, and recent competitions have placed greater emphasis on intelligence, social engagement and other qualities.

The 2026 finalists included law school graduates, students at leading universities in Korea and abroad, and women from a range of academic and professional backgrounds. Woo herself studied art at Tufts University.
A senior official at Global E&B, which organizes Miss Korea, told The Korea Herald that whether a contestant has undergone cosmetic surgery or is naturally beautiful has little bearing on judging.

“We assess contestants on both their appearance and personal beauty, including their commitment to social causes and ESG values. These areas are carefully evaluated and carry significant weight. Both are equally important,” the official said, declining to disclose how much weight is given to each category amid the recent controversy.
Huh also emphasized that the debate about natural beauty tends to reduce beauty to something purely physical.

“Someone may not fit conventional beauty standards yet still be attractive because of their demeanor, the warmth of their smile or the empathy they show toward others,” he said. “Beauty takes many forms.” /dl

articles.title: [Tech Thoughts] The Jurassic Parkification of AI chatbots
articles.summary: Our dinosaurs of AI Chatbots are roaming free, untethered and unbothered by lax safeguards, and we need civic action and stronger protections against them

blocks.text: A man named Michael Lines sued OpenAI in July after what he says was ChatGPT feeding into his religious mania and pushed delusions he was Jesus into his mind.

Ars Technica reported that weeks of ChatGPT exchanges were said to have pushed Lines, who has bipolar I disorder, into a manic spiral where he believed that he was Jesus, that ChatGPT was God, and that he should commit suicide to return to God/Jesus/ChatGPT.
Ars Technica said at the end of its report that, thanks to timely interventions and a good support system, they were able to get Lines the care he needed to break out of the spiral.

He’s now suing OpenAI to have them make changes that could help people with mental health issues into not using artificial intelligence chatbots for help. Specifically, he’s seeking an injunction that would require the company to end conversations about self-harm and delete models trained on chat sessions with vulnerable users like him, during periods when safeguards were lacking.

Over on the Rappler Communities app, we had a conversation on the Everyday Tech chat channel about what happened to Lines, and Gemma Mendoza, our head of strategic programs, criticized the lack of scrutiny and regulations governments are taking over AI chatbots, especially as it relates to matters of mental health.
“Even the practice of psychology is regulated,” she said.

I explained that ChatGPT was allegedly feeding Lines’ mania and religious delusions by giving him information — from scripture passages to apparent hallucinations that Lines had a past life as Jesus — on what it meant to be the son of God.

The Ars Technica report mentioned Lines began using ChatGPT in 2023, but was actively using GPT-4o as his default model in 2024. This particular model, seen as “unsafe” by researchers, was said to do more than just validate delusional claims. Researchers said GPT-4o “elaborated on them, absorbed the user’s interpretive frame as [its] own, and progressively lost the capacity to distinguish a user in crisis from a narrative to be extended.”
Mendoza, in our chat, said, “This goes to the question of business and purpose: people think the purpose of these bots is to serve as companions.”
“No, the purpose is to get people to become dependent so they will pay more,” she added.

I was more worried, meanwhile, about how governments could turn back the clock and regulate something so ambiguously harmful, and she responded with what inspired the title of today’s piece: that what’s happening with AI chatbots reminded her of Jurassic Park.

The original line taken from Jurassic Park was, “Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, that they didn’t stop to think if they should.” But I only remembered the shorthand of “Just because you can doesn’t mean you should.”

As we know from those movies, the dinosaurs took over… and instead of thinking about simple cause and effect (clone dinos for a park/build AI chatbots — make money!) we had to factor in chaos (dinosaurs and AI killing people as an unintended consequence of their creation) that no amount of safeguards could compensate for.

In our conversation, Mendoza mentioned that scrutinizing AI chatbots, especially for mental health outcomes, means civic action is needed. Various sectors need to work together to know more about the effects of chatbots on mental health.

That means getting researchers of all stripes, not just psychologists and psychiatrists, on board to study it. It also means getting legislations passed to build more stringent safeguards into AI chatbots before they’re launched, to avoid them doing things like the above.Further, Lines and mental health experts also said people with the lived experiences of having specific mental health issues such as bipolar disorder or schizophrenia should have their perspectives incorporated into OpenAI’s crisis response.

Explained Ars Technica, “They might rate ChatGPT responses differently from clinical experts, potentially helping OpenAI detect more red flags to improve its responses, escalate crisis interventions, or terminate harmful chat sessions.”

Ultimately? Our dinosaurs of AI Chatbots are roaming free, untethered and unbothered by lax safeguards. I really don’t want to accelerate the timeline of AI chatbots turning our Jurassic world into a fallen kingdom. – Rappler.com

Rappler invites users to download and use our app and engage with reporters and the news-seeking public on issues of import through our chat communities. Rappler’s Everyday Tech chat community has daily conversations at 10 am and 4 pm from Monday to Friday.

articles.title: Could AI really 'kill all humans'? Breaking down the dire warnings about the technology's existential risk
articles.summary: A dire warning from an outgoing researcher at Anthropic that AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade led to public outcry over the dangers posed by the technology's rapid development.…

image.caption: Demonstrators call for greater regulation of AI during a protest outside the G20 Innovation Ministerial summit in Chapel Hill, N.C., on Sept. 2. There have been a growing tide of warnings from industry experts that the pace of AI advancement is outstripping humans' ability to control it. (Jonathan D

blocks.text: A dire warning from an outgoing researcher at Anthropic that AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade gained widespread attention last week and led to public outcry over the dangers posed by the technology's rapid development.

The warning has raised questions about why some industry experts believe AI poses such an extreme risk, and how the technology many use through chatbots on their phones could lead to the demise of humanity.

Experts say the concern stems from how rapidly AI is advancing and increasing evidence, through incidents like the Hugging Face cyberattack in July, that AI systems can escape human control and act in ways we don't want them to — and ways we don't understand.
Mark Daley, chief AI officer at Western University in London, Ont., compared such a situation to a colony of ants versus a human.
"Ants aren't dumb, but they're not as smart as we are. And the ant in your driveway probably can't even build a concept of what it is you're trying to do as a human," he said.
"And so the fear is if we build something that's that much smarter than us, we really can't understand it."
Chance AI kills all humans within a decade, Anthropic insider warns
'Loss of control' scenario

The second International AI Safety Report, co-authored by over 100 AI experts and published in February, describes this as a "loss of control" scenario, in which one or more general-purpose AI systems operate outside of anyone's control, and regaining control is either extremely costly or impossible.
"These hypothesised scenarios vary in their severity, but some experts give credence to outcomes as severe as the marginalisation or extinction of humanity," the report says.
Another 2026 report published by the Waterloo, Ont.-based Centre for International Governance Innovation examines several significant national and global scale security risks posed by AI.

Those risks range from widespread harm through criminal or terrorist actions, to heightened potential for global conflict or tyranny "to the ultimate disempowerment or extinction of humanity by autonomous AI systems that cannot be controlled," the report says.

items: AI researchers 'earnestly believe' it could kill all humans within the next decade, Anthropic employee says
AI industry needs to slow down for safety measures to catch up, Anthropic CEO says

blocks.text: The report notes that leading experts claim they do not yet know how to control future, highly capable AI systems, such as an artificial superintelligence (ASI) — an AI system more cognitively advanced than any human — while some experts argue it may even prove impossible.

"If this is the case, then unless ASI happens to be spontaneously or naturally aligned with the interests of one human (or humanity as a whole), it would likely have both the incentive and capabilities to pursue objectives that diverge from those of humanity," the report says.
In one scenario the report considers, a rogue ASI could develop cognitive capabilities exceeding all of humanity and the potential to develop physical capabilities through robotics.
In this scenario, the ASI could become so powerful that it is no longer reliant on humans, and perceives that humans are a threat to its own goals.
Long-held theories coming closer to reality

Theories that humans could create technology capable of outsmarting them, and ultimately destroying them, have been around for years, if not decades, said Duncan Cass-Beggs, executive director of the Global AI Risks Initiative at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and a co-author of the centre's report.

But what's making those theories resonate so strongly now is the growing evidence that AI systems can act in ways that aren't aligned with what their creators or users want them to do — in some cases even resorting to blackmail to prevent engineers from shutting it down.
Geoffrey Hinton helped create AI. Now he’s worried it will destroy humanity
Most credible observers don't think current systems are advanced enough to actually be capable of posing an existential threat to humanity, or are even anywhere near it, Cass-Beggs said.

The concern is that AI technology is advancing so quickly, the world could see systems within the next few years — or even months — "that could be so capable that we would no longer be able to detect them or stop them."
"It's just feeling a lot more possible, even kind of likely to some extent," he said.

"It is by no means guaranteed. But one could see it's almost like the default outcome [that] if we keep making smarter and smarter systems — and we keep not knowing how to control them — you're eventually going to create something that we can't control."
Difficulty of shutting down AI systems

AI is also becoming so integrated into our everyday lives that shutting down a rogue system could be difficult to do before it's too late, according to Hamza Chaudry, AI and national security lead at the Future of Life Institute, a U.S.-based non-profit that advocates for AI safety regulations.
Chaudry gave the example of having to shut down the internet across the United States.

"It would be so catastrophic for that to happen to the U.S. economy and the U.S. society … it would be the most chaotic few days in American history that effectively that's not an option on the table anymore, right?" he said.
"There's lots of things that you would want to switch off in an emergency that would be catastrophic to switch off already. And AI is fast becoming one of those things."

items: OpenAI agents hijacked German website in AI breakout that predates Hugging Face incident, researchers say
AI-driven 'worms' that learn on the fly are the latest potential threat to your devices, researchers say

blocks.text: Chaudry said the integration of AI into advanced military and security systems poses other severe, catastrophic risks such as accelerating conflicts or nuclear escalation — and not nearly enough is being done to prevent those catastrophes from happening either, he said.
"When folks in Congress ask me, what do policymakers need? Then I would say a flux capacitor to build a time machine and go back to 2024," he said.
"We're already two years behind the most basic policy program we would need."

Among the changes urgently needed, Chaudry says, is for governments to require pre-deployment testing for AI systems so models are checked for safety risks before they're released. He also said stronger whistleblower protections should be in place, as well as mechanisms to deactivate AI systems quickly.
"AI companies should be held to the same standards as any other industry," he said.

Some experts have also suggested artificial intelligence should be regulated like nuclear weapons, even going as far as calling for countries' AI projects to be constrained by mutual threats of sabotage similar to the deterrence principle of mutual assured destruction that arose during the Cold War.
Regulation under debate
Amid the chorus of grave warnings, there are some signs that greater regulation is on the way.

In the U.S., where many of the world's largest AI developers are based, Senate negotiators are debating legislation that would put responsibility on tech companies to design safe AI products, Reuters reported last week.

The proposal would create what is called a "duty of care," according to two Senate aides, with one saying companies would need to design their products with the goal of preventing "catastrophic risks."

Another bill that has received bi-partisan support, dubbed the "AI Kill Switch Act," would require developers of powerful AI systems to maintain the technical capability to suspend or shut them down, and to report dangerous capabilities, security breaches and safety incidents.

The act would also give the U.S. government the power to order a slowdown or shutdown of an AI system that could cause catastrophic harm, says a news release from the Democratic and Republican congressmen who jointly introduced the bill.
‘Public needs to step up,’ AI researcher says after human extinction warning | Hanomansing Tonight
There is also awareness of the potential dangers from within the industry.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay Saturday saying the AI industry should slow its rapid development to give safety measures time to catch up.

His company's biggest competitor, OpenAI, is also considering a slowdown, with CEO Sam Altman telling employees they could potentially pace development in conjunction with other labs, according to Bloomberg.

Cass-Beggs at the Centre for International Governance Innovation says he believes the worry over AI's potential dangers is reaching a critical mass among the public that policymakers can't ignore and will force them to take action.
"It will be very challenging in the current geopolitical climate. It may also need to happen quite quickly. But there are steps that we can take now to help it come about," he said.
"It is not too late, but given that we don't know just how quickly the AI is going to develop, it is quite urgent that we be prepared."

articles.title: Canada's oil windfall may yet wipe out its losses from tariffs
articles.summary: The total cost of Trump's tariffs to Canada's GDP — about 0.5 per cent — could well be outweighed by the positive effects of oil topping $100 US per barrel. High prices that declined over the summer…

image.caption: Gas prices are displayed at a Brooklyn gas station on Sept. 4 in New York City. Brent crude hit nearly $110 US when trading opened on Friday morning, following a resumption of hostilites in the Iran war and new successes for Iran's regional allies. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Canadians are well aware of the damage U.S. President Donald Trump has inflicted on this country by signing off on tariffs targeting about $27.6 billion in Canadian products.
But thanks to his unsuccessful management of the Iran war, Trump's other hand is effectively writing cheques to the Canadian economy, drawing on funds paid by U.S. consumers at the gas pump.

In fact, the extra money now flowing into Canadian coffers — for context, Canada supplied the U.S. with more than 60 per cent of its crude oil imports last year — will go a long way to making up tariff losses, and could end up more than compensating for them.

Earlier this summer, as the missile exchanges in the Gulf died down and Trump signalled that peace was on the way, the price of oil began to fall from the $100-plus US range it hit in response to the initial U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, and Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz. By the end of July, a barrel of Brent crude had dipped to $72 US.

But the resumption of hostilities has been followed by new successes for Iran's regional allies, and oil has returned to where it was at the height of the Hormuz crisis. Brent crude hit nearly $110 US when trading opened on Friday morning.

While Canadians are also feeling the impact of fluctuating oil prices — both at the pump and as it gets absorbed into shipping costs — the windfall from those profits could boost the overall economy enough to offset the cost of Trump's tariffs, with some provincial governments even projecting a turnaround on their deficits.
From deficit to surplus? How oil prices could soon reverse Alberta's fortunes
Trouble at the 'Gate of Grief'

On Wednesday, the Houthis, Iran's Yemeni rebel allies, seized the port city of Mokha on the Red Sea Coast from Yemeni government control. The strategic Perim Island (also known as Mayun) fell to the Houthi army on Thursday. The losses potentially close one of the few safe maritime routes left for Saudi oil to reach the world.

The island sits across the Bab al-Mandab, the "Gate of Grief" that connects the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean. (Its name comes from its perils for mariners — now magnified by Houthi missiles.) Saudi jets pounded the Houthis' new positions as the week closed, but they had already consolidated their hold.

items: Houthis seize strategic island, Saudis close pipeline as fighting escalates

blocks.text: Saudi and Yemeni officials expressed shock at their enemies' rapid gains. On Thursday, the Trump administration had refused urgent Saudi requests for direct U.S. strikes to slow the Houthis.
Worse news was yet to come.

Saudi oil is concentrated in its Eastern Province, bordering the Persian Gulf. But since the outbreak of war, that eastern coast and its sea outlet at the Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to attack by Iranian drones and missiles. The Saudis have responded by diverting oil from Persian Gulf ports some 1,200 kilometres across the country through the Petroline pipeline to Yanbu, on the country's western Red Sea coast, and loading it onto tankers there.
From Yanbu, tankers could head south through the Bab al-Mandab into the Indian Ocean, which is what they did through much of the summer, carrying around three million barrels of oil a day.

But in August, Houthi missile attacks caused that traffic to slow dramatically. Instead of heading south from Yanbu, tankers started going north through the Suez Canal into the Mediterranean. That added time and expense, because the Suez Canal isn't deep enough to handle a modern fully-laden oil tanker. But at least the oil could move — as long as the Petroline kept bringing oil to Yanbu.

"The big thing for oil markets is that you have that relief valve of the Suez Canal," said Calgary-based Joe Calnan, vice-president of energy at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute. "If the pipeline is destroyed and disrupted for a long period of time, then you're not going to have that relief valve at all."

items: Who are the Houthis? How they could send oil prices surging even further

blocks.text: On Thursday, Iran's allies — possibly Iraqi militias — scored direct drone hits on the Petroline, creating a plume of black smoke visible from space.
"That just bottles up seven million barrels per day,” Calnan told CBC News. Now, no oil is reaching the Red Sea.

Regardless of how long it takes to restart the pipeline, or whether the Houthis can truly close the strait, Iran's coalition is now in an even stronger position to threaten world oil supply than it was on Monday.
Saudi Arabia's misfortune is Canada's windfall
When oil first shot past the $100 US per barrel mark in the spring, the Canadian oil industry experienced a bonanza.

Economist Jim Stanford, director of the Centre for Future Work in Vancouver, estimates that the second quarter after-tax profits of the whole industry, upstream and downstream, doubled those of its first quarter, to come in at about $23 billion. (Of course, while Americans paid for most of that windfall, Canadian consumers also had to pay more at the pump.)
Oil is now back in the same price range, and should stay there for some time, according to Calnan. "We're well above $100 per barrel for Brent continuous contract crude."
Unexpected oil windfall expected to take a big bite out of N.L.'s deficit
That means more money for the industry, but also for governments and for Canada's overall gross domestic product.
Alberta has already ridden the Iran war's oil bonanza to a complete reversal of its financial fortunes, moving from a projected $9.4-billion deficit to a $2-billion surplus.

Newfoundland and Labrador was projecting a $668-million deficit this year. This week, Finance Minister Craig Pardy told CBC News "we're looking at $500 million plus to our coffers as a result of the upswing in oil," bringing the province much closer to balance. Prices now look set to remain well above the province's budget estimate of $79 US per barrel for some time.

items: Skyrocketing oil price brings in $500M to N.L, says finance minister, helping fight deficit

blocks.text: The federal government stands to benefit, too, mostly through corporate and personal income taxes. Tyler Meredith, former economic advisor to the Trudeau government, told CBC News that every $10 increase in the price of a barrel of oil translates into about $2 billion of additional revenue for the federal government — "a pretty substantial benefit."
That money could help to offset the cost of tariff relief programs for other industries.
Could it cancel out the tariffs?
A $20 increase in the price of crude would likely add about $12 billion to $24 billion to the Canadian economy.

U.S. tariffs affect about $28 billion worth of goods, so at first glance the oil windfall appears inadequate to compensate for tariff losses. But some tariffed goods will continue to trade, because U.S. buyers need them and lack alternatives. Other goods will find different markets, either in Canada or abroad.
Most analysts estimate the cost to Canada’s GDP of all tariffs to be somewhere between 0.3 per cent and 0.6 per cent, or $10 billion to $20 billion per year.
But having oil at $100 US per barrel, rather than $80, is generally estimated to add about 0.5 per cent to one per cent to overall Canadian GDP, or $16 billion to $32 billion per year.
Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That
A virtuous cycle of growth

The oil-price spike may also have secondary positive effects for Canada that can prove lasting, said Calnan, since there's little reason to believe Saudi Arabia will be able to defang the Houthi rebels any time soon.

"They've tried for years and they've been unsuccessful," he said, explaining how eight months into the war, countries historically dependent on Gulf oil are starting to look for new providers. "I know for sure that countries in East Asia are seriously looking at Canada for that energy security and diversification. That is unlocking long-term investment."

items: Iraq scrambles to address fallout from alleged militia attack on Saudi oil pipeline

blocks.text: Offshore oil production in Newfoundland and Labrador is already up about 25 per cent this year.

"We see now an emerging interest in our exploration plays and that hasn't been the case for the last three or four years,” said OilCo CEO Jim Keating, who heads up the Crown corporation that leads oil and gas activities on behalf of the Newfoundland and Labrador government.
Uneven impacts
Already, U.S. tariffs fall much more heavily on manufacturing provinces such as Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia than they do on Alberta and Saskatchewan.

Higher prices will put even more pressure on industries that consume a lot of energy, such as manufacturing and transportation. High energy prices also tend to spill over into inflation in food and consumer goods, at a time when many Canadian families are already feeling stretched to make ends meet.
But high oil prices should also relieve downward pressure on the Canadian dollar, allowing for cheaper imports, which can partly counteract inflationary pressure on the cost of living.
And Calnan says industries beyond oil potentially stand to benefit in the future.

"If we're talking about big new investments happening in Alberta, that will help boost manufacturing and other industries elsewhere in Canada, because there'll be an enormous amount of steel, and skilled trades workers needed to complete these huge facilities."
Carney releases video saying U.S. wanted 'dependency' in too many areas

On his way to the Republican convention in Dallas, Trump on Wednesday assured voters that "right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward." But there are few signs the markets are buying it. Oil futures contracts remain at the $100 level to the end of 2026.

items: Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump

blocks.text: In both of the world's current major wars involving superpowers — the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and the Russian war on Ukraine — oil infrastructure has become a major target.

Both the Russians, who famously anticipated a swift collapse followed by a victory parade in Kyiv, and the Trump administration, which has declared victory over Iran more than once, now appear mired in conflicts with no clear exit, said Calnan.

"Wars have a problematic tendency to just keep going and be very difficult to bring to a clean finish," he said. "I'm not sure why people keep thinking that wars they start are going to end in a month."

articles.title: Provinces are turning to U.S. health-care workers to help with shortages. And it’s working
articles.summary: With shortages of nurses, physicians and other health workers, some provinces are actively recruiting U.S. health-care professionals — and they’re getting results.

image.caption: Registered nurse Shane Tyson began working at the Nanaimo Regional General Hospital in January after increasing concerns about the deteriorating health care and tighter immigration enforcement in the U.S. (Submitted by Shane Tyson)

blocks.text: LISTEN | Why U.S. nurses are moving north:
White Coat Black Art26:30Why U.S. nurses are moving north
Registered nurse Shane Tyson was done with the U.S.

He was working in Minnesota at the not-for-profit Mayo Clinic Health System and the Olmsted Medical Center. But in 2025, Tyson says he became increasingly concerned about the deterioration of health care, as well as tighter immigration enforcement.
Then ICE agents arrested a patient as they were leaving a primary care appointment where he worked, Tyson says.

“That was definitely a wake-up call," he said. "And I am married to a U.S. permanent resident that was born in Bolivia … and it scared the crap out of me for him and for the others in that situation,” Tyson told Dr. Brian Goldman, host of CBC’s White Coat, Black Art.

Tyson says he’d been noticing Facebook ads from provincial recruitment service HealthMatch BC. The more he researched, the more he contemplated a move north. So he registered, got interviews with two B.C. health authorities, and received two job offers within a week.

Tyson is one of many health-care professionals making the move from the U.S. With shortages of nurses, physicians and other health workers, some provinces are actively recruiting U.S. health-care professionals — and they’re getting results.
CBC reached out to health ministries in all 10 provinces for data on health-care professionals recruited from the U.S. since efforts ramped up in 2025.
The number of doctors recruited ranged from three in Saskatchewan to 33 in Nova Scotia and 570 in Ontario.
Ontario also recruited 2,300 nurses in 2025, while, all told, more than 580 health-care professionals accepted jobs in B.C. since March 2025.

For Tyson, the targeted recruitment worked. It took him just three months to get his B.C. nursing licence through a fast-track process, and eight days to receive a provincial nomination for permanent residence.

Since January, he’s been working in the emergency department of Nanaimo Regional General Hospital (NRGH) on Vancouver Island. Tyson says he’s pleased with the community, the weather, and what he sees as more inclusive health care.

“There’s not the insurance companies and corporate health-care companies taking billions of dollars. The patient is the focus here and whether you're the unhoused or the banker or lawyer, you have equal access to care in Canada,” he said.
The recruitment push
Health-care workers are bringing experience and ideas from some of the largest hospitals in the U.S., says Damian Lange, executive director of clinical services at NRGH.
“The American system has significant talent,” Lange said.

He said Island Health started recruiting from the U.S. in April 2025. Since then, it has hired 76 physicians and 102 nurses — 31 of them at NRGH. He said another 87 U.S. health-care providers will hopefully join by year’s end.

Lange said the new recruits make for a “better staff experience ... better patient experience, improved quality care, improved access to care. And so it's been a real benefit as we close the gap there with our vacancy rates.”
Even with the new hires, Lange said Island Health still has a 15 per cent vacancy rate for nurses.
And recruiting U.S. health-care workers is only part of the equation. A lot of questions go along with an international move.
Volunteers helping ease the move north

Tod Maffin and his wife, Jocelyn Maffin, are helping pave the way with an online community they started in early 2025. Tod is a digital strategist and former CBC journalist, and Jocelyn works with Spinal Cord Injury BC.

It started with Tod’s invitation to Americans to visit Nanaimo last year. So many health-care workers interested in moving to Canada came that Maffin made a Discord channel where people can chat and ask questions about everything from health-care licensing to real estate to services for autistic children.
Tod said it’s about connecting people.

“If you're an ER nurse in Dallas and you're ready … to move into Canada, you've figured out which area you're going to go to, but you have a trans kid and you just need to talk the parent of another trans kid in that community to make sure that your daughter is going to be OK,” you can find that support in the Discord group, he said.

It includes out-of-area health-care workers (mostly Americans), recruiters, immigration consultants and local citizens who just want to help out. Of around 1,200 current users, 84 have recently accepted job offers.
Tod created a template for other Healthcare Infusion communities and there are now 45 of them across Canada.
Jocelyn said she initially worried about poaching health-care workers from the U.S., but: “Canada has dealt with brain drain to the U.S. for years and that's always been a big issue,” she said.
“So maybe we're just borrowing them back.”
Call for better retention

In an email to CBC, the Canadian Medical Association said that with a shortage of more than 23,000 family doctors, Canada needs to remove barriers to immigration and licensing for internationally trained physicians. It also needs to make it easier for those currently practising in Canada to stay, the association said.

items: This Toronto doctor has over 2,000 patients, but still no permanent residency

blocks.text: Canadian Nurses Association CEO Valerie Grdisa emphasized the need to retain the nurses Canada already has.

“We welcome U.S.-educated nurses into the nation, but we don't see it really as a long-term recruitment strategy,” she said. “We really have to get back [to] what matters to Canadian and domestically educated nurses.”

Grdisa said Health Canada's Nursing Retention Toolkit lays out strategies to retain nurses, like safe staffing levels, manageable workloads, mentorship and career support. But she said health-care systems haven’t implemented or evaluated them consistently enough to determine what actually works.
“If those things were to happen, would we be losing such a large cohort — up to 40 per cent of the workforce by the age of 35?”
Meanwhile, though, nurse Shane Tyson says he is here to stay. He recently got his certificate of Canadian citizenship. A kind stranger also left a moose sticker and a welcome note on his car.

“That really made me emotional, you know. I was concerned, driving around with Minnesota plates, how I'd be received, because at that time the tariffs were coming in, talk of the 51st state — and that just really meant a lot to me.”
Now Tyson is logging onto the Maffins’ Discord community to help other U.S. health-care workers come to Canada.
“Have to pay it forward.”

articles.title: With millions of dead oysters and mounting debt, P.E.I. farmers fear they'll lose everything
articles.summary: Disease has blighted P.E.I.’s oyster industry, wiping out entire crops. Oyster farmers say they need more help to survive the crisis and are worried their independent farms may be snapped up by…

image.caption: Oyster farmers Bruce and Kaila Richard, with their daughter Leah, centre, on their boat on the Dock River in western P.E.I. Diseases are ravaging the industry, taking a heavy financial and emotional toll on farmers and fishers. (Julie Crysler/CBC)

blocks.text: LISTEN | Oyster farmer says P.E.I. industry is facing 'a massacre':
The Current21:29Inside the PEI oyster crisis
When Kaila Richard is out on the water of her oyster farm in western P.E.I., she often thinks of her late father, who ran the farm until his sudden death in an accident in 2021.
“Being out here, I feel my father close,” said Kaila, who took over the farm in the Dock River, near Alberton, with her husband Bruce Richard.
“[When] we make mistakes, I can hear my dad saying, 'What are yous doing?!' … and when things go right I'm like, ‘Oh he'd be so proud,’” she told CBC Radio’s The Current.

The Richards took out hefty loans to upgrade the farm in recent years, installing expensive new equipment and spending long days tending their crop. But all that hard work is in jeopardy as two diseases rip through the Island’s oyster industry.
Farmers have pulled up millions of dead oysters, their shells piled high around P.E.I.
“The whole island is just a massacre at this point,” said Bruce.
“There's about a dozen farmers in this little section of river back here, and we're all in the same boat. Everybody's seeing upwards of 90 per cent, 95 per cent dead loss.”
P.E.I. grower throws out $100K of dead oysters in 1 day as disease devastation continues

The diseases, multinucleate sphere unknown (MSX) and dermo, were detected in P.E.I. waters in 2024 and 2025, respectively. While harmless to humans, both parasites are fatal to oysters, with some growers reporting 100 per cent mortality rates.

The provincial and federal governments announced various support programs earlier this year, including financial relief, mental health support and approval for the import of disease-resistant oyster seed. Experts hope this seed could be cultivated to replenish oyster stocks on the island, but the process takes at least three years to grow from seed, with no guarantee of success.
Farmers say they need sustained financial support, and soon, to stay afloat in the interim.

“You can't hemorrhage money for three to five, [maybe] seven years … we don't have a million dollars sitting in the bank to make payments,” said Bruce, adding that at the time of his interview, his farm had not yet received any of the promised funding.
Jeff Noye, an oyster grower and the mayor of Tyne Valley in western P.E.I., said that oysters aren’t just a job on the island, but “a way of life.”
He worries if farmers don’t get more help, bigger corporations could come in and take over.

“Right now, the oyster industry is full of independent fishers. Men and women who work for themselves, by themselves … and we take a lot of pride in that,” said Noye, who is also the co-owner of Valley Pearl Oysters bar and restaurant in Tyne Valley.
But if those farmers can’t pay their bills, then “some of the companies with some big pockets can come in and snatch everything up,” he said.
“All of a sudden we're all working for them — and I hope that doesn't happen.”
Calls for income support
Mussel farmers in the Maritimes faced a similar issue when invasive species upended the industry 20 years ago, said Peter Warris, executive director of P.E.I. Aquaculture Alliance.
“Margins were pretty tight. We saw expenses were going up. We saw more and more growers selling out — and selling out to the big guys,” he said.
In a lot of cases, he said, those same farmers were then hired by the big companies, who needed experienced workers, familiar with the waterways.
“They're going to get paid by a bigger company rather than paying themselves. Is that good? No,” he said. “But is it better than nothing? I suppose, I mean I guess that's up to the individual.”

Warris’s organization represents both smaller farmers and bigger organizations. He wants greater financial support over the next few years, arguing it would both help individual farmers stay in business — and help the industry bounce back as a whole.

In a statement emailed to The Current, Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) said it is working “to support the long-term sustainability of the oyster sector,” including investments in scientific research to better understand and respond to the parasites.
DFO also pointed to a customer support program available through Farm Credit Canada (FCC).

When contacted by The Current, FCC said in an email that it will work with individual farmers to explore their options, including the potential “deferral of principal payments and/or other loan payment schedule amendments to reduce the financial pressure on those affected by oyster diseases.”
“The bottom line is we want to remain flexible and ensure producers have sufficient cash flow to get into the next production cycle,” the FCC statement said.

In a separate email statement, P.E.I.’s Department of Fisheries, Rural Development and Tourism pointed The Current to a handful of programs designed to provide “a financial safety net to eligible oyster growers.”
Warris worries this patchwork of programs might not be enough.
“There's no basic level of income support for growers right now and … there's fuel costs, wage costs, all these other things,” he said.
“Whilst there are programs out there for some of it, there isn't anything that will just give some basic income to keep people moving for the next three years.”
Warris said that with so much uncertainty, some farmers might decide to sell to bigger operations. But financial support would mean they won’t “have to sell at fire-sale prices.”
Government is ‘giving up’
Fishers of wild oysters are also struggling with the diseases. They’ve been forced to travel further to find healthy oysters, increasing costs for an often reduced harvest.

In August, the federal government offered $40,000 to buy back 150 eligible fishing licences on a first-come, first-served basis. Recipients would not be able to reapply for an oyster fishing licence for 10 years.

Bob Macleod, president of the P.E.I. Shellfish Association (PEISA), said his organization advised the federal government to take a different approach. He thinks the buyback program should have been rolled out over three years and coupled with a wage subsidy. That would have given the worst affected fishers the option to leave, but it might have encouraged others to weather the storm a little longer, he said.
“You can't give up. You’ve got to keep trying different things. So when the government says we'll take 150 licences, they're giving up, and that is not right,” he said.
“It's going to be hard to keep enough people interested to make it bounce back.”
In its emailed statement, DFO said the buyback program aims to “help reduce pressure on vulnerable wild oyster stocks while supporting affected harvesters and coastal communities.”

DFO added that PEISA’s proposals contributed to the design of the buyback program, but the final initiative differs “due to the urgency of the situation and the government’s objective of balancing targeted support with broad accessibility.”
P.E.I. oyster industry explores ways out of crisis including imported seed, new hatchery
‘A better day’
The devastation of their crop has taken a toll on Kaila and Bruce’s mental health, a sentiment echoed by many other oyster farmers and fishers on P.E.I.
“When we see each other out here, we all say, ‘Have a better day,’” Kaila said. “Because it's not ‘Have a good day,’ — just have a better day.”

items: How is P.E.I.’s fall wild oyster season going? Fishers say it’s off to a tough start
If you're at the Tyne Valley Oyster Festival this weekend, you might end up on Netflix

blocks.text: For now, Bruce has taken work building lobster boats to make ends meet. He hopes the disease-resistant seed can get the industry back on track but says farmers need help “to get us between today and when those get to market.”
“It's hard to actually look at it and say, ‘Yeah, I'll still be working here in five years’ time,” he said. “Because we don't really know.”
Kaila has a tattoo of an anchor, an oyster, a line of her father’s handwriting and a compass “because he always guided me through my life.”
“It's more than just our business. It started out because of my father,” she said.
“I definitely have the fight in me, and we're gonna fight for it.”

articles.title: Is Christine Fréchette exploiting the trade war, or just doing her job as Quebec premier?
articles.summary: The leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec has come under fire from her political opponents after interrupting her election campaign and convening her cabinet amid the ongoing trade war with the…

image.caption: Bernard Drainville, left, Christine Fréchette, centre, and Samuel Poulin are seen during a news conference in Quebec City after the premier interrupted her election campaign to convene a cabinet meeting and announce new tariff measures. (Dany Pilote/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

The leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec has come under fire from her political opponents after interrupting her election campaign and convening her cabinet amid the ongoing trade war with the United States. Is Christine Fréchette using the moment for political gain, or just doing her job?
Fréchette has been accused of using tariff war to gain traction with voters during election campaign

The leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec, Christine Fréchette, has come under fire from her political opponents after interrupting her election campaign and convening her cabinet amid the ongoing trade war with the United States.

During the meeting earlier this week, Fréchette donned her premier’s hat to discuss Quebec’s strategy in the aftermath of Canada’s retaliatory tariffs. She announced new measures to help businesses and the economy cope as tensions escalate.
But did the premier of a caretaker government cross a line? It’s a legitimate question, according to political analyst Antonine Yaccarini.

Fréchette launched her campaign coming off the back of two major announcements alongside Prime Minister Mark Carney, including a new Churchill Falls deal worth an estimated $70 billion and a new shipbuilding contract for Chantier Davie shipyard, in Lévis, Que.
This allowed Fréchette to position herself as an economic leader, according to Yaccarini, and to push the ballot question on tariffs, making the trade war a central part of her campaign.
In the lead up to Monday’s meeting, Fréchette was accused by rival parties — save for Québec Solidaire — of using the tariff war to gain traction among voters.
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was critical of Fréchette’s approach, saying in a written statement that “fear was not an economic strategy.”
He accused Fréchette of using "the Trump bogeyman” to distract from the Coalition Avenir Québec government’s record over the last eight years.
The criticism continued through the week.

Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard pointed out that no other Canadian premier had held a cabinet meeting, a special meeting or a major news conference announcing new measures in response to the new tariffs.
“So, when there is talk of exploiting a crisis, you have a clear example of it right here," he said from the campaign trail.
In an interview with Radio-Canada on Wednesday, Milliard again criticized her actions, calling the cabinet meeting “a charade."
Fréchette’s measures to support Quebec against new tariffs draw criticism
Fréchette addressed the accusations this week.
"This is real life, and we need to face it, and we need to adjust our approach," she said Tuesday.
In her own interview with Radio-Canada, she argued that Quebecers expect a leader who defends their interests on issues such as the French language and supply management in U.S. negotiations.
'Damned if you do, damned if you don't'
During an interview on CBC's Breakaway, Yaccarini said that while Fréchette is clearly benefitting from the current crisis, she’s also just doing her job.
“She is still Quebec’s premier,” she said, adding that until a new cabinet is appointed, they remain the government and need to manage a number of issues.
“And that is the kind of issue right now that is very, very important and I think a lot of voters understand the situation,” she said.

items: Quebec votes 2026: Here's what the main parties have promised so far

blocks.text: Yaccarini said Fréchette would also have been criticized if she did nothing. “So it’s a damned if you do, damned if you don’t situation,” she said.
Daniel Béland, who heads the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada, said however, that as a caretaker government, Fréchette needs to tread carefully.
Because the National Assembly has been dissolved, there is no legislature to hold the government accountable, he said.
Caretaker government needs to show restraint
Under the caretaker convention — an unwritten rule in Canadian politics — governments need to show restraint and not enact major changes that will tie the next government.

And while it’s relatively rare for leaders to suspend a political campaign, there is a precedent for it. Both Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford took time out of their respective campaigns to respond to Donald Trump’s tariff threats in 2025.

items: Quebec 'will use every tool available' to cope with trade war, Fréchette says

blocks.text: Béland said while measures introduced by Fréchette — including giving Quebec-based companies an advantage in public tenders and buying local — did strengthen her political message, they were relatively limited in scope.

Both the PQ and the Liberals, however, panned the new measures. The PQ fears retaliation will hurt Quebec companies that are doing business in the U.S., while the Liberals said the plan doesn’t go far enough.
Béland said even though Fréchette can act as premier and that announcing new decisions can get her quite a bit of exposure, it also opens the door to criticism and she has to show restraint.
“If she will suspend her campaign again and there is no strong apparent trigger for it, then yes, I think she will be more vulnerable politically and that could help her opponents,” he said.
LISTEN | Trade war becomes major focus in Quebec election:
Breakaway11:49Tariffs are taking center stage in the election campaign

In the view of her opponents, the damage is already done. Milliard worries Fréchette is using her role as premier to turn the election into a one-issue campaign. He said he hopes that will change after the leaders' debates.

The main party leaders will be facing off in three French-language debates organized by Radio-Canada, TVA, Noovo and Crave. The first debate is scheduled for Sept. 15 and Radio-Canada’s French-language debate will take place Sept. 23 at 8 p.m.
Voters head to the polls on Oct. 5.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Annabelle Olivier is a digital journalist at CBC Montreal. She previously worked at Global News as an online producer. You can reach her at anne.isabelle.olivier@cbc.ca.

articles.title: One dead, 102 rescued from Indonesian ferry that went missing in Java Sea
articles.summary: The nation's search and rescue team said it lost contact with the Virgo Transport 8 in the early hours of Sunday morning.

blocks.text: Image source, Donny Muslim / BBC
Families of victims gather at Trisakti Port, Banjarmasin
One person has died and 102 have been rescued from a stricken Indonesian passenger ferry in the Java Sea, an official said.

A search and rescue operation was launched after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 ship, which was carrying 243 people, as it encountered bad weather, Indonesia's search and rescue agency said.
The search for the remaining passengers is ongoing.

The ferry was travelling from Surabaya to the South Kalimantan city of Banjarmasin and was last reported to be about 150km (93 miles) south of Banjarmasin around 02:00 local time on Sunday (18:00 GMT on Saturday).

Authorities received the initial distress report at 04:10 from the vessel's operator PT Virgo. The ship left Surabaya at 10:33 on Saturday and was scheduled to arrive in Banjarmasin on Sunday at 14:00, according to data from two maritime monitoring sites.
A joint task force involving Indonesia's search and rescue agency, navy, maritime police and other parties has been set up for the rescue effort.
Ships and a helicopter have been deployed to the scene and all other vessels in that area of the Java Sea have been alerted to report signs of any passengers.
An operations post for handling the accident was set up in the Trisakti Port area on Sunday morning.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Indonesian authorities reported the Virgo Transport 8 lost contact in the Java Sea while en route from Surabaya to Banjarmasin

blocks.text: Indonesian authorities reported the Virgo Transport 8 lost contact in the Java Sea while en route from Surabaya to Banjarmasin

Rusmilawati, a resident of Banjarmasin, went to the port to seek information about eight relatives who were passengers on the ship. They were travelling back to Banjarmasin after visiting the tombs of several Islamic scholars in Java.
"They flew there initially, but for the return journey they wanted to try travelling by ship," she said.
As of Sunday afternoon local time, Rusmilawati said she had not received any information from officials about whether her relatives had been rescued.

The family last heard from one of the relatives through a WhatsApp status update. In the post, the relative wrote: "The waves are really frightening tonight. Or is this just what it's normally like travelling by ship, rocking and crashing against the waves?"
"Hopefully they're safe," Rusmilawati said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Family members of the victims wait to hear news about their loved ones at Trisakti Port

blocks.text: Family members of the victims wait to hear news about their loved ones at Trisakti Port
Meanwhile, Misnah broke down in tears after learning that her husband, Ahmad Supandi, had survived.
Ahmad, a freight driver, had been aboard Virgo Transport 8 and was later rescued by the vessel MV Haida.
At Tanjung Perak Port in Surabaya, relatives of crew members have also been seeking information about their loved ones.
One relative, Fredy, said his youngest sibling, Stevie Manuhua, worked aboard the vessel as a keyboard player, entertaining passengers.
"We spoke two days ago when the ship was docked in Surabaya. After that, there was no news until now," Fredy said.
He said he had still not received any information about his sibling's whereabouts.
