The night was a "a tense, tearful, joyous affair probably even more so for the singer than for her loyal audience," writes The Telegraph's Neil McCormick, external.
She started out slow, he says. "Her voice sounded fragile and exposed, but at least it was her distinctive voice, not some autotuned approximation."

"At first, she was clearly struggling to hold herself together," he continues. "Her vocals wobbled dangerously, as if about to crack or collapse. But she was gaining confidence with every moment back on stage."
She broke down in tears as the audience roared in approval after the first song, and addressed the crowd in both French and English during the set.
"This was a high-stakes, high-wire return, perhaps the riskiest comeback in the history of showbusiness," McCormick continues, referring to her health condition.

But he concludes: "I honestly think I prefer this less superhuman Céline. Her voice is still great, but a bit more raw and real, with a rougher tone, less smoothness in the runs and more edge to her whoops and shrieks."
Sarah Leavitt, reporting from Paris for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), external, said the crowd "was left without words" by the stunning performance.
She noted that she didn't want to cry, but "of course she cried right away."
Dion also "endeared herself" to the crowd by saying during one song that she wanted to stop and start over.
Will Hodgkinson at the Times of London, external writes in his review, "miraculously, her art will go on," that the performance was "overwhelming".
She "looked suitably humbled and tearful" as she emerged, he said, going on to praise the stage direction.
"Truly, she was throwing the love at the crowd, who threw it right back at her. There was no holding back. It was quite overwhelming, actually," he writes.
The performance was "complete with both costume, key change and air of tragic, important romance".

"Céline Dion's strength lies in being a diva with the common touch while being as French as they get, even if she is Canadian. She fulfilled that role with all the verve you could hope for," writes Hodgkinson.
"The concert had a spiritual feel, with visual interludes steeped in biblical imagery alluding to a pilgrimage," Elsa Keslassy writes for Variety., external

In video clips, Dion is seen wandering in a desert. "The set design was highly cinematic, with a monumental staircase sweeping up one side and a moon dominating the stage, while the backdrop appeared to have a stark, almost brutalist gray texture."
The star, known for power ballads like My Heart Will Go On and Because You Loved Me, has said she will not let her diagnosis control her life.
"The way I see it, I have two choices. Either I train like an athlete and work super hard, or I switch off and it's over," she told French Vogue magazine, external in 2024.
"I've chosen to work with all my body and soul, from head to toe, with a medical team."
When Dion announced the first leg of her Paris residency back in March, nine million fans signed up for early access tickets to the concerts, French outlet FRI reported.
The shows sold out so fast that her management company soon announced an additional 10 shows scheduled for May 2027, which have also since sold out.
Fans who were unable to snag tickets to one of the highly anticipated shows have not been left out entirely - events honouring Dion's comeback have dominated Paris in recent weeks.
Céline Dion tribute boat cruises on Seine - complete with costume contests, sing-alongs, DJ sets, are happening throughout September.
Ahead of Saturday's show, fans gathered outside Dion's Paris hotel, LeRoyal Monceau, as early as 06:00 local time to catch a glimpse of the star.
Paris City Hall organised a massive karaoke event on Friday night, attended by thousands, to celebrate Dion's return to the stage.

"I couldn't get tickets to the concert. I'm still keeping my fingers crossed and hoping, but I thought to myself: at least I can share a moment here with all the fans," Rania, a participant at the event, told Reuters.
Earlier this week, thousands of fans also gathered at a historic theatre in central Paris for two nights of karaoke and activities inspired by Dion's music.
And Paris venues and night clubs are hosting Dion-themed events around the city on Saturday night for fans who couldn't get tickets to the actual show.

articles.title: One dead and more than 30 missing after ferry sinks off Vanuatu coast in rough seas
articles.summary:
Prime minister’s office tells families of those missing ‘the nation stands with you’ as search and rescue efforts continue

One person has died and more than 30 are missing after a ferry sank…

blocks.text: One person has died and more than 30 are missing after a ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu, the country’s government says.
The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail with more than 40 passengers and crew on Friday from the island of Santo to Ambae island in very rough seas, but did not arrive.
“Our hearts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones,” Vanuatu prime minister Jotham Napat’s office said in a statement on Sunday.
“Search and rescue operations are continuing.”
Fifteen of those onboard have been “accounted for alive” and one body has been recovered, the statement said.
“Over 30 people remain missing at sea,” it said.
“To the survivors, we ⁠pray for your strength and recovery. To the families of ​those ​missing and those we ​have lost, please know that the nation stands ​with you ‌in this time ​of ​grief.”
An investigation into potential negligence has been launched.
“This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel,” the statement added.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in New Caledonia said it was assisting with the search, and a French Armed Forces aircraft was deployed on Sunday morning.
The centre said 12 people were located on Sunday morning.
Matai Seremaiah, the member of parliament for Luganville who is assisting in the search, said efforts would concentrate on the south-east coast where currents may have carried survivors.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: PH joins India-led coalition to boost disaster-resilient infrastructure
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is turning to an India-led global coalition for technical expertise and possible financing to build infrastructure that can better withstand floods and other…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is turning to an India-led global coalition for technical expertise and possible financing to build infrastructure that can better withstand floods and other disasters, according to Malacañang.
President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Saturday met with officials of the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) in New Delhi as Manila formally joined the group as its 71st member.
Marcos is currently in India to attend the 18th Brics Summit as this year’s chair of the Association of the Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The membership comes as the Marcos administration faces growing pressure to improve the country’s flood-control and other disaster mitigation infrastructure amid increasingly adverse weather events worsened by climate change.

Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Secretary Dave Gomez said the CDRI could help the Philippines learn from other countries how to design and build roads, bridges and ports that can withstand disasters and climate-related risks.
“First and foremost, they will teach us—this is essentially a sharing of experiences among coalition members on how to deal with disasters and how to build disaster resilience,” Gomez said.
The coalition could also help the Philippines access financing for projects meant to make infrastructure more resilient, he added.
According to Gomez, investing in stronger infrastructure before disasters strike would be more beneficial in the long run than spending heavily on reconstruction and recovery after calamities.

The Philippines has been dealing with recurring flooding, particularly in Metro Manila and other urban and low-lying areas, with the government pursuing large-scale flood-control and drainage projects while also reviewing existing infrastructure.

The CDRI membership provides the Philippines an opportunity to tap the experience of other countries in addressing such challenges, particularly in designing infrastructure that can withstand extreme weather and other hazards.
CDRI Director-General Amit Prothi welcomed the Philippines’ membership and said he looks forward to working with Philippine institutions on disaster-resilient infrastructure.
He cited the Philippines’ extensive experience and knowledge in dealing with flooding, earthquakes and volcanic activity.
Knowledge sharing

Prothi said the country’s long-standing efforts to address these challenges could provide valuable lessons for other countries, especially in its experience in disaster risk management, preparedness, response, and resilient recovery.

Launched by the Indian government in 2019, the CDRI is a voluntary and nonbinding global partnership that brings together governments, international organizations, financial institutions, private companies and academic institutions.
It seeks to promote the sharing of expertise and best practices, strengthen technical capabilities and encourage investments in infrastructure that can withstand disasters and climate change.

The coalition also focuses on shaping policies and financing, integrating risk-aware development, scaling up resilience actions, and building stakeholder capacity to protect vulnerable communities and high-risk regions.
$10 trillion global investment

By 2050, CDRI aims to drive $10 trillion in resilient infrastructure investments and services to improve environmental quality, livelihoods and well-being for more than three billion people worldwide.
Overall, the CDRI is composed of 71 members, including 59 countries and 12 partner organizations.
The Philippines is the second Southeast Asian country to join the coalition after Vietnam.
The Department of Public Works and Highways has been designated to represent the Philippines in the CDRI.

The country’s participation in CDRI also forms part of the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership and aligns with the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023-2028, the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) 2023-2050, and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan (NDRRMP) 2020-2030. /gsg
/gsg

articles.title: Zelensky offers to meet Putin at G20 in Miami
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he would travel to Miami if his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, attended the Group of 20 (G20) leaders’ summit scheduled for December.…

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he would travel to Miami if his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, attended the Group of 20 (G20) leaders’ summit scheduled for December.
Zelenskyy replied enthusiastically when DW’s correspondent Misha Komadovsky posed the question on Friday.
“Yes, of course. We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” he said.
Zelenskyy added that what he was going to say to Putin mattered less than results.
“It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. […] Results matter. That’s it.”
Zelenskyy and Putin have not met in person since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its smaller neighbor in February 2022.
The Kremlin has so far declined to say whether Putin would go to Miami for the meeting.
The Russian leader has not personally attended a G20 summit since 2019.
Last month, Russia’s Finance Minister Anton Siluanov was however invited by the US to attend a meeting of G20 countries in North Carolina in a move that upset European officials.
100-year partnership declaration with Canada
First up, however, Zelenskyy spoke of the deals he signed on Thursday with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, including a 100-year partnership declaration.

Zelenskyy underlined the importance of the deal, which he said covered numerous sectors, “from security, financing, energy, very important energy, veteran policy, and culture, and relationships and humanitarian issues.”
“So it’s a global decision, a really historic decision, and I’m happy that we have it,” he said.
Zelenskyy said he had also signed a deal on collaboration on drone production with the Canadian leader involving a number of Ukrainian companies.
Zelenskyy pushes for more Patriot missiles ahead of winter
Zelenskyy’s interview with DW comes as summer is nearly over and Ukraine is gearing up for the cold months of winter.
The Ukrainian president has conceded that his country has been struggling to counter flying jet-propelled drones that Russia has been increasingly deploying.
“They [US] have political will to sell and to help, but the production is not too big. So it means that stocks is a variant,” he said.
“Will Americans be ready to give us (Patriots)? I don’t know. We will see.”
Patriot missiles are powerful weapons that are currently the most effective defense against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
What Zelenskyy needs from US and European allies
“Russia [currently] produces 140 ballistic missiles per month. So, according to the rules of NATO, if you want to destroy 140, you need a 1-to-2 [ratio], 280 missiles,” Zelenskyy told DW.

“You will never have 280 missiles per month, and between us, it’s a huge challenge to have [even] 100 missiles per month. This is what I want. I want to have 100-120 for these difficult months, especially the cold months.”
Germany earlier this week said it was going to send Patriot missiles from its national stock, without specifying how many missiles that would be.
Zelenskyy called on Kyiv’s European allies to provide more support.
“They have to give as much as possible. With all respect to them, they have to give to Ukrainians to save their lives.”
Zelenskyy also spoke of having secured agreements with several European companies to develop a Ukrainian-led anti-missile system called Freya.
He said he was hoping that the first test phase would begin by the end of December, stressing that time was short.
Ukraine in ‘good position for negotiations’
Zelenskyy said that it was a “good signal” that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv earlier this week, and not just Moscow.
He said he had made clear to them that his country was well-placed for negotiations on ending the conflict, with Russia estimated to be losing more than 30,000 soldiers a month.
Zelenskyy said this meant that Moscow was paying a “big price” for small gains on the battlefield.
“So that’s why we think that we have now good position for negotiations,” he said, adding that his country was stronger than last year.

blocks.caption: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Zelenskyy in KyivImage: Ukrainian Presidential Press Office/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Grain and energy top priorities
The other concern that has been coming up steadily over this summer is the shipment of grains through the Black Sea, with Moscow and Kyiv currently targeting each other’s ships and hindering exports.
Russia’s de facto blockade of Ukraine’s Black Sea ports in the Odesa region has led to a 76% fall in Ukraine’s grain exports year-on-year so far in August.
Zelenskyy said he had spoken with the two envoys about an energy and grain ceasefire that could provide a starting point for peace.
“What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve,” he said.

Misha Komadovsky US Correspondent Roshni Majumdar Roshni is a global breaking news writer and digital editor for DW, based in Germany. Timothy Jones Writer, translator and editor with DW’s online news team.

articles.title: India’s BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
articles.summary: India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019. The summit comes…

blocks.text: India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019.

The summit comes at an important moment for India. As New Delhi’s year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia, and its relationship with Washington remains difficult.

Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.
But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi’s diplomatic gains.
New Delhi and Beijing locked in ‘armed coexistence’ and competition
Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order.
Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India’s engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi’s longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy.
“These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers,” Kantha told DW.
However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal.

blocks.caption: India’s geopolitical strategy is heavily impacted by its relationships with both the West and fellow BRICS powersImage: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier.

International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access.
The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment.
Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset.

“The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard,” said Kantha.

“It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple ‘elephant and dragon’ story,” he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world’s two most populous nations.
BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow
India’s presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11.

blocks.caption: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit

blocks.text: With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran.
Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis, forcing India to issue a unilateral chair’s statement instead.
With Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage.

“Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground,” says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation.
“BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common,” he added.
Fears of Chinese dominance
The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China.

India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. However, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West.

India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency.
“Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation,” Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking ‘de-dollarization.'”
“Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements.”
India’s ‘America Plus’ strategy

Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China.
India’s diplomatic course is not a pure “multi-alignment” approach but an “America Plus” strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW.

“India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons,” said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University.
But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns.
“A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia’s growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance,” he said.
In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West.

The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India’s power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform. /dl

articles.title: Canadian boxer George Chuvalo, who faced Muhammad Ali in his prime, dead at 89
articles.summary: George Chuvalo, the iron-chinned Canadian heavyweight who took the best punches from the giants of boxing without ever falling, has died. He was 89.

image.caption: George Chuvalo poses for a portrait in 2016 ahead of events commemorating his historic 1966 match facing Muhammad Ali. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: George Chuvalo, the iron-chinned Canadian heavyweight who took the best punches from the giants of boxing without ever falling, has died. He was 89.
Chuvalo suffered from dementia late in life and had been residing in a long-term care facility in Toronto. He died Saturday according to multiple online posts by family and friends.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who said the boxer was a family friend, shared condolences on social media Saturday.
"My thoughts are with all of George's family and loved ones as we mourn his passing," he said.
Chuvalo went the distance with Muhammad Ali in bouts in Toronto and Vancouver, and absorbed the hardest shots sluggers Joe Frazier and George Foreman had to offer, without being knocked down.
It was unfathomable family tragedy after he retired that brought him to his knees.

"If you added up every punch I took and multiplied the total by 10,000, it wouldn't begin to equal the pain of losing three sons and a wife to drugs and suicide," he said in his 2013 autobiography Chuvalo: A Fighter's Life, co-written with Murray Greig.
The son of Croatian immigrants was born Sept. 12, 1937, in Toronto's Junction neighbourhood. He became intrigued by boxing after seeing The Ring magazine at a newsstand.
Chuvalo was 10 years old the first time he stepped through the ropes, and a growth spurt combined with an interest in weightlifting saw him develop into a six-foot, 210-pound fighter.
After a brief amateur career, he turned pro in 1956, winning notice for performances at the Jack Dempsey Tournament at Maple Leaf Gardens.
But by the early 1960s, Chuvalo's career had stagnated under ineffective guidance, until Toronto poultry magnate Irv Ungerman took over as his manager.

Chuvalo parlayed several wins into an attention-getting 11th-round stoppage over contender Doug Jones at Madison Square Garden in 1964. He returned to that mecca of boxing the next year, narrowly losing a decision to former champ Floyd Patterson in a bout The Ring named best of 1965.
'He just keeps coming and coming'
Chuvalo's style was inexorable without being reckless. He moved forward with thudding blows from both hands to the head and body, producing stoppages in 88 per cent of his wins.

"You can't believe his strength," Canadian fighter Bill Drover once told a writer. "There's no way to stop him. He just keeps coming and coming. The only way you can stop him is with a stick of dynamite."

Chuvalo would always insist his defence was better than advertised, but it was his durability that was remarkable. He was able to absorb the shots, he said, thanks to a 17.5-inch neck strengthened through exercises.

Chuvalo found himself fighting for the heavyweight title in 1966 as a replacement foe when Ali's affiliation with the Black Muslims and controversial anti-Vietnam-War stance made him a pariah in the U.S.
The challenger's prospects were described in a New York Times headline: Bettor's-Eye View of Chuvalo: A Big Bum With a Lot of Heart.

While Chuvalo failed to become Canada's first heavyweight champion since Tommy Burns in the early 1900s, he earned praise for a gritty performance. Ali famously called him the toughest man he had faced up to that point, but Chuvalo was ambivalent being the first to take the champ 15 rounds.
"In a crazy way, that fight is what defines me for a lot of my fellow Canadians but it took a long time before I came to appreciate how good it made me feel," he said.
Never knocked down

With wife Lynne and five children at home, Chuvalo appreciated the paydays the Ali performance begat. He would beat contenders Jerry Quarry and Manuel Ramos, losing close bouts to Oscar Bonavena and Jimmy Ellis.

Chuvalo was stopped for the first time in 1967 by Frazier, requiring a silicone implant to keep an eyeball from drooping. The loss to Foreman in the fourth round three years later was also notable, with the referee stepping in before Chuvalo's "never knocked down" streak might have been ended.

Chuvalo's loss to Ali in Vancouver in 1972 was not as compelling or as close as the first bout. He retired for good on a winning note six years later, finishing with a record of 73 wins, 18 losses and two draws, with 64 of his wins coming by knock out.

Unlike with Ali and others, the toll of concussive blows wasn't evident on the surface. Chuvalo was articulate and spoke in rapid-fire bursts, with a quip or self-deprecating joke usually at the ready.

But like many fighters, he had a tough time transitioning to the "humdrum" nature of life, as he once described it. At various points, he opened a nightclub, got his real estate licence, promoted fights, hosted a TV show and took cinema's worst ever arm-wrestling defeat in a cameo in David Cronenberg's The Fly.
George Chuvalo's date with destiny and Muhammad Ali

Chuvalo told CBC Radio in 1968 he didn't want his four sons boxing for a living, but it was outside the ring where he couldn't protect them. The youngest, Jesse, became hooked on heroin after a prescription for pain medication ran out and was just 19 when he fatally shot himself in 1985.

Older brothers George Jr. and Steven had by then also become users of the drug and involved in petty crime to feed their habits. Steven Chuvalo described a feeling of "worthlessness" he and his two addicted brothers felt in an interview with CBC's the fifth estate in 1995.
"My dad spent quite a few years chasing us around the city, Georgie and I in particular, and dragging us out of drug houses and heroin houses and basically just trying to keep us alive," he said.
George Jr., three days sprung from jail in Kingston, Ont., overdosed on Halloween 1993.
Just four days after that, 49-year-old Lynne Chuvalo swallowed pills and left a suicide note.
"I never thought she'd do it, but I'm not surprised," Chuvalo told the New York Times a short time later, adding his wife never got over the first burial of a child.
Steven Chuvalo, who spoke on the fifth estate of wanting to make his father proud, would overdose and die eight months after that program aired.

Chuvalo would persevere, marrying again, and cherishing time spent with oldest son Mitch, daughter Vanessa, and his grandchildren. He would travel the country, speaking bluntly to students, as captured in a CBC Radio report in 1998.
"I'd like to think if you're ever tempted with the idea of doing drugs, or you ever flirt with doing drugs, I hope you think of me, George Chuvalo, and what drugs did to my family."

In 2017, reports surfaced of family drama involving Chuvalo's surviving children and the fighter's second wife, Joanne, who he was divorcing. Some of the disputes centred around the state of Chuvalo's cognitive decline and his future care.
On a podcast five years later, Mitch Chuvalo said his father no longer recognized him when he visited.
By that time, his legacy had been recognized by the City of Toronto, with the official opening in 2019 of the 7,000-square foot George Chuvalo Community Centre, located in the Junction.

articles.title: Trump while in Ireland: Reunification would be ‘fantastic’
articles.summary: DUBLIN — US President Donald Trump said Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic” as he waded into a complex and politically charged subject during a weekend visit to a…

blocks.text: DUBLIN — US President Donald Trump said Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic” as he waded into a complex and politically charged subject during a weekend visit to a tournament at his Irish golf course.
At a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the United Kingdom’s Northern Ireland.
“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told a reporter who sought his opinion on the issue. “It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing,” the Republican president said, adding that “the U.K. will have something to say about it, obviously.”
The Irish unity debate is heated
Competing visions of Northern Ireland — whether Irish or British — drove decades of violence in the six-county region that has a Protestant majority and has remained part of the U.K.
Previous American presidents, including Democrat Joe Biden, who has strong emotional ties to Ireland, have avoided commenting directly on the subject.

Ireland, long dominated by its bigger neighbor Britain, became a self-governing Catholic-majority country a century ago. Northern Ireland was split between two main communities: nationalists, most of them Catholic, who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British. Tensions eventually exploded in the Troubles involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops.

A 1998 peace accord that the United States was instrumental in negotiating largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland’s ultimate status unresolved. That agreement allows for a vote on unification if it appears likely a majority of people would vote for it. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that the U.K. would only consider allowing a referendum “when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered.” Burnham’s office referred back to that comment when asked about Trump’s statement.

Trump’s comments Saturday, along with recent statements about the Falkland Islands, a small British overseas territory in the South Atlantic Ocean that Argentina calls Las Malvinas, could also be viewed as a dig at Britain, given his anger over London’s refusal to be drawn into the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
Trump also talked about the Falkland Islands

Trump once more raised the prospect of conflict between the U.K. and Argentina over the Falklands. Argentina’s President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, has recently restated his country’s claim to the territory of about 3,500 people, which is about 300 miles (480 kilometers) east of the southeast coast of Argentina.

Trump has previously said Washington could reconsider its neutral stance on the islands’ sovereignty. On Saturday, he expressed skepticism that Britain would be able to retake the Falklands as it did after Argentina invaded in 1982.
“I’m sure I’ll be called into that potential disaster, but if they do, I’ll probably be able to settle, settle it out,” he said.
A meeting with the Irish president who criticized Trump

Trump also held talks in Dublin with Irish President Catherine Connolly, a left-wing politician who joined protesters when Trump visited Ireland in 2019 during his first term in office. She is now Ireland’s elected, largely ceremonial head of state. A supporter of the Palestinian cause, Connolly has in the past has criticized U.S. policy in the Middle East and called Trump a “bully.”

blocks.caption: Protesters show placards during a demonstration against the visit of U.S. President Donald Trump in Dublin, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. Associated Press

blocks.text: Connolly said in a statement after the meeting that she conveyed to Trump “the strong view of the Irish people that the normalization of war and genocide can never be accepted.” She gave Trump several gifts, among them a collection by the late Irish poet Michael Longley that includes the sonnet “Ceasefire.”
Asked about the meeting, Trump first had his protocol chief, Monica Crowley, answer before he was pressed and said it was “very nice.” “We discussed a lot of things, quickly,” Trump said.
Trump’s presence irks some Dubliners
Police put up a cordon around Dublin’s 1,750-acre (700-hectare) Phoenix Park, where Connolly, Martin and U.S. Ambassador Edward Walsh have residences and welcomed Trump.
A protest march drew thousands to central Dublin. He had left the city and was on the way to his Doonbeg golf course on the country’s Atlantic coast by the time the demonstration began.
Many in the crowd waved Irish or Palestinian flags and chanted “Donald Trump not welcome here” and “Irish government, shame on you!”
Paula Butler said she came with a contingent from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre to oppose the American president’s “attitude to women, to refugees, to migrants.”
She was unimpressed by Trump’s support for Irish unity, a popular cause in Ireland.
“What he knows about Irish unity, I’d say I know more on my little finger,” Butler said.
Kim Mathis, who moved from Florida to Dublin last year with her partner, said “part of the reason we moved to Ireland was to get away from Trump and all of his horrific policies.”
She said dealing with Trump is “a global conundrum” for governments. “It would be really nice if politicians would just say, ‘Stay home.'”
Eric Trump defends family’s presence in Ireland
Speaking to Irish national broadcaster RTE on Friday in Doonbeg, Trump’s son Eric said the course is the largest employer in the area.

“Go down to Morrissey’s tavern in Doonbeg and hear from a real Irish person as to whether or not they like President Trump and the Trump family, go have them attest to what we’ve done for the country and what we’ve invested in the country and the love and respect that our family has always shown them,” he said.
Trump’s visit is the latest example of blending his official duties and personal interests.

He spends most weekends playing golf at his clubs in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events and having a hand in organizing some of them in ways that benefit his family business. His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have hosted professional golf tournaments this year.

Last year, Trump went to Scotland for five days to play golf at his club in Turnberry and later inaugurated a Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire. During that visit, he held talks with the British prime minister and the president of the European Commission.
Asked if he would return to Ireland next year for the Ryder Cup, Trump said, “I will. Absolutely.” /dl

articles.title: Houthis claim attack on Saudi base as fighting flares with Yemeni forces
articles.summary:
Iran-allied Houthis say drones and missiles used in attack that targeted ‘weapons depots and command and control centres’ in southern Saudi Arabia

Houthi fighters on Sunday said they used…

blocks.text: Houthi fighters on Sunday said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in southern Saudi Arabia as renewed fighting with Yemen’s government forces led growing numbers of civilians to flee.

The attack at the southern Sharurah base targeted “weapons depots and command and control centres that are managing the aggression against our nation and people”, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree wrote on X.
The date of the operation was not specified. Clashes have increased this week between the Iran-allied Houthis and Yemeni government forces, which are backed by Riyadh.
On Saturday, the government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha, and later attacked other Houthi positions in the south-western part of the country.
“Air Force of the Armed Forces targeted positions and barracks of the terrorist Houthi group with three airstrikes” in the Taiz region, the Yemeni military said Sunday in a post on X.
The US news site Axios also reported that Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman twice called Donald Trump to request strikes on the Houthis last week, but that the request was rejected.

The ongoing clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the group capturing the remainder of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and several strategic islands, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab strait at the sea’s southern entrance.

The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade on the strait of Hormuz at the start of the Middle East war.
The Houthis have recently declared their own maritime blockade of Riyadh’s Red Sea ports.

The government news agency Saba reported on Saturday that Yemeni “forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia” near the port of Mocha, and quoted a spokesperson for the forces as saying they had also struck Houthi targets just outside the city.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said on Saturday evening that over the past 48 hours, “Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 airstrikes” on areas under their control.
Yemen’s civil war, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sana’a, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but roared back to life in July.
Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration.

On Saturday night, Saudi authorities said a Houthi projectile fell in an area near the border, hours after issuing alerts warning of the risk of possible attacks. The civil defence directorate said the incident resulted “in two injuries and material damage to a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles”.
The Yemeni civil war has uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes.
The fall of Mocha to the Houthis on Thursday drove many residents to Aden, where the internationally recognised Yemeni government is based.
The UN’s migration agency said on Saturday that 76,000 people had fled the fighting since July, a figure that had quadrupled since last week.
About 1,400 people had fled to Djibouti, the country’s minister of economy and finance Ilyas Moussa Dawaleh said on Saturday.
The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.

Trump on Saturday acknowledged speaking to the de facto Saudi leader but said the Houthis had also “called us and they don’t want to fight with us”. He did not elaborate on whether Washington would take any action, but told reporters that “everything’s gonna work out fine and dandy” in the region.
In 2025, the US conducted a seven-week bombing campaign against the Houthis in response to their repeated attacks on Red Sea shipping in support of Hamas in the Gaza war.
That ended with a negotiated ceasefire, though the Houthis kept up their missile and drone attacks targeting Israel.
More recently, the group has resumed attacks on ships in the Red Sea after declaring their maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia.
In Yemen’s capital Sana’a, Houthi supporters celebrated the freeing of 210 prisoners held in areas that fell to the group and had spent up to eight years in jail.

articles.title: A funny limp turns into giant steps against cancer
articles.summary: SYDNEY — At first, Kelly Hennessy thought her daughter Mileah was just trying to mimic her beloved older cousin with her ”weird, long-legged skip”. Mileah was an energetic, advanced…

blocks.text: SYDNEY — At first, Kelly Hennessy thought her daughter Mileah was just trying to mimic her beloved older cousin with her ”weird, long-legged skip”.
Mileah was an energetic, advanced little girl who loved being outdoors and spending time with her close-knit family, including her cousin who had been performing a similarly unusual skip.
When daycare reported the two-and-a-half-year-old was dragging one side after a minor fall, she thought it might be a sprain, so she brought her doctor’s appointment forward.
But the Sydney mother never imagined the cause was an aggressive bone cancer that would leave her little girl amputated above the knee.
An X-ray revealed a large dark mass around Mileah’s left knee and femur.
A pediatrician told Ms Hennessy it appeared to be either an infection or a tumor.
”I’ve never had a feeling like it,” Ms Hennessy tells AAP.
”You know how you get that sick feeling or a nervous feeling? It’s like that, is the best way I can explain it. It was accompanied with complete sadness and fear.”
Mileah and Ms Hennessy spent a week in hospital while doctors carried out investigations, with the first biopsy coming back inconclusive.

After about two weeks waiting for a second biopsy, they were told Mileah had osteosarcoma, a rare and aggressive bone cancer.Amputation had already been raised as a possibility because of Mileah’s young age and the position of the tumor.
”I couldn’t even process the X-ray, let alone everything else that was still coming to me,” Ms Hennessy said.
Within days, Mileah had a central line inserted and began chemotherapy.

The treatment was brutal, with fevers, vomiting, mucositis and repeated hospitalizations for infections. Her chemotherapy regime included doxorubicin, known as the ”red devil” because of its toxicity.
”She got very sick from her chemotherapy,” Ms Hennessy says.
After two cycles of chemotherapy, Mileah traveled with her orthopedic surgeon to Melbourne for surgery.
She underwent a Van Ness rotationplasty, an unusual limb-salvage procedure in which part of the leg is removed and the foot rotated 180 degrees and attached to the thigh.
Her heel then functions as a knee joint inside a prosthetic leg.
But for Ms Hennessy, the worst part was returning to Sydney and watching her daughter deteriorate as chemotherapy continued.”That was the hardest,” she says.
”That was when all the infections came. That was when she was on a lot of different drips for medication and for pain tolerance.”The experience consumed the family’s life.
Ms Hennessy stopped working and faced financial pressures, while friendships changed and her relationship broke down, as she focused on getting Mileah through the treatment.
”Life still goes on,” she reflects.
”You’ve got your financial issues because you’re not working. There’s all these little things that still are going on around the outside but your focus is just on making sure your kid gets better.”
Mileah was so young when she became sick, that Ms Hennessy tried to make the experience simple.
”You’ve got a leg that’s very sick, we need to get it better, we’ve got to give you special medicine but then we’re going to give you a new leg,” she told her.
Now approaching her fifth birthday, Mileah has finished treatment and is thriving.
She is back at preschool, preparing to start kindergarten next year, and is already on her third prosthetic leg as she grows.
She can walk almost normally and is working on running and riding a bike.
”A lot of the time, when her pants are on, you can’t even tell she’s an amputee,” Ms Hennessy says.
Her latest lung scans, taken as part of her regular cancer monitoring, were also clear.

Ms Hennessy hopes Mileah will remember as little as possible of the worst parts of her treatment. Instead, her daughter is more interested in choosing colourful patterns for her prosthetic, including mermaids, Barbie and Disney characters.
Mileah’s young age may also mean she will never have to remember what it was like not to have a prosthetic leg.

In a boost for other young Aussies facing their own fight against the Big C, the government on Friday announced it was committing $5 million to support Australian participation in the LifeArc Worldwide CAR-T Pathfinder Trial and Paediatric Cell Therapy Accelerator.
CAR-T is a type of immunotherapy used in laboratories to re-engineer a patient’s white blood cells so they can destroy cancer cells.
“It will help bring world-class international CAR-T clinical trials closer to home for Australian children and young people with cancer,” Health Minister Mark Butler said in a statement.
The funding is part of its $300 million investment in the Australian Cancer Research Program announced earlier in 2026.
Professor Brendan Murphy, the chair of Children’s Cancer CoLab that promotes a collaborative approach to funding research to fight the disease, welcomed the announcement.
The CoLab says 1000 Aussie kids are diagnosed with cancer every year, three children die from the disease every week, and 80% of those who survive have long-term effects from their treatment.
“It is very encouraging to see the Australian government investing in new treatment options for children and young people with cancer,” Prof Murphy said.
Mileah’s family is now sharing her story to boost the corporate sector’s involvement in the fight against cancer.
2025 Dare to Cure events in Sydney and Melbourne raised $1.7 million, funding the equivalent of 16 senior researchers.

The CEO Dare to Cure event, run by the Children’s Cancer Institute, challenges business leaders and senior executives to step outside of their comfort zones while raising money for childhood cancer research.
Chris Dutton, who is founder of CEO Magazine and an ambassador for CEO Dare to Cure, said the event gives business leaders a chance to make a difference.
”CEO Dare to Cure is the number one event that any CEO or leader should seriously consider doing,” he says.
”It’s a chance to come together to help children with cancer. There’s nothing better really.”
For Ms Hennessy, the challenge offers more than an opportunity to raise vital funds.
Children facing cancer are pushed far outside their comfort zones every day, through scans, chemotherapy, surgeries and hospital stays.
She believes asking people who have been fortunate enough not to experience that reality to challenge themselves, even briefly, can help foster empathy as well as raise money.
”It makes an incredible difference because these kids are getting put out of their comfort zone every single day, 24-7,” Ms Hennessy said.

”To have such an amazing campaign where you can have a laugh and raise money at the same time and also watch people being put out of their comfort zone in a safe and welcome environment, I think makes a huge difference.” /dl

articles.title: France: Attack ruled out in train derailment
articles.summary: More than 40 were injured when a train derailed between Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, on Friday evening. Investigators say there is "no indication" the incident was deliberate.

image.caption: An 18-year-old woman was seriously hurt in the accidentImage: Guillaume Saligot/AFP

blocks.text: A train derailed on Friday evening between the cities of Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, authorities said.

The public prosecutor of Rouen, Sebastian Gallois, said Saturday evening that there was "no indication of a malicious act carried out with the deliberate intention of derailing the train, and certainly not of an attack," according to reports in the French media.
Gallois' remarks came after some politicians had suggested earlier on Saturday that the incident might have been the result of sabotage or other criminal activity.

At least 44 people were injured in the accident, which occurred near the municipalities of Cleon and Tourville-la-Riviere at around 7:30 p.m. local time (18:30 UTC), the Seine-Maritime prefect said in a statement.
One of ​the injured, a young woman, was in a critical state and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen, the local authority added. Her condition has reportedly improved in the hours since.
The train was carrying around 180 passengers when it derailed, national rail company SNCF and the prefect said.
What else do we know about the train derailment?
French Transport Minister Tabarot said 140 firefighters were at the scene.
Local authorities had urged the public to avoid the area.
The French rail network operator SNCF Reseau said traffic on the line had been suspended.
"The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions," SNCF Reseau said.
​A police spokesperson had said the train derailed after hitting an unidentified object.
A piece of rail that might have been involved has been found on the track, according to police reports.

blocks.caption: Five carriages derailed and one overturnedImage: Guillaume Saligot/AFP

articles.title: 2 men detained after altercation on Doha-bound flight from Melbourne
articles.summary: MELBOURNE — Two men have been restrained on a flight from Melbourne to Doha after being involved in a physical altercation. Qatar Airways, which operated the flight, confirmed the men were…

blocks.text: MELBOURNE — Two men have been restrained on a flight from Melbourne to Doha after being involved in a physical altercation.
Qatar Airways, which operated the flight, confirmed the men were handed over to local authorities on arrival.
“We can confirm that two male passengers were involved in a physical altercation on board flight VA7 from Melbourne to Doha on Friday,” the airline said in a statement.
“Both passengers were restrained and, upon arrival in Doha, were handed over to local authorities.”
Media reports said the men made violent threats towards passengers and crew, including claiming they had a gun.
A passenger on the plane told Nine newspapers the men were repeatedly getting in and out of their seats and later began arguing and fighting.
“The men would not comply with instructions from the crew, and ultimately had to be restrained,” the woman said.
In its statement Qatar Airways said “the safety and wellbeing of our crew and passengers remain our highest priority”. /dl

articles.title: China threatens to cancel summit if US approves new arms sales to Taiwan
articles.summary: China has told the United States that it intends to cancel a planned meeting between their leaders later this month if Washington approves any new arms sales to Taiwan by then, multiple sources…

blocks.text: China has told the United States that it intends to cancel a planned meeting between their leaders later this month if Washington approves any new arms sales to Taiwan by then, multiple sources familiar with bilateral ties said Saturday.

U.S. President Donald Trump, apparently eager to showcase some diplomatic achievements ahead of November’s midterm congressional elections, places great importance on holding the summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
While preparing for Xi’s upcoming trip, China has restated its position that the Taiwan issue is a “red line” in bilateral relations, according to the sources.
China claims the self-governing democratic island as part of its territory, to be reunited by force if necessary.
When Xi met Trump in Beijing in mid-May, he told the U.S. president that Taiwan is the “most important issue” in the countries’ ties, warning of a potential conflict if it is mishandled.

At the time, Trump said in a TV interview that arms sales to Taiwan could be “a very good negotiating chip” in his dealings with China, which raised doubts about Washington’s longtime security commitments to its allies in Asia.
China’s increased military activities in and around the Taiwan Strait have raised fears of a potential invasion and a broader regional conflict involving the United States and its allies.

Under the Taiwan Relations Act, enacted by the U.S. Congress after Washington severed diplomatic ties with Taipei in favor of Beijing in 1979, the United States supplies Taiwan with arms to help it maintain a sufficient self-defense capability.
In December last year, the Trump administration announced an $11 billion package of arms sales to Taiwan, the largest ever, which triggered an angry reaction from China.

Trump has said he will host Xi and his wife at the White House on Sept. 24 and organize a state dinner in their honor. The Chinese government has not made an official announcement regarding Xi’s visit to the United States.
The U.S. war against Iran could also be one of the major agenda items at the meeting, since China is Tehran’s key economic partner.
As the war Trump started with Israel in late February drags on with no immediate end in sight, his administration has pressured China not to do business with Iran.
But one of the sources said, “China has shown a cooperative stance and is not hindering dialogue with the United States.”

The Treasury and Commerce departments have been leading Washington’s negotiations with Beijing, and many key economic issues are expected to be discussed by the two presidents, including an envisioned deal to reduce tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from each side.
A framework for dialogue on the safety of artificial intelligence is also likely to top the agenda, according to the sources. /dl

articles.title: They lost their jobs after posting about Charlie Kirk, but some have no regrets
articles.summary: Some people fired in the wake of Kirk's assassination have won big settlements from employers, others have had to start over from scratch.

blocks.text: In September 2025, Gerald Bourguet felt he was finally living his dream life: he and his wife had bought a house with a pool, they had just welcomed a baby boy, and he was writing about professional men's basketball as his full-time job.

But all of that changed after he made a series of online posts critical of the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk hours after he was fatally shot on 10 September, while speaking on the campus of Utah Valley University.

In the posts, Bourguet described Kirk as an "evil man" and suggested he had dedicated his life to hateful causes. He also criticised Kirk's supporters saying they had not been vocal about school shootings.
"I had seen the way that people were talking about this person - kind of eulogising him and lionising him and it bothered me based on a lot of the things that he had said," Bourguet told the BBC.

Kirk, who founded Christian youth organisation Turning Point USA, was a divisive figure in US politics. For many on the political right, he was charismatic and had a unique skill in making conservative ideas appeal to young people. But for his opponents, his comments on a large swathe of issues from race to immigration, gun control and gender identity were deeply offensive.

Screenshots of Bourguet's critical posts went viral quickly. He was fired from his job, his address was exposed online, and he began receiving threatening text messages, he said. Concerned for their safety, the family fled the state with their four-month-old. They returned months later to sell the house and permanently relocated.
A year later, he says he doesn't regret what he said, but acknowledged: "My life will never be the same after this".
"At age 35, I am having to start over in a lot of respects… I wouldn't wish this on my worst enemy," Bourguet said from his new location, which the BBC agreed to not disclose.
PHNX Sports, Bourguet's former employer, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Bourguet was one of hundreds fired or disciplined over critical comments of Kirk after his death. While some of those who have lost their jobs have been reinstated or received restitution - sometimes in the millions - others like Bourguet have had to rebuild from scratch.
In the aftermath of Kirk's assassination, most people kept their feelings to themselves, or shared them with close friends.

But on polarised social media, people rushed to laude, or denounce, the controversial activist. Some called the criticisms, posted hours after his death, tasteless. But others called for swift action, arguing they were callous, mocking, and could even incite further violence.
Laura Loomer, an influential right-wing commentator with nearly 2 million followers on X, warned Kirk's critics to "prepare to have your whole future professional aspirations ruined".
The push for punishment also came from the highest levels of US government.
"When you see someone celebrating Charlie's murder, call them out," Vice-President JD Vance said days after the assassination. "And hell, call their employer," he added.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told the BBC: "Anyone who engages in or endorses political violence or assassination culture must be condemned in the harshest terms possible."

Critics on the left said there was a difference between criticism of Kirk and celebrating his death. Some accused these conservative leaders of hypocrisy, as many had previously bemoaned the rise of "cancel culture" – where people who voice controversial opinions face severe consequences at work and socially.

"Cancel culture can be good, it's bad when it's applied in the wrong ways," Jordan Pace, a Republican member of the South Carolina House of Representatives, told the BBC. "If you are someone who celebrates political assassinations and the murder of an innocent man with two young children in a way that many people did, then yeah, that's an appropriate way for society to function, to shame those people."

Pace had previously called for defunding universities in his state if they didn't take actions against employees who made comments about Kirk. One of his posts was re-shared by US President Donald Trump.

Across the nation, some employers – private and public – acted swiftly to the pressure campaign. Reliable figures on the number of people fired or disciplined are hard to come by, but a Reuters tally last November found more than 600 instances. It is likely an under-count because not all cases received national or local press attention.

The specific actions that led to these disciplinary decisions run the gamut. In Tennessee, anthropology professor Tamar Shirinian was suspended and later fired for a Facebook comment saying "the world is better off" without Kirk.

A Delta Air Lines flight attendant was fired after posting "good riddance" in response to Kirk's killing. Office Depot supply store fired an employee for refusing to serve a customer who had wanted to print flyers for a Kirk vigil. Delta Air Lines declined to comment. Office Depot did not respond to a request for comment.

Others were disciplined even if they did not make any direct comments about Kirk or his death. Darren Michael, a theatre professor in Tennessee, was fired after he posted a screenshot of a news article from 2023, that covered Kirk's controversial speech on gun control. In the article, Kirk is quoted saying protecting citizens' rights to own guns was worth it even if it led to some gun deaths every year.
Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission fired biologist Brittney Brown after she reposted a meme that also satirised Kirk's position on gun violence in light of his own shooting.
"I was absolutely gutted," Brown said about her firing to the BBC. "It was like the entire world just completely flipped on its head in a moment."

In the year since Kirk's killing, dozens of lawsuits have been filed across the country by people fired for their comments about the activist, arguing their terminations violated their rights to free speech. The suits have led to substantial pay outs in some cases.
Brown agreed to a $485,000 (£355,000) financial settlement – about 12 times Brown's annual salary.
Darren Michael was reinstated by the Austin Peay State University and in January, the school agreed to pay him $500,000 to settle legal claims. The school did not respond to a request for comment.

In the largest settlement reviewed by the BBC, the University of Tennessee agreed to pay $1.9m to resolve a lawsuit brought by anthropologist Tamar Shirinian, over her "better off" comment. As part of the settlement, she will not be reinstated and has agreed to not reapply for future positions at the school.

Recently, an arbitrator ordered The Washington Post to rehire, with back pay, opinion journalist Karen Attiah, who was fired for her online posts that said in part she was not going to engage in "performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence".
Several other lawsuits remain pending, the BBC found.
Most of the legal actions have been pursued by employees of government institutions, or unionised workers, who have some free-speech protections.
But in the US, most private sector employees work under "at-will" contracts, which means they can be can be fired without reason.
Even those who have scored some victories don't see it as a win.
"All I wanted was my job back," biologist Brown said. "How much taxpayer money did they waste on this when I barely made $40,000 a year? So no, it does not feel like justice."
Shirinian told the BBC she too had wanted to return to her job but felt a legal case could be a lengthy affair.

"I took a settlement because this allows me to move on with my life," she told the BBC. "The one small regret that I have is that I will not see my day in court and justice will not be served in that way. But I think that the number of the settlement actually speaks to that anyway."
The University of Tennessee and Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

As an at-will employee at a private company, Bourguet is unlikely to prevail in a lawsuit challenging his dismissal. A year on, he said he has struggled to find work. The new state he lives in has a professional basketball team, but he believes the ordeal has made him unemployable in the small world of sports writers. Instead, he's started his own podcast, although he doubts he can earn enough through it to pay the bills.
"I have accepted that that life is over and that I need to start a new one." Leaving the country is now on the table, he said.
Despite the huge personal and professional costs, those who spoke to the BBC said after months of reflection, they did not regret their actions.
"I have a right to say what I want to say," Brown said. "They are the ones who should have the regrets, not me," she said referring to her former employer.
Shirinian apologised to the university days after her suspension. She told the BBC her comment was "an emotional outburst" that was not intended to be public and that she regretted the tone used.
"I don't regret the sentiment, however" she said, adding "the sentiment was that I am not sad. And I refuse to be made to feel like I have to be sad that someone who was so hateful was killed".
Bourguet also said he does not regret his comments although he has conflicting thoughts about its consequences.
"I don't regret that line of thinking because I think it's important to push back on things that are steeped in hatred," he said, referring to Kirk's political message.
"I don't regret what I said. I don't regret the way that I said it. I do regret the ripple effects that came from it and the way that they impacted me, my career, my family, and my son."

articles.title: Russians seek answers over hundreds missing after Ukraine's 2024 incursion
articles.summary: Officials say more than 300 Russians remain missing after the 2024 Kursk offensive, but no-one really knows the true figure.

blocks.text: "The state channels were convincing viewers that 'everything is under control: two or three days, and it'll be just as it was before'," she recalls.

She still fails to understand why Russian authorities could not stop Ukrainian soldiers storming two border checkpoints in August 2024, taking around 40 prisoners and bombing a convoy carrying Russian soldiers.
Within six days they had overrun more than 777 sq km (300 sq miles) of Russian territory, as Ukraine's military sought to divert Russian forces away from their front-line offensive.
For most of the next eight months, mobile and internet links were down.
Russia's foreign ministry repeatedly accused Ukraine of war crimes against civilians: allegations rejected in Kyiv as completely unfounded.

Nearly 200 Russians sent a letter to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, Russia's President Vladimir Putin and the United Nations, asking them to organise a humanitarian corridor to evacuate civilians.
It never happened and, by late autumn, battles raged as Russian forces sought to retake the territory.
Lyubov and others who had lost contact with their loved ones began to form groups.

One resident, whose family friends had also stayed behind, began compiling a list of people she saw on videos published by the Ukrainian military and journalists. Then she began detailing those believed to have died and where they were buried.
"At first, in a panic, you try to do something – anything – to find some sort of information," she said. "Taking action brings a certain sense of relief, and that's how you can cope with the stress."
Soon about 1,000 names were on the list.
Lyubov wrote to the Red Cross and Kursk interior ministry appealing for help, but had no response.

Early in 2025, Russia's human rights commissioner published a list of 517 Kursk residents reported missing. The list mixed up names of the missing with those who were searching for them, and the families said it was like a "slap in the face".
"Publishing something like this is the height of incompetence and a lack of basic respect for people," said one young woman whose parents had gone missing, in a video shared online.
Heavy fighting had been reported in late 2024 in the village of Darino, where Lyubov and mother were from, and authorities said that 90% of it had been destroyed.
The Russian military regained control of the village and then began evacuating those who had survived, and the bodies of those who had not.

One of the evacuees got in touch with Lyubov, telling her she had lived with her mother for the past few weeks. Her mum had passed away, she explained, following a head injury in circumstances that remain unclear.
A few other elderly people had also died, she said, unable to cope with wartime conditions.
Lyubov waited in vain for her mother's body to be brought out, while other families had no idea if their relatives were alive or dead.
People complained no-one was searching for their loved ones and that there was no single list of those missing.
Lyubov heard that the bodies of neighbours who died alongside her mother had been taken away from Darino in April, but her mother's body was still missing.
She tried and failed to get an answer from the authorities: "They wouldn't listen, and everyone just kept saying that it was dangerous there, and no-one was going to deal with it right now."
The head of one local village council, Yuri Tkachev, was among volunteers who went to retrieve the bodies of civilians, from the streets or from nearby fields.
"It's hard for people to know – or rather not to know – what has happened to their loved ones, whether they're being held captive or have died, and where they died," he said.
Body bags and fuel for vans taking part in the evacuations were paid for either by the volunteers themselves or with donations, but not by authorities.
Although regional officials met the group searching for the missing several times in the second half of 2025, relatives complained it made little difference.
Lyubov was still searching for her mother's body, until she visited the mortuary last October during a trip to the regional capital Kursk.
"I just asked: 'A woman born in 1949 from the village of Darino – are there any unidentified bodies?'"
The official turned his laptop screen towards her and immediately she recognised her deceased mother in a photograph from April 2025.
She was lying on her side in the street, her knees bent. Lyubov tried not to look too closely. She recognised her mum's face and an old jumper, which she wore while she worked.
She had provided a DNA sample in January but was told it had been lost, so her mother's body had been in the mortuary unidentified for several months.
She had wanted to bury her mother in their home village, but for now that is impossible, so she has been cremated and her ashes sit in Lyubov's apartment in Belgorod, about 100 miles away.
She is bitter that the government failed to stop the incursion, that it did not evacuate residents when it could, and that it persuaded them the situation was not serious.
Asked by the BBC to comment on this story, there was no response from the Kursk governor, Russia's human rights commissioner or the Russian Red Cross.
The command of Ukraine's Territorial Defence Forces and Ukraine's human rights commissioner of Ukraine said all the civilians they had evacuated from Kursk region had been handed over to Russia.
Lyubov thinks back to when she used to ride her bike across the border into Ukraine to shop for sausages, yarn and ice cream.
"We went to see them, and they came to see us. And now not one of these villages exists any more."

articles.title: New statues added to controversial Prime Minister's Path in Wilmot, Ont.
articles.summary: Four statues of former Canadian leaders were added to the Prime Minister's Path project in Wilmot, Ont., on Saturday. Not everyone was pleased.

image.caption: Statues of Sir John Abbott, Sir John Thompson, Sir Mackenzie Bowell and Sir Charles Tupper were unveiled at a park in Baden, Ont. on Sep. 12, 2026. Sculptor Nathan Scott calls these prime ministers "the unfortunate four." (John Dalusong/CBC)

blocks.text: Kitchener-Waterloo·New
Four statues of former Canadian leaders were added to the Prime Minister's Path project in Wilmot, Ont., on Saturday. Not everyone was pleased.
Protesters decried the project as insensitive and poorly conceived

The contested project, now run by Createscape Waterloo Region, held an afternoon unveiling with the leadership of Wilmot Township at a municipal park by Castle Kilbride in Baden, a small community west of Kitchener.
"Obviously we're very happy that [the project] has found its footing once again," Don Bourgeois, chair of the board and president of Createscape Waterloo Region, told CBC News.

"Our purpose is to help create public art that has that emotional attachment, but also gets people... to have discussion about the future of Canada, the history of Canada, of art and what art is about."

The four new statues depict Sir John Abbott, Sir John Thompson, Sir Mackenzie Bowell and Sir Charles Tupper. They join statues of Sir John A. Macdonald, Kim Campbell, Sir Robert Borden, William Lyon Mackenzie King and Lester B. Pearson.
Around a dozen protesters attended, decrying the project as insensitive and poorly conceived.

items: Wilmot Township moves forward with Prime Ministers Path project

blocks.text: Project's rocky path
The Prime Ministers Path project was first proposed in 2013. The project aimed to honour former Canadian leaders with 22 bronze statues placed in a park to celebrate Canada's 150th birthday.

The project faced controversy from the beginning, however, with Kitchener councillors rejecting the idea of having the statues at Victoria Park in 2014 and Waterloo's Wilfrid Laurier University backing out of the agreement to put the statues at the school in 2016.
The statues would later find a home at Castle Kilbride in the village of Baden that same year.

By 2020, the statue of Sir John A. Macdonald was put in storage after a public call for it to be removed for his role in the residential school system. The project was then cancelled by the township's council in 2021, leading to the removal of the statues.

Last April, Wilmot council voted to proceed with the project. The vote involved giving Createscape Waterloo Region custody of the nine statues it owns, as well as entering into an agreement with the group to display the statues in municipal parkland for the next 20 years.

items: Work underway to re-install Prime Ministers Path in Wilmot Township
Createscape shares its plans for Prime Ministers Path in Wilmot

blocks.text: The project now includes an added educational component, with the Six Nations of the Grand River playing an important role, Bourgeois said.

"The Six Nations [of the Grand River] will be involved in making sure that our website, which will include historical educational materials, reflects the issues that resulted from decisions of the prime ministers over the last century and a half," he said.
But the addition of an educational component is not enough, said Benny Skinner, who uses they/them pronouns, and led Saturday's protest.

"If you actually take the time to learn about the prime ministers, the history of who they are and what they've done, and you learn proper authentic history that includes Indigenous peoples history, what you'll realize is that this is an extremely insensitive and poorly thought-out project," they said.
Indigenous people included 'from the beginning'
The project has been criticized as insensitive to Indigenous people since its inception.

When Wilfrid Laurier University declined to host the statues in 2016, opponents of the project said there had been insufficient consultation and celebrating the country's past prime ministers would be culturally insensitive given the university is built on land that traditionally belonged to Indigenous people.

items: Wilmot's Prime Ministers Path will continue, but now as a community-led project

blocks.text: Bourgeois insists that Indigenous perspectives have been taken into account.

"They were included in a sense right from the beginning, that issue with respect to how Canada, through the prime ministers' leadership, have dealt with First Nations was part of the discussion," Bourgeois explained.
"But clearly, we failed to communicate that properly. We failed to do it in a fashion that was sufficiently collaborative."
That has changed, he said: "Today, thankfully, we're down on a different path."
But Skinner, who was co-lead for the consultancy the last time there was a community engagement for the project, said concerns raised during consultations were not heeded.
"They're looking for an Indigenous person to check off that it's fine so that they can continue to do this project the way that it is," Skinner said.
"None of the Indigenous people I have spoken to, in the hundreds, about this project, want this project on these lands."

Sculptor Nathan Scott believes it is important to highlight all aspects of Canadian history. He sculpted the four newest statues in 2019, referring to them as "the unfortunate four" for what he sees as their limited achievements in office.
"I'm a proud Canadian. I love our history," he said. "It wasn't always done perfectly. It's the good, bad and sometimes there's ugliness to it, but it's who we are."
"And if we don't have history, if we try to erase it, who are we? Who are we at all?"
13 statues to go

Future changes to the project could yet win over opponents, Skinner said. They proposed changing its name, moving it to a hidden area so people don't have to see it and better collaboration with Indigenous people.

For his part, Bourgeois said the educational aspect of the project will remain important. This includes hosting educational symposia where the history and work of each prime minister will be discussed.
For now, the long-term goal remains completing the remaining 13 statues, he said.
Though Canada has had 24 prime ministers, Justin Trudeau and Mark Carney won't be included in the current project — to avoid it becoming "a little bit too political," Bourgeois said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
John Dalusong is a journalist for CBC Kitchener-Waterloo. Have a story? Reach him at john.dalusong@cbc.ca.
With files from Joe Pavia, Carmen Groleau and Kate Bueckert

articles.title: Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI slowdown
articles.summary: Elon Musk and OpenAI chief Sam Altman say they agree with Amodei's view that safety measures need time to catch up to AI's rapid development, after a recent hacking incident by AI agents.

image.caption: Amodei founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela in 2021 [FILE: 2025]Image: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP

blocks.text: The CEO of artificial intelligence (AI) safety and research company Anthropic, Dario Amodei, has called on AI firms to slow the technology's development.
His remarks on Saturday come amid mounting concerns over the risk of "superintelligent" computer software systems.

In a blog post, Amodei said he was concerned that a so-called swarm of autonomous software systems, or AI agents, could be capable of taking over the "entire internet" within six to 12 months, potentially causing billions of dollars' worth of damage.
"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," Amodei wrote.

Amodei's comments come in the wake of AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who joined Anthropic from rival firm OpenAI, leaving the sector in protest at the US companies "gambling with our lives" in the race to come up with AI models that are capable of self-improvement.
Amodei calls for industry-wide action, Musk and Altman agree
The Anthropic chief called for a coordinated, industry-wide pause, but said he would not wait for his firm's rivals to act.
As a first step, he said he would permanently allow independent observers into Anthropic to assess the safety of its models during the training phase.
Sam Atmant, the chief of ChatGPT developer and Anthropic rival, OpenAI, as well as Elon Musk, who owns xAI, said they agreed with Amodei's assessment.
"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," Sam Altman wrote on X, adding that OpenAI "will do the same."
