Musk, for his part, said "Dario is right" in a post on the platform he bought in 2022.

blocks.caption: Musk (left) founded OpenAI with Altman, but the pair are now rivalsImage: La Nacion/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Why are industry leaders calling for AI development to be slowed?
In early June, Anthropic had called for AI development to be slowed or suspended amid safety concerns over AI agents.
More than 1,000 employees at AI companies, including Amodei, called on the US government to help slow the pace of development of automated AI.

Then in July, OpenAI revealed that during testing, AI agents had independently broken out of a secured environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site used to store and develop code, as it tried to find answers to a task it had been assigned.
The AI models had exploited software vulnerabilities and coordinated among themselves during the incident, Amodei explained.

"A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand," he said in his blog.
Amodei said he was concerned that an AI swarm with more capabilities would have caused "catastrophic damage."
"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way," he said.
America's AI boom: Who pays the price?

articles.title: DR Congo’s worst Ebola epidemic ever passes 7,000 cases
articles.summary: KINSHASA, DR Congo – More than 7,000 Ebola cases have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s worst outbreak of the deadly disease ever, according to figures released Saturday…

blocks.text: KINSHASA, DR Congo – More than 7,000 Ebola cases have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s worst outbreak of the deadly disease ever, according to figures released Saturday by Congolese authorities.
But the government also suggested that the spread of the disease may already have peaked, despite the virus having been confirmed in a seventh province earlier this week.
The DRC officially detected the latest outbreak in mid-May, with nearly 3,400 people killed in its 17th epidemic of the highly infectious virus.

It began in the northeastern Ituri province before spreading to conflict-plagued, remote eastern and northern regions where armed groups have roamed for decades, the presence of the state is weak and health infrastructure is lacking.
The disease was confirmed in South-Ubangi, which borders the Central African Republic and Congo-Brazzaville, earlier this week.
According to the latest figures from the Congolese authorities, 7,022 cases have been recorded since the beginning of the epidemic. Of that number, 3,398 people have died and 1,671 have recovered.
“The peak was reached at the beginning of the third week of August,” Congolese government spokesman Patrick Muyaya wrote on X on Saturday.
“All the indicators show a decrease in the number of cases,” he added, specifying that “10 of the 61 health zones” affected by the epidemic have not recorded any new cases “for at least 21 days”.
Most of the recorded cases are in Ituri, where Ebola has been detected in schools in the days after the post-summer holiday return to classes, causing alarm among parents and health workers.

“We are very worried because we don’t know which child comes from which family or what the health status of the members of that family is,” Angele Magani, the mother of a student in Bunia, Ituri’s provincial capital, told AFP.
“We are so scared, even though the school authorities reassure us about the health measures that have been put in place,” she added.
Bunia school official Roger Mungimbo said “there is a mandatory hand-washing system with soap, and we have also done everything possible to have a maximum of 30 pupils per classroom.”
“We regularly make the children aware that they must not touch each other” and wash their hands regularly, he added.

Ebola, which has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the last 50 years, is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and can cause severe internal and external bleeding and organ failure.
The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Several treatments and vaccines are being tested.

blocks.text: Western Australian police have said a man had been shot at a residence on Owen Place in Hamilton Hill, around 4.35am this morning.
In a statement, police and St John WA responded and provided emergency first aid to the victim.

double quotation markThe man has been conveyed by St John WA to hospital with serious injuries. Police believe two males, dressed in all black clothing, were involved in the shooting. Significant police resources have been deployed and are conducting a thorough search of the area. Members of the public are asked to stay away from the area. Those in the area are advised to lock their doors and windows and remain inside.
Police said anyone who sights the two males or sees any suspicious behaviour is urged not to approach the men, but to call police via Triple Zero immediately.
We will update when we have more information.
Bowen: Conflict in Middle East will impact fuel prices in Australia
We’ll be hearing from federal politicians later this morning but before we do, a quick update on one of the big challenges to the global economy: fuel security.

Conflict in the Middle East is again placing pressure on the supply of crucial oil exports. On Friday, Saudi authorities said drones launched from Iraq led to a temporary closure of a crucial oil export route used to bypass the lockdown of the strait of Hormuz.

Nearly 50,000 people have also fled a sudden advance by Houthi forces in western Yemen, with entire villages emptied and families trapped near frontline fighting with depleting food supplies, according to aid workers.

On Saturday, the energy minister, Chris Bowen, sought to reassure Australians about the nation’s supply reserves. He said Australia had 41 days worth of petrol in strategic reserve and 42 days worth of diesel:

double quotation markThe situation is getting worse in the Middle East. The dispute involving Saudi Arabia and the Houthis and the ongoing war in Iran is doing nothing to improve the fuel supply around the world and is pushing up prices of oil. We’re seeing that in the markets even overnight, and that will inevitably also flow through to Australia. However, the Australian government will remain firmly focused on ensuring our fuel security, just as we have for the last more than six months since this crisis began.

articles.title: Fire at nursing home in Chile kills 16
articles.summary: SANTIAGO, Chile – A fire at a nursing home in Chile that had previously violated regulations has killed 16 elderly residents and left others hospitalized, authorities said Saturday. The blaze…

blocks.text: SANTIAGO, Chile – A fire at a nursing home in Chile that had previously violated regulations has killed 16 elderly residents and left others hospitalized, authorities said Saturday.
The blaze began on Friday night at the single-story care home in the Araucania region, 640 kilometers (400 miles) south of the capital Santiago, and was extinguished early Saturday.
Images shared on social media showed massive flames rising above the building in the darkness, while a fire truck sprayed water to tackle the flames.
“We express our sorrow and dismay at the deaths of 16 elderly people in this tragedy,” authorities in the municipality of Pitrufquen said in a statement.
A total of 26 elderly residents were in the nursing home. Ten of them survived and were taken to the local hospital, the statement said.
On Saturday, firefighters were still clearing debris and removing collapsed corrugated metal roofing. Police cordoned off the area for safety.

“It is a situation that fills our souls with great sorrow and pain. We have been… providing support to the families,” said local mayor Jacqueline Romero, who said that municipal health and public safety teams, firefighters and police were deployed.
The cause of the fire remained unclear.

“We are currently carrying out investigative procedures, including examining the scene and conducting inquiries, to determine the origin and cause of the fire, as well as to rule out third-party involvement,” Jorge Granada, the prosecutor assigned to the case, told local media.
The owners of the private care home were summoned to give statements.
An official at the regional health secretariat said there had been previous operational problems at the care home.
“It was an unregulated facility; it had faced administrative proceedings and fines since 2019, and was a repeat offender,” the official, Jose Bravo, said.

“In February, the municipality had sent a letter specifically calling for an inspection because the facility was not in compliance with regulations — it was subject to sanitary enforcement proceedings,” Romero told local networks.

On his X account, Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast demanded that the truth be uncovered and “necessary corrections be made to do everything possible to prevent a tragedy like this from happening again.”
He said he had ordered “urgent measures” to review conditions at nursing homes across the country.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte lawyers’ bid to have charges refiled opposed
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution and lawyers of the victims of the drug war of then President Rodrigo Duterte objected to a motion by his lawyers before the International Criminal Court (ICC)…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution and lawyers of the victims of the drug war of then President Rodrigo Duterte objected to a motion by his lawyers before the International Criminal Court (ICC) seeking to have the charges against him refiled, saying they cannot revisit that matter at the trial stage.
In a filing on Aug. 31, Duterte’s lawyers asked Trial Chamber (TC) III to have the charges “properly inform…the accused of the case he needs to meet.”

The defense said it wants the scope of the charges defined in terms of how many counts they constitute. It also seeks an “exhaustive list of underpinning acts” to represent the entirety of the charges. The former president faces three counts of crimes of humanity of murder.

Duterte’s lawyers were referring to the prosecution’s document containing the charges, which accused Duterte of being criminally responsible for the killing of 76 individuals in 49 incidents during the drug war.
Reopening the charges?

In separate filings dated Sept. 10, the prosecution and the common legal representative of victims (CLRVs) opposed the defense’ motion, saying that questions on the “adequacy” posed by the defense were already determined and affirmed by Pre-Trial Chamber (PTC) I.

“To the contrary, the three counts each have a clear temporal, geographical and material scope, and this is consistent with the requirements of article 74(2) of the [Rome] Statute,” the prosecution said in its 10-page response, referring to the 2002 treaty which established the court.
It added “The…mere disagreement [of the defense] with the analysis of the [PTC] is insufficient to show any defect.”
The CLRVs sought the outright rejection of the motion for being “procedurally misconceived.”
They said the defense cannot just ask TC III to reopen the issue “under the guise of a motion concerning the ‘form’ of the charges.”

“[S]hould the Chamber consider that the defence genuinely seeks to challenge defects in the [document containing the charges], such objections belong to the pre-confirmation stage and cannot now be raised before the trial chamber,” they said in a 10-page response.
They said the defense merely reiterated its disagreement with PTC’s earlier decision and “advance[d] no argument” to warrant a reversal.
Another defense motion
The trial of Duterte, who is detained in The Hague, is scheduled to begin on Nov. 30 and is seen to continue until next year.
A third status conference will be held on Sept. 16 to discuss the prosecution’s list of witnesses and evidence, the number of hours it needs to present its case and its disclosure of evidence.

The prosecution last week also opposed a proposal by the defense to authenticate its evidence from open source and user-generated materials, saying this step is “unnecessary and burdensome” and even risks delaying the start of the trial.

It said the prosecution should have the discretion to determine whether a certain piece of evidence from open source or user-generated materials should be accompanied by a certification from an expert.

It cited as an example information from open sources that are credible sources—such as the United Nations, nongovernment organizations and government websites—and should not require authentication by experts. /cb

articles.title: Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters
articles.summary: Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen were adopted from orphanages in Mumbai in the 1980s and grew up in the Netherlands.

blocks.text: Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.
Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each other in the Netherlands, have now discovered they are biological sisters.
Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen, born in the early 1980s, were adopted from two different orphanages in the western Indian city of Mumbai within months of their birth.
When they first met in their early teens at an event hosted by the adoption agency their parents had used, they were struck by the uncanny similarities in their appearance and mannerisms.
Meena, now 43, remembers the day clearly.
"All the adopted children were brought together to hang out and bond and have dinner."
Both Meena and Minal were with friends who noticed how similar they looked.
"They said, 'Look at yourselves in the mirror'.
"And I was like, 'Oh my God, she has my nose! We have the same laugh'.
"At dinner, I kept looking at her the whole time," Meena told the BBC from her home in the Netherlands.
The following day, the girls exchanged telephone numbers and addresses and promised to keep in touch.

Even though there was no indication they were related by blood, their connection was instant, and for years they wrote each other letters, often addressing each other as "Sis" because "we felt that way".
They wrote about school, friends, boys, going out and dancing. They told each other about the sports they played and discussed music, discovering they both loved Backstreet Boys.
Then 15 years ago, they lost contact. Minal had moved to France. And Meena had recently had her first child and got busy.

In 2017, Meena attended another meeting of adoptees from India where she heard about DNA testing and decided to take a test herself. But she never found any matches and earlier this year, deleted the app because her phone storage was full. Then on 20 May, Meena received a message from Minal on Facebook.
"'Remember me?' she asked.
Minal had taken a DNA test in April while visiting her parents in the Netherlands and attached a screengrab of her test result.
"I reinstalled the app. I was so nervous I entered wrong passwords 10 times before I was able to log in," Meena says.
The result couldn't have been clearer - the two women were "a 100% match".

"I had a 'full sister' which means we shared the same biological mother and father," Meena explains. "It was like I had an adrenalin shot. I cried. Minal was my missing puzzle piece I had waited so long for. We had called each other sister.
"This DNA match was the confirmation that all our intuition was right."
On a fine sunny day in August the old friends met for the first time since discovering they were sisters.

"It was amazing. It felt like homecoming," Meena, now a mother to three children, says. "For years, Minal and I had felt a big hole in our hearts. We feel like we've been completed. Everything now feels like it's supposed to be."
Reporting on their "emotional reunion", Reuters said "tears, hugs ​and laughter punctuated their ​meeting... followed by their first selfie together".

Minal, 44, who lives in France with her partner and two sons, told the agency that when her ⁠DNA results came in April, she had initially not realised her match was the same teenage girl who had clung to her when ​they first met 30 years ago.
It only sank in when she looked at her photos on social media. "'Meena: Sister.' I couldn't believe it. We were friends before we were sisters.
"We were sisters the whole time," she said, "but we didn't know."
Since May, Meena and Minal have been speaking every other day. They've met each other's spouses, children, brothers and parents.
"Everyone notices how we finish each other's sentences, how we move our heads or walk similar," Meena says.
The fact they are siblings is still sinking in, she says.
"Sometimes we talk for two hours and lose track of time, suddenly remembering that we have to do groceries or pick up children from school."
One thing she and her sister would "love to do", Meena says, is return to the place where it all began.
"We'd love to go to India together sometime, to walk through the streets of Mumbai together.
"There were times when we both felt very lonely, like when I lost my dad or went through a heartbreak," she says.
"I regret we couldn't be with each other - we could have shared happiness, helped each other in tough times."

articles.title: Swimming pigs draw tourists to Greek island
articles.summary: GREECE — On a beach at the small Greek island of Atokos in the Ionian Sea, tourists frolic in the azure waters like most visitors do in the popular Mediterranean country at this time of year. The…

blocks.text: GREECE — On a beach at the small Greek island of Atokos in the Ionian Sea, tourists frolic in the azure waters like most visitors do in the popular Mediterranean country at this time of year. The difference is that they are surrounded by a herd of black pigs.

The island lies a short distance from Ithaca, the island home and kingdom of the hero Odysseus in Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” And like Ithaca, Atokos has become a social media sensation, drawing visitors from around the world who come to swim alongside, and even feed, the docile animals.
The pigs mostly mind their own business as they scour the sand for anything edible, before taking short dips in the sea to cool off.
‘Piggy Island’
“They seem to be in their [environment], and they don’t try to bite if you don’t touch them,” said Francesco Ferrari, a 22-year-old tattoo artist from Italy.
The visitors have been ferried over by tour operator Renato Bisha, who makes several such trips over from Ithaca every day.
With the “Piggy Island” experience gaining popularity over social media, similar day trips are organized from the nearby islands of Lefkada and Kefalonia.
“The island has become viral because of the pigs. Many people actively ask to come to Atokos,” said Bisha, throwing fruit to attract the animals to his boat.
“This is so amazing, I recommend it to anyone,” said American visitor Jamie Jackson. “Never in my life had I ever thought I’d be doing this.”
Little known before images of the swimming pigs went viral on Instagram and TikTok, Atokos now has thousands of visitors, especially during the busy summer months.
“I think [the pigs] are having as much fun as we are,” said another American visitor, Michael Mcanelly.
“It’s something unique, worth coming over to see,” added Simos Gleridis, a 33-year-old accountant from Thessaloniki. /cb

articles.title: Marcos seeks India expertise for PH railway, space projects
articles.summary: NEW DELHI, India — President Marcos is seeking India’s technical expertise and cooperation on major railway projects and space technology development in the Philippines. On the sidelines of his…

blocks.text: NEW DELHI, India — President Marcos is seeking India’s technical expertise and cooperation on major railway projects and space technology development in the Philippines.

On the sidelines of his participation in the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India on Saturday, Marcos held separate meetings with Rail India Technical and Economic Service Ltd. (RITES) and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).
The summit is ending on Sunday, Sept. 13, which also happens to be the President’s 69th birthday.
Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Acting Secretary Dave Gomez said Marcos met with RITES representatives to explore possible cooperation on at least three railway projects.

The priority projects being considered by RITES are the Mindanao Railway Project, a mass rail system in Cebu and the extension of the Philippine National Railways (PNR) system from Tutuban commercial center in Tondo, Manila.
Gomez said RITES could participate in the projects as a consultant or through a public-private partnership (PPP), while also helping the Philippines explore official development assistance (ODA).
“They will look into them and we will study them),” he said after the meeting.
RITES, a Government of India Enterprise under the Ministry of Railways, provides consultancy services in the fields of transport, infrastructure and related technologies.
It has been listed as among the top 500 Indian companies, establishing itself as a preferred choice for clients in over 55 countries across Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East.
Marcos also met with ISRO officials to discuss cooperation with the Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) in support of the country’s long-term goal of launching its own satellite. —Philippine News Agency

articles.title: Trump's comments on a united Ireland may have targeted audience across the Atlantic
articles.summary: Nobody could have predicted that today's main global headline would be Trump's desire to see a unified Ireland.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
US President Donald Trump is visiting Ireland
ByCaitriona Perry
Chief PresenterReporting fromin Dublin
When another world leader meets US President Donald Trump the only certainty about what might happen is the uncertainty about what might happen.
This was exactly the case ahead of President Trump's two-day visit to Ireland.
Nobody could have predicted that by the end of the first day, the main global headline would be his desire to see a unified Ireland.

As the shockwaves of his remarks rippled through this island and Great Britain, it was unclear whether this represented a new US administration policy, or an off-the-cuff remark from a president who likes to take questions from reporters, and likes to give answers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, President Trump with the Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin

blocks.text: President Trump with the Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin
Former Republican Congressman Mick Mulvaney was Trump's special envoy to Northern Ireland in his first term in office.
He cautioned against anyone reading too much into the president's remarks.
"This does not represent a shift in US foreign policy," he said.
"We're still very much committed to the Good Friday Agreement."
Democratic Congressman Brendan Boyle agreed.
"There is bipartisan support for that deal, and that is not going to change."
Although both agreed that Donald Trump was probably right to say that "eventually" unification would happen, that did not mean the US was about to start pushing for it.
Watch: President Trump says he would 'love' to see Ireland unified

Giving an answer to a question that is asked at a free-flowing press conference is one thing, but Donald Trump repeated his sentiments a short time later when he was delivering a speech to an invited audience at the US Ambassador's residence.
In fact it was almost the first thing he mentioned, hinting that maybe he realised he had kicked over a can of worms at his earlier appearance.
The rest of that speech was curious. It was billed as a 20-minute address to Irish and Irish American business leaders, but was about twice that and strayed largely into domestic US matters.
President Trump has a speaking style that he describes himself as "the weave".
He can bounce from topic to topic during any speaking engagement, veering off the script and then returning to the matter at hand.
Today he lauded his own achievements, as he sees them, such as clamping down on illegal immigration, doing deals and boosting defence production.
He repeated his criticisms once again of what he views as the UK's lack of support for his military operation in Iran.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Donald Trump meets Irish President Catherine Connolly

blocks.text: Donald Trump meets Irish President Catherine Connolly
Midterm elections fast approaching
But who was his target audience? The gathered business leaders in Dublin or a US audience tuning in before it was even dawn in much of that country?
This November's crunch midterm elections are fast approaching and the Republican party is under intense pressure because of the president's policies.
They may lose control of one or both houses of Congress.
About one tenth of the US population claim Irish heritage but they are not a homogeneous voting bloc.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bill Clinton alongside former Irish President Mary Robinson in 1995

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Bill Clinton alongside former Irish President Mary Robinson in 1995
Was he trying to target Irish-American independent or swing voters in the US, of which there are many who have flip-flopped between the Republican and Democratic party in recent years?
Some of them do support a unified Ireland and so in this time of chasing every vote, perhaps that played a part.
Bill Clinton secured a lot of Irish-American support when he was running for president, by promising to get engaged in the peace process.
They voted for him and he followed through on his promise and much of that work led to the foundations of the Good Friday Agreement.
But, Irish America is a different place now. Indeed, America is a different place now as politics have become more polarised.
The November election campaigns show no indication that will change anytime soon.
But political leaders in Ireland will be hoping the only debate tomorrow is about the play on the golf course.

articles.title: Afghan woman deported from US in first use of 'alien terrorist' court
articles.summary: The legal US resident was never charged with a crime, but was deported due to her family links to terrorism.

blocks.text: An Afghan woman living in Texas with legal US permanent residency has been deported from the country in the first-ever use of a secretive court.
Nazira Haji Zada, 47, chose to leave the US rather than continue to argue her case before the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ) and her lawyers.

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created in 1996, but had never heard a case before the proceedings in July. It is meant for non-US citizens facing terrorism-related charges when the evidence is confidential and related to national security.
Lawyers for Haji Zada argued that the case violated her right to due process under the US Constitution.
Afghanistan citizen Haji Zada was never charged with a crime, but prosecutors had tried and convicted her son and son-in-law for terror offenses.

Her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhed, were both found guilty of a plot to carry out a mass shooting on Election Day in 2024, inspired by the group calling itself Islamic State.
Haji Zada, who has been living in Fort Worth, Texas, was accused by prosecutors of being the "matriarch" of the group, who had worked "to radicalize the family".
In a statement on Friday, the justice department said she "conceded that she is an alien terrorist and waived appeal of the removal order, terminating her previous [immigration] status".
"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," said US Attorney General Todd Blanche.

"Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States, and this first-ever case before the ATRC shows how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country."
Court-appointed lawyers for Haji Zada said they were denied access to the evidence in her case.

"Our client's choice to consent to removal should not be seen as an endorsement of this court's legitimacy," public defenders Matthew Farley and Mary Manning Petras said in a statement to The Washington Post.

"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process. We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue," they said.

articles.title: Cayetanos back from Singapore trip: 'We just wanted to rest'
articles.summary: Senator Alan Peter Cayetano said he and his family traveled to Singapore simply to take a break, amid questions over their trip abroad.

blocks.text: Published September 13, 2026 4:51am
Senator Alan Peter Cayetano on Sunday said he and his family traveled to Singapore simply to take a break, amid questions over their trip abroad.
In a Facebook Live early Sunday, Cayetano said the trip was private and that there was no reason why they could not travel.
“Private yun at gusto lang magpahinga (It was a private trip and we just wanted to rest),” Cayetano said.
The Cayetano siblings were seen arriving at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport early Sunday.
He said “responsible” public officials, including those from the Bureau of Immigration and the Office of the Ombudsman, had said there was no reason why they could not travel.

Cayetano said he was surprised that their “routine, quiet and short” trip became an issue, which he attributed to what he described as the country’s increasingly “toxic” political environment, where people are quick to create conflict and controversy.
The Senate minority leader’s trip abroad raised questions amid reports linking him to the controversy over the construction of the cauldron, or “kaldero,” used during the 2019 Southeast Asian Games.

Senator Panfilo Lacson has also submitted to the Ombudsman case studies, supported by official documents, detailing the supposed “systemic anomalies” in flood control infrastructure projects in Taguig City, the political bailiwick of the Cayetanos.
Cayetano also referred to what he described as Lacson’s “persecution” of him and his family, as well as Taguig.
“Pinapaubaya ko na sa Panginoon (I leave it to the Lord),” he said.
He said threatened cases, investigations and what he described as constantly changing accusations were part of the cost of fighting for the country.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Legarda spox calls Ombudsman probe 'political persecution'
articles.summary: A spokesperson for Senator Loren Legarda has described the Ombudsman"s investigation into the senator and her son, Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste, as “lawfare” and “political persecution.”

blocks.text: A spokesperson for Senator Loren Legarda has described the Ombudsman’s investigation into the senator and her son, Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste, as “lawfare” and “political persecution.”
Legarda and Leviste are facing complaints before the Ombudsman over Leviste’s solar power firm.

In a statement on Friday, Atty. Antonio “Tony” La Viña said Legarda was facing “classic lawfare,” which he described as the weaponization of the law for political purposes and noted that it had traditionally been used against government critics and opposition figures.

“This is classic lawfare, the weaponization of the law for political purposes. Sadly, this is not the first time it has happened. Previous administrations have done it as well to opposition politicians, government critics, journalists, Supreme Court justices, and social and political activists,” said La Viña, a former dean of the Ateneo School of Government.

La Viña, who said he has worked with Legarda for three decades, cited the senator’s environmental legislation and said she had never been investigated or charged with corruption or similar offenses during her decades as a public official.

The Office of the Ombudsman announced in July that it had launched an investigation into Legarda and Leviste following allegations that Leviste’s renewable energy company failed to supply electricity as mandated by its legislative franchise.

Prior to the Ombudsman probe, the Department of Energy (DOE) filed a complaint with the Department of Justice (DOJ) against Leviste and five executives of Solar Para sa Bayan Corporation (SPBC) for alleged violations of the Public Service Act.

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla claimed Legarda was linked to the case because her son’s company could not have secured its 2019 franchise without her influence as then-chairperson of the Senate finance committee.

La Viña defended Legarda, emphasizing that no formal charges have been filed against her or Leviste. He said, however, that the Ombudsman’s public pronouncements already conveyed an “unmistakable impression that liability has already been assumed,” even though the matters involving them remain at the preliminary investigation stage.
Both Legarda and Leviste have filed their counter-affidavits.
In his radio program on dzRH on Saturday, Remulla said it appeared that Legarda, who is currently on medical leave, did not want to return home from France.
La Viña, in response, said, “Walang sinabi na ganyan sa akin si Senator Loren (Senator Loren never told me anything like that).”
Timing
According to La Viña, Legarda’s inclusion in the Ombudsman’s probe and its timing raise questions about whether the scrutiny is based on evidence or driven by political motives.

“The subsequent inclusion of Senator Legarda in an Ombudsman preliminary investigation, and the timing with which that proceeding emerged, inevitably raise questions about whether the scrutiny against her is grounded in evidence of her own acts or is being driven by the wider political issues surrounding her son,” La Viña said.

He noted that Legarda does not own, run, or participate in SPBC or any Solar Philippines company, adding that being both a parent and a senator does not establish that she benefited, acted improperly, or committed a crime.
“Senator Legarda should not be shielded from scrutiny because Leviste is her son. But neither should motherhood become evidence against her,” he added.
La Viña said Legarda should only be scrutinized based on concrete evidence showing that she improperly intervened with government officials or benefited from the grant of the franchise.

“But the record establishes important facts: the franchise was non-exclusive, it did not provide for government subsidy, its implementation depended in part on regulatory actions assigned to the DOE, and Senator Legarda herself did not vote for its passage,” La Viña said.
‘Out-of-the-box entrepreneur’

La Viña also defended Leviste, maintaining that he did not commit any illegal acts and describing him as an “out-of-the-box entrepreneur” who introduced “new ideas and approaches to fast-track the energy transition.”

“In any case, Leandro introduced new ideas and approaches to fast-track the energy transition, and there may have been policy gaps that prevented the successful implementation of some of those ideas,” La Viña said.

“But that is not a criminal act. He should be praised, not punished, for that. In the same way, he should be lauded and not harassed for his crusade against corruption. Note that harassment against them started only in late 2025 when Leandro exposed corruption,” he added.
La Viña also pointed to the sequence of events leading up to the complaints against Leviste.

He said that after Leviste publicly exposed corruption in late 2025 and called for government-wide investigations, a steady stream of allegations and “investigations” targeting his projects began to surface.
“In conclusion, I reiterate my earlier point that lawfare—weaponization of the law for political ends and gain—is always wrong and in fact unlawful,” La Viña said.
“What is going on is clearly political persecution,” he added. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Céline Dion fans prepare for comeback concert in Paris
articles.summary: Fans of the Canadian singer greeted her as she left her hotel on Saturday.

blocks.text: Céline Dion greeted fans today as she left her hotel, hours before she kicked off her comeback concert in Paris.

The Canadian singer returns to the stage on Saturday for her first full concert in six years, to open a sell-out Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder put a pause in her career.
Some fans arrived as early as 06:00 to get a spot in front of LeRoyal Monceau hotel to catch a glimpse of the star before she left.
She is one of the best-selling music artists of all time and is due to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months.

articles.title: Baghdad confirms attack on Saudi pipeline came from Iraq
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia has said it will not relatiate and wants Iraq to "take the necessary measures." Baghdad is under pressure from the United States to rein in Iran-backed militias.

image.caption: The Iraqi government is under US pressure to rein in Iran-backed militiasImage: Iraqi Prime Minister's Press Office/Handout/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Iraq's government confirmed on Saturday that Friday night attacks on a key Saudi oil pipeline had been launched from Iraqi territory.
Saudi Arabia said that it shut down the pipeline on Friday, calling it a "precautionary measure" over a drone attack that occurred the previous day.
Riyadh said that it would not retaliate, stressing that it wanted to give Baghdad "an opportunity to take the necessary measures."
Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices
Who is behind the attacks on the Saudi pipeline?
No group has claimed responsibility for the attacks.
The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an alliance of Iran-backed Iraqi militias, denied any involvement.
The militias are formally part of Iraq's security forces, but some of the groups occasionally act independently.

Also on Saturday, US President Donald Trump said Iran was "probably" responsible for the pipeline attack, while also seemingly downplaying the US and Saudi Arabia's conflict with the Houthis, an Iran-backed militia that control swathes of Yemen.
"The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," Trump said. "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through."

The Houthis and some of the Iraqi Shiite armed groups are part of what Tehran dubs the "Axis of Resistance," a group of Iran-backed militias in the Middle East that oppose the United States and Israel.
The Yemeni armed group has imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabia since July and seized the Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday.

The Houthis have previously targeted international shipping in the Red Sea, citing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza amid Israel's offensive in the territory, but have said they do not intend to do so as part of their recent advances along Yemen's coast.

blocks.caption: The Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia group has said it will not comply with Baghdad's order to disarm by September 30 [FILE: September 2014]Image: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Iraq under pressure to disband Iran-backed militias

Iraq has been under pressure from Washington to rein in Iran-aligned Shiite armed groups, as some of the militias have hit US-linked targets in the region since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28.
While Baghdad has set a September 30 deadline for their disarmament, several militias have said they will not comply with the order,
The deadline coincides with the date set for the withdrawal of the remaining US-led coalition forces from Iraq.

One of the most influential militias, Kataib Hezbollah, has heavily criticized the disarmament plan and called for guarantees that US forces would never return and measures would be implemented to rid Iraq of US influence on political or economic decision-making.

articles.title: 13 seen as voting threshold in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: Thirteen votes could be enough to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial if only 20 senators are considered active and eligible to participate in the proceedings, law professor…

blocks.text: Published September 13, 2026 12:27am

Thirteen votes could be enough to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial if only 20 senators are considered active and eligible to participate in the proceedings, law professor and litigation lawyer Howard Calleja said on Saturday.

Calleja said the two-thirds voting threshold for conviction should be based on the number of senators who are present and able to perform their functions, rather than automatically using the full 24-member Senate.
“If 20 na lang ang natira, I think the 2/3 of 20 is 13 point something, so 13 din ang gagamitin natin as the number for conviction,” Calleja said at the Saturday News Forum.
(If only 20 remain, I think two-thirds of 20 is 13-point-something, so we would use 13 as the number of votes needed for conviction.)
Calleja said the 1987 Constitution does not specifically require 16 votes for conviction, noting that it requires the “concurrence of two-thirds of all the members” of the Senate.
“The Constitution didn't state ‘16’ or ‘24’ — it admits to the moving number of members of the Senate,” he said.
Calleja made the assertion as the Senate impeachment court seeks the opinion of amici curiae before deciding on the voting threshold for Duterte's conviction in the ongoing impeachment trial.
According to Calleja, the term “concurrence” means senators must be capable of participating in the proceedings.
He said senators who are suspended, unavailable or otherwise unable to perform their legislative functions should not automatically be included in determining the threshold.
Calleja cited suspended senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, saying their suspensions remove their rights, functions, obligations, responsibilities and privileges as members of the Senate.

He also questioned whether Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa should be included in the count, citing his status as a fugitive and questions over whether he took the oath required to serve as a senator-judge after the 2025 elections.
If the three senators are excluded, 21 senators would remain for purposes of computing the two-thirds requirement, Calleja said.
He also raised the case of Senator Loren Legarda, who is on medical leave abroad.
If Legarda returns and participates in the proceedings, Calleja said she should be included in the count. If she does not return, however, he said she should not be counted.
This would leave 20 senators, resulting in a two-thirds threshold of 13 votes, according to Calleja.

Calleja maintained that his interpretation would not amount to changing the rules in the middle of the impeachment trial, saying the Constitution itself does not fix the number of senators to be counted at 24.
He said the number could change depending on which senators are present and capable of participating in the impeachment proceedings.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Burial of King Oyo takes place in Uganda as news anchor prepares for throne
articles.summary:
Royal guards carry casket through streets of Fort Portal amid row over appointment of Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma

Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest…

blocks.text: Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest monarch, has been buried among the tombs of his royal forebears as ⁠his Tooro kingdom looked to put ⁠a bitter succession battle behind ​it.

Oyo’s appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.
Oyo made global headlines in 1995 when he took the throne at the age of three. Images of the toddler king wearing a crown and royal robes sparked curiosity and adoration around the world.

blocks.caption: King Oyo of the Toro kingdom was for a long time the world’s youngest monarch. Photograph: Sipa/Shutterstock

blocks.text: He died last month at 34 ⁠in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.
Uganda is led by an elected head of state but retains several kingdoms that pre-date the ​British colonial era and are regarded as bulwarks of traditional identity ‌and heritage.
At a church service before ‌the burial, Oyo, who became a UN goodwill ambassador championing the fight against HIV and Aids, was eulogised as a reserved but jovial young man.
“Although ‌he became king and carried responsibilities far beyond what most people ever experience, he never completely lost the young boy who loved to have fun,” said his sister, Ruth Komuntale.

Royal guards clad in orange shawls then led the hearse carrying Oyo’s casket through the streets of the kingdom’s capital, Fort Portal, to the royal tombs, as thousands of mourners joined the procession on foot.
The burial, which was held 31 years to the day after Oyo’s coronation, followed days of bickering within the notoriously fractious royal family.
A committee consisting of members ‌of the royal clan announced on Wednesday it had chosen Oyo’s cousin, Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC, as king.

But the late king’s immediate family said his hitherto unknown son should succeed him, as called ​for in his will. Oyo never married and was not known to have any children until the kingdom’s prime minister said in the statement announcing his death that he had a son.

blocks.caption: UBC news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma. Photograph: UBC Uganda

blocks.text: Supporters of Kijanangoma’s succession say Oyo’s family has not been able to produce basic information about the purported son.

A source with knowledge of crisis talks over the matter said Ugandan authorities had successfully pushed through Kijanangoma’s succession on Friday. A government spokesperson could not be reached for comment.
The archbishop of the ⁠Church of Uganda, Stephen Kaziimba Mugalu, called for unity.
“Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict,” he ​told mourners. “It can even destroy the legacy ​of the king we are mourning.“
Oyo himself took the throne after a protracted succession battle that finished in court.

In ​addition to his ceremonial responsibilities and campaigning ‌against HIV and Aids, ​Oyo cultivated close ties with former ​Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whom he named a special adviser to the monarch. Gaddafi donated money towards refurbishment of the royal palace.
The 56-year-old Kijanangoma, who maintained a lower profile as the succession battle played out, has been described by fellow Ugandan journalists as quiet and humble.
Besides the throne, the new king will inherit a considerable royal estate including swathes of land and sizeable cash payouts from the central government.

articles.title: Ukraine: Several killed in series of Russian strikes
articles.summary: Local authorities said several civilians were killed and dozens more wounded across Ukraine by Russian strikes. Meanwhile, the Kremlin has rejected Volodymyr Zelenskyy's proposal to meet with the…

image.caption: Dozens of people were injured in a Russian attack on a residential area in OdessaImage: Nina Liashonok/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russia continued on Saturday its constant strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure, killing at least four people and wounding dozens more.

According to Ukrainian officials, two people were killed in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, while steelmaker ArcelorMittal reported that two more people were killed at its plant in Kryvyi Rih, a city in the center of the country.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said that a Russian strike on an apartment building in Odesa wounded 37 people and that rescue teams are searching for two missing individuals.

blocks.caption: The southern Ukrainian port city of Odesa is a frequent target of Russian attacksImage: State Emergency Service of Ukraine in Odesa Region/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: He added that ten regions came under Russian attack last night and that Russian attack drones are still flying over many of them.
Ukraine retaliates by hitting chemical plants

In response to Russian attacks, Kyiv is fighting back. According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine has attacked "chemical enterprises" in the Perm region of the Urals and in the Samara region, which is located southwestern Russia.

The General Staff in Kyiv also reported a fire at a rubber factory in Togliatti, located in the Samara region. According to their statement, the company specializes in producing synthetic rubber important for tactical and ballistic missiles.
Togliatti Mayor, Ilya Sukhih, said that one person was hospitalized following a massive attack on the city. He added that several multi-story residential buildings were damaged.
Kremlin rebuffs Zelenskyy's meeting proposal

In an exclusive interview with DW, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he is willing to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Group of 20 (G20) leaders' summit in Miami in December.
Zelenskyy backs Putin meeting at Miami G20: 'Results matter'

However, on Saturday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Moscow has yet to decide whether Putin will travel to the summit. "We don't know yet ​whether we'll be going to ​Miami," Peskov said, according to Russian media.
Commenting on Zelenskiy's proposal, Peskov reiterated Moscow's longstanding position that if the Ukrainian leader wants to meet with the Russian leader, he should come to Moscow.
