articles.title: Celine Dion's return to the stage draws thousands of ecstatic fans to Plenitude Arena in Paris

image.caption: Fanny Sucheyre wears her wedding dress on the way into Dion's show. (Sarah Leavitt/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Thousands of devoted fans flocked to the Paris suburb of Nanterre on Saturday as Celine Dion returned to the stage for her first full concert in six years, opening a sellout Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder sidelined her career.
Dion, 58, kicks off sellout residency after stiff person's syndrome diagnosis
Céline mania in Paris ahead of Canadian star's sold-out comeback tour

As the sun began to set in the Paris suburb of Nanterre on Saturday, concertgoers made their way through thousands of feet of barricades, past security and into Europe's largest indoor concert venue. They wore anything from jeans and graphic T-shirts to sparkly mini skirts and floor-length gowns.
For Céline Dion, one woman wore her wedding dress.
"I cancelled the party with all my family and friends to come see Céline," said Fanny Sucheyre, who celebrated her one-year wedding anniversary at the concert.
"I said to myself, if one day I had the chance to see her, I would wear my best dress. So it's my most beautiful dress."

Thousands of devoted fans travelled to Nanterre's Plenitude Arena to watch Dion return to the stage for her first full concert in six years. The show opens a sellout Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder sidelined Dion's career.
Outside the venue, fans belted out lyrics in both French and English. Several said they had loved the Canadian singer since childhood.
Inside, special edition Céline champagne glasses sold out within minutes and the lines for champagne itself stretched more than 30 metres. Even the men's washroom had snaking line ups.

"It's a dream. I haven't slept for three days. I'm 50 years old and right now I feel like I'm 15," said Guylene Richardson, heading into the arena with her daughter, both in Dion concert tees. "With [Dion's] disease, I didn't think she would come back, so it's great. I'm really happy for her. I'm happy for us."

One of the best-selling artists of all time, she announced a diagnosis of stiff person’s syndrome — which causes stiffness and muscle spasms — and disappeared from the spotlight in 2022. She broke her hiatus to perform Edith Piaf's Hymne à l'amour from the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the 2024 Paris Olympic Games.

Dion is scheduled to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months. The City of Light has buzzed with anticipation for the singer's comeback, with signs dotting the length of the Champs-Élysées or along the famed river Seine.
With files from Sarah Leavitt and Carly Thomas

articles.title: Six Nigerians extradited to US over $6M online romance scam
articles.summary:
Alleged members of Black Axe criminal network that swindled US women out of $6m flown from South Africa

Six Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled…

blocks.text: Six Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American women out of more than $6m through online romance scams were extradited to the United States on Friday.

South African police confirmed they were to be extradited earlier on Friday, while local news in Africa confirmed that the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, known as the Hawks, facilitated their handover to officials from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation and Secret Service at Cape Town international airport, in collaboration with Interpol South Africa.
The men, who were arrested in the South African city of Cape Town in 2021, face wire fraud and money laundering charges.

They are accused of belonging to a criminal network known as the Black Axe, which Interpol describes as being among criminal groups responsible for a significant share of the world’s cyber-enabled financial fraud, typically through romance, cryptocurrency and investment scams.
According to South African police, the men are alleged to have targeted more than 100 women in the US, defrauding them of more than $6m through online romance or love scams.
Among the alleged victims were pensioners and businesspeople who were reportedly targeted through sophisticated online relationships.

“Through the coordination of Interpol South Africa, the six will today be transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town to Cape Town international airport, where they will be handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service, who arrived in South Africa this morning,” said police spokesperson Katlego Mogale.

A recent operation by Interpol targeting west African organized crime groups led to the arrest of 58 people and the identification of 263 suspects linked to various criminal networks involved in similar crimes, the multinational police body said last month.
The operation aimed to disrupt money laundering, identify high-value targets, seize assets, and support arrests and prosecution.
In South Africa, authorities raided seven locations in the city of Johannesburg linked to a syndicate that ran romance and investment scams targeting retirees in English-speaking countries.
In that operation in South Africa, police arrested 39 people, seized $2.67m and froze more than 250 bank accounts, Interpol said.

articles.title: Ombudsman: Philippines should secure extradition treaties with European countries
articles.summary: Following reports that former Ako Bicol party-list congressman Zaldy Co is hiding in France, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday said it was time for the Philippines to secure extradition…

blocks.text: Published September 12, 2026 10:00pm

Following reports that former Ako Bicol party-list congressman Zaldy Co is hiding in France, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday said it was time for the Philippines to secure extradition treaties with European countries.
Aside from Co, Senator Loren Legarda and her son, Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste—both the subjects of plunder investigations before the Ombudsman—are also in France.
Speaking on dzRH, Remulla lamented the lack of an extradition treaty between the Philippines and France.

Remulla said Co, who is facing criminal charges over his alleged involvement in the flood control mess, was even able to buy an apartment on Avenue Montaigne in France. The Ombudsman also commented that Legarda, who is currently on medical leave, did not appear to want to return home.

“I think we should. At saka maraming Filipino doon,” Remulla said when asked whether he thought the Philippines should pursue more bilateral agreements or extradition treaties with European countries.
(I think we should. And there are many Filipinos there.)

Remulla is scheduled to travel to France, where he plans to meet with several international law enforcement agencies, including the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). He said he hopes to raise his concern that Europe could be turning into a hiding place for individuals facing criminal cases in the Philippines.
“They protect human rights. But will they protect white-collar criminals and those who got their money from corruption and are storing it within the country?” Remulla said.
His brother, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, is also scheduled to travel to France to meet with Interpol officials.
The Ombudsman may also travel to Brussels or The Hague in the Netherlands to meet with representatives from the European Union.

Remulla made no promises that he would return home with Co. However, his younger brother, Jonvic Remulla, expressed confidence that he could bring Co back to the Philippines. —Jean Mangaluz/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: IDF soldier filmed shooting Palestinian in leg amid West Bank settler standoff
articles.summary:
Incident is latest to raise questions over Israel’s ability or willingness to stop violent settlers in occupied territory

An Israeli soldier shot a Palestinian man, wounding him in the leg,…

blocks.text: An Israeli soldier shot a Palestinian man, wounding him in the leg, as settlers confronted villagers by grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land in the town of Faqqua in the occupied West Bank.

Eyewitnesses said that a group of settlers had entered the area with their livestock, prompting residents to try to stop them. Israeli forces then intervened and, according to men at the scene, opened fire at residents. One of them shot Qassem Hussam, a Palestinian man in his mid-30s, wounding him in the leg.
Reached by the Guardian, the IDF confirmed it had received a report of the incident and that the person who fired was one of its soldiers.

“Earlier today [Saturday], a report was received regarding friction between Israeli civilians and Palestinians near the area of Faqqua,” the IDF said. “An IDF force that was at the scene fired into the air and toward a Palestinian.”
Mohammed al-Sheikh, 34, who was standing next to Hussam, told the Guardian the confrontation began when villagers encountered Israeli settlers grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land.

“Then the Israeli soldiers came,” al-Sheikh said. “They started shooting. One soldier shot Hussam and he fell to the ground. We immediately went to help him and move him away. We couldn’t get an ambulance to the area, so we took him to hospital in a private car.”
Hussam was taken to hospital in a light-to-moderate condition, according to the Palestine Red Crescent.

The Israeli military said the incident was being reviewed by commanders and that its findings would be forwarded to the relevant authorities for examination. The IDF added that the military was investigating the soldier who shot the Palestinian man, apparently in breach of army protocol, according to the Times of Israel.
Video of the incident shows a group of Israeli soldiers and settlers confronting unarmed Palestinian men before shots are fired.
The incident is the latest to raise questions over the Israeli government’s ability or willingness to curb violent settlers in the occupied West Bank, where attacks have continued to increase.

On 8 September, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act, “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.

Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, and announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.

The dramatic shift in the UK’s position came after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of rising settler violence in the West Bank, which led 12 countries, including France and Canada, to announce sanctions.

After Miliband described violent Jewish settler activity in the occupied West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” carried out with the tacit backing of the government of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, announced retaliatory measures including the closure of the consulate and entry bans on several MPs.
It marked the latest stage in a rapidly worsening dispute between the two countries, with diplomatic relations at their lowest point in years, even as violence in the West Bank has continued.

Israeli forces also carried out raids across Jenin governorate on Saturday, arresting six people and injuring a 14-year-old boy, who suffered a broken hand, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Soldiers also raided several villages around Jenin, while forces entered at least five towns in Bethlehem governorate and set up a checkpoint at Za’atara.
East of Ramallah, Israeli settlers attacked the outskirts of Burqa, throwing stones at homes and vehicles.

On 4 September, two Palestinian teenagers were shot dead in al-Mughayyir after settlers entered the village under police and military escort and took dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, residents and Israeli activists said.
The victims were Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19. Three other pupils from their 470-strong school had already been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers this year.

According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 1,111 Palestinians, including at least 243 children, have been killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 7 October 2023.

articles.title: Bulgaria: Fire at factory making munitions for Ukraine
articles.summary: Bulgarian authorities are investigating a fire at a munitions factory for links to an explosion at a similar facility in August. Arms maker EMCO says no human error was involved, as investigators…

image.caption: EMCO's owner has been targeted for assassination by Russia, and its factories and warehouses targeted due to its supplying of arms to UkraineImage: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP

blocks.text: Bulgarian authorities are investigating a fire at a munitions storage facility operated by arms maker EMCO.
Police say the blaze broke out Friday night and follows a similar incident at another EMCO site in August.
EMCO's munitions are used in Ukraine and sabotage has not been ruled out.
The full extent of the damage is not yet known but no casualties have been reported.
"At present there is no danger to the population," said local police, adding that employees had been evacuated and the area cordoned off.
EMCO has ruled out any chance of human error in the incident.
This is a developing story, stay tuned as we update...

articles.title: Trump visits Ireland, says unification would be 'fantastic'
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump's trip to Ireland to watch a golf tournament has also included meetings with leaders there.

image.caption: Trump (in blue suit) received a military welcome upon arrivalImage: Kylie Cooper/REUTERS

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has said he would "love" to see the Republic of Ireland, an EU member, unite with British-run ⁠Northern Ireland as he faced reporters' questions on a range of issues on Saturday.

Trump is taking the weekend trip largely to watch the Irish Open golf tournament held on a course he owns on the country’s Atlantic coast, but he met as well with the Irish president and prime minister, or taoiseach.
The US leader also spoke optimistically about his country's war with Iran and its trade conflict with Canada, among several other topics.
What did Trump say about Ireland?

After a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in the capital, Dublin, Trump said he very much supported what he said would be the eventual unification of the two parts of the island of Ireland.
"Well, I don't want to ​cause any problems, ​but ‌I will tell you, I'd love to see ‌it unified," Trump told ‌reporters.
"The way I look at it, it's ⁠going ​to happen ​eventually ... I think it would ​be a ‌fantastic thing," he added.
"Now the UK will have ​something ⁠to say about it ... but ⁠I think ​it would be a great thing."

The British government responded swiftly to the remarks, with Prime Minister Andy Burham's office saying that in his view, there was no majority public support for a referendum on the issue and that there would not be another one until that changed.

Previous US presidents have avoided touching on the subject in view of the delicate nature of the issue, with Northern Ireland seeing decades of of deadly sectarian violence in the 20th century over the question of whom it should belong to.

blocks.caption: Micheal Martin (L) has led Ireland twice since 2020Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: What did Trump say about the Iran war?
Trump also said that the US war with Iran, which began on February 28, would "end very soon" — a view he has frequently expressed in the past without it becoming reality.
He also said that the end of the conflict would mean that the price of oil, which has soared as a result of the war, would "come tumbling down."
However, he vehemently defended his decision to mount the military operation against Iran.
He said that the US attacked because "Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon", adding: "They were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon."

"If they had it, they would have blown up Israel, they would have blown up the Middle East, and they would have hit some [...] in my opinion, [of] Europe's cities and beyond cities, and they would probably hit us soon before we put out the fire. But they cannot have a nuclear weapon."
The war with Iran is not supported by a majority of the US population, particularly in view of promises made by Trump on the campaign trail to keep his country out of foreign "forever" conflicts.

blocks.caption: Trump and Martin held talks in Farmleigh House in Phoenix Park in DublinImage: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: What did Trump say about Canada?
The president sounded a similarly optimistic note regarding the US trade war with Canada.
He said Canada was keen to make a deal and that one could be struck "fairly soon," while reiterating his claims that Canada had treated US farmers unfairly with its tariffs.
"Canada ‌wants to make a ‌deal ​very badly," he said.
"Canada has ​to treat our farmers better. ​They can't ‌charge our farmers tariffs," he said, ​adding: "You'll ⁠probably see a deal with Canada ⁠fairly ​soon."

articles.title: Uganda lays 'boy king' Oyo to rest amid succession row
articles.summary: A funeral is underway for King Oyo Nyimba, who was crowned in the Tooro Kingdom in 1995 aged just 3. His death at 34 has triggered a dispute over a successor, as rumors abound of possible heirs born…

image.caption: The funeral has been taking place of King Oyo Nyimba, seen here aged 18 in 2010Image: Marc Hofer/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Uganda has concluded a nine-day period of mourning for King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, with a funeral for the Tooro Kingdom's late monarch due to take place in the western city of Fort Portal on Saturday.

Oyo, who once held the unofficial title of the world's youngest king, ascended the throne as a young child in 1995 and died last month of cancer aged just 34, with his death prompting a bitter succession dispute.

blocks.caption: Oyo's coffin lay in state at the Karuziika Royal PalaceImage: Michael Muhati/REUTERS

blocks.text: How is Oyo to be laid to rest?

The casket carrying the king's body, which was draped in the blue-and-yellow Tooro flag, was carried by hearse from the royal palace in Fort Portal in a procession accompanied by royal guards dressed in orange tunics and beating wooden sticks.
The ceremony in St. John's Cathedral was to be attended by hundreds of mourners, including senior Ugandan government officials.
After the service in the cathedral, Oyo was to be buried at the site of the royal tombs.
At the burial ceremony, tradition dictates that the successor should throw nine coffee berries into the grave.

blocks.caption: Oyo's death has caused widespread griefImage: Abubaker Lubowa/REUTERS

blocks.text: Dispute over Oyo's successor
However, the question of that successor has aroused considerable controversy, and it was in doubt until late on Friday who would carry out that rite.
On Wednesday, a committee made up of members of the royal clan announced it had chosen Oyo's cousin, Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, as the new king.
Kijanangoma, 54, is a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC.
But the immediate family of the late king said that the latter's will had called for a son who was born out of wedlock and has yet to be identified to succeed him.
Additionally, there have been claims on social media that there are at least two possible heirs alleged to be Oyo's children.
Those supporting Kijanangoma say Oyo's family has so far failed to come up with concrete information on the alleged son, while traditionalists also favor the choice of an adult as new monarch.
A source with knowledge ⁠of ​crisis talks on the matter said authorities had managed to get Kijanangoma officially accepted as successor on Friday.

blocks.caption: Mourners queued before the royal palace to view the king's bodyImage: Abubaker Lubowa/REUTERS

blocks.text: Beloved traditional monarchs
Queen Mother Best Kemigisa said in a statement that the succession battle undermined the family's ability to mourn the king's death.
"I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: Please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."

Although Uganda is led by an elected head of state, it still possesses several kingdoms that were restored in 1993 after being banned for some three decades following the country's independence from British colonial rule.
The monarchs of such kingdoms are often beloved but hold no formal power. Instead they are seen as guardians of traditional identity and heritage.

articles.title: BRICS summit leaders urge 'maximum restraint' in Middle East
articles.summary: The joint delcaration at the BRICS 2026 summit expressed 'deep concern' over escalation of tensions in the Middle East. China's President Xi.Jingping said the Iran war was not in the bloc's interest.…
articles.byline: Karl Sexton, Felix Tamsut, Midhat Fatimah

image.caption: Xi Jinping is expected to meet Narendra Modi at 5.45 p.m. local timeImage: Mukhtar Khan/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 12, 2026
What does the joint declaration say?
On the first day of the BRICS Summit, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the adoption of a joint declaration.
The joint declaration adopted by the BRICS coalition stresses on the need to cooperate to maintain the smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy.

"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia and, recalling our respective national positions, call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation," the statement read.
The member states have reiterated their commitment to peaceful resolution of international disputes through dialogue, consultation and diplomacy.
The declaration also advocates for a multilateral approach that respects diverse national viewpoints and positions on crucial global issues.
The bloc expressed its concern about the growing risks of nuclear danger and conflict.

articles.title: Russian GRU spies behind failed Leipzig attack: reports
articles.summary: A German newspaper has cited reports tying a failed attack at Leipzig Airport to Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency. One suspect's ties to GRU were known when he entered the country, yet he…

image.caption: Bomb experts were able to disarm an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport in a failed attack now definitively attributed to Russia's GRU military intelligence agencyImage: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: Germany's Welt am Sonntag (WaS) newspaper has cited intelligence reports tying the recent failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport directly to Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency.
In an article published on Saturday, Welt am Sonntag said that a man with known ties to the GRU was responsible for operational logistics in the attempted attack.
Further, it said those ties were known to German authorities when the man entered the country from Turkey, nevertheless, he was not surveilled after arrival.
Classified security assessments cited by the paper say the Russian national is now in his home country after departing to Serbia on a flight from Berlin-Brandenburg Airport.
A second man, a Belarus citizen, was also cited as an accomplice in the report.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig
Explosives thought to have entered Germany from Bulgaria and Serbia

German intelligence sources said that the explosives used in the incident were likely smuggled into Germany via truck from Bulgaria and Serbia and then stored in underground depots once they arrived in Leipzig.

Berlin quickly made clear that forensic evidence found at Leipzig/Halle Airport — including drone configuration, explosives and trigger mechanisms used in other Russian hybrid attacks — pointed to a Russian plot.

In early August, German tabloid BILD reported that authorities had found DNA traces on the drone's remote control antenna. Those samples were said to have matched DNA found at the scene of a July 20, 2024, arson attack at a Leipzig logistics facility operated by German courier company DHL.
Leipzig attack averted but Russian escalation will continue

The incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport — a hub for military aid destined for Ukraine — occurred on the evening of August 4 and involved an explosives-laden drone that was found near a Ukrainian transport jet.
Authorities were able to disarm the drone and after public speculation that Moscow was behind the incident the German government officially blamed Russia in early September.
Saturday's article said Berlin made the attribution on the basis of the intelligence reports cited.
In response to its conclusion, Germany announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn.
The Kremlin in turn reacted by closing Goethe Institutes — a German cultural exchange outfit — across Russia.
As in numerous similar hybrid attacks prior, Russia has denied any involvement in the incident.
Putin denies Russian involvement in Leipzig drone attack

articles.title: Xi Jinping gets red carpet at Brics summit amid thaw in India-China relations
articles.summary:
Chinese president’s arrival in Delhi seen as step towards reconciliation after deadly 2020 military clash

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a…

blocks.text: The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.

The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.

The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which ‌20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.

Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.

Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.

Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.

But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but ⁠was unlikely to ​name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.

China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.

Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.

“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title: Alberta separatists expect a win, regardless of numbers that say otherwise, poll suggests
articles.summary: A political scientist and pollster say that mismatch of expectations has consequences for what comes next and Albertans shouldn’t expect this issue to be put to rest with this one vote.

image.caption: Pro-unity and pro-independence signs in Airdrie, Alta. A poll of Albertans done during the first week of September suggests that supporters of separation believe their side will prevail in the October referendum. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·Exclusive
A political scientist and pollster say that mismatch of expectations has consequences for what comes next and Albertans shouldn’t expect this issue to be put to rest with this one vote.
Pollster also finds many support Option 2 for reasons other than full independence
Alberta separatists think they’re going to win a referendum that surveys suggest they are poised to lose by a wide margin, according to exclusive new polling.

And that mismatch of expectations has consequences for what comes next — including the likelihood that Albertans shouldn’t expect this issue to be put to rest with this one vote, say the pollster and a political scientist.
Abacus Data CEO David Coletto presented the results of the new poll, done during the first week of September, to CBC’s West of Centre on Friday.
On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on a question with two choices: Option 1 is to stay in Canada, while Option 2 supports commencing the legal process to hold a binding referendum on Alberta separation.
That ballot question will be in addition to nine others that focus on constitutional and immigration issues.

Coletto’s poll found 64 per cent of respondents would vote to remain a province in Canada and 24 per cent would vote to start the separation process. Nine per cent were undecided and three per cent said they would skip the question.
But the poll also found that Option 2 supporters have surprisingly high expectations, believing that the separatist option will garner a winning 57 per cent of votes.
Coletto chalks it up to the political bubbles people live in and the natural hopefulness that comes with their strong support of the separatist camp.
Lisa Young, a political science professor at the University of Calgary, says that inflated expectation is worth noting — especially in the context of post-referendum ramifications.
"What he found, I think, should be setting off alarm bells in all of our heads," Young told West of Centre.

"If you do walk into this with the expectation that Option [2] is going to get 57 per cent and the actual outcome is 28 per cent ... the first question is going to be, 'Was this a proper result? Can we trust the outcome?'"
Premier Danielle Smith has said the upcoming referendum will be a gut-check of where Albertans stand, and that the province can hold a vote and move on.
But Young and Coletto don't see it that way.

In the event that the winning side supports remaining in Canada, the poll found many Option 2 voters expect the separatist movement to keep growing. Only six per cent of them said they expect the issue will be settled.
"There seems to be this assumption in the UCP premier's office ... that if you let this group let off steam, it will make the issue go away," Young said.
"This does not simply go away afterward. We're going to live with it one way or another for the next months, if not years."
Who is the typical Option 2 voter?
According to the polling, the typical Option 2 voter is a conservative partisan, somewhat more likely to be a man and tends to be slightly older than the provincial average.

They are more likely to live in small cities or in bedroom communities around Calgary and Edmonton. While rural Alberta contributes more than its share, the communities ringing Alberta's main metropolitan centres provide the most voters.
But the group is more distinguishable by its grievances than its demographics, the poll suggests.

It says Option 2 supporters are far more likely to put being an Albertan ahead of being a Canadian, and have a more favourable view of the United States and Donald Trump. That said, the group is split on whether Alberta should become a U.S. state.

The group also shares near-unanimous agreement that Alberta contributes more to Canada than it gets back, the province’s interests are ignored in Ottawa, and the rest of the country does not respect Alberta, the poll suggests.
Young said she wonders if the separatist camp is adequately reflected among people who were polled.
"I did start thinking back to 2016 in the United States," Young said. "People wouldn't tell a pollster that they were going to vote for Trump because it was seen as sort of socially unacceptable."
Coletto said he's confident his poll factored in as many Option 2 voters as possible, but he also acknowledged this is not a typical election.
"Partisan politics can get divisive. But this is being felt much more deeply and much more emotionally on both sides."
"Whatever side you're on, you've still got to live together no matter what happens going forward."
Do they actually want to leave?

What Option 2 voters hope to get out of a favourable result varies significantly. When asked to identify their main motivation for choosing to commence the process for a binding referendum, only 26 per cent said independence.
The rest are voting for leverage, to send a message or on principle, Coletto said.
"For many Albertans who are inclined to look at Option 2, it's not just a black or white, in and out."
That result aligns with recent messaging from the separatist camp.
“Independence isn't actually on the ballot,” Keith Wilson, with independence group Let Alberta Decide, told West of Centre last month.
“Voting Option 2 sends a message that no, we can do better. We want a more respectful and balanced and fair relationship with Ottawa.”
“Others are prepared to vote for Option 2 when they don't even support independence. And that's why I have some optimism we're going to win on Oct. 19.”
Methodology

Abacus Data surveyed 1,000 Alberta adults online from Sept. 4 to 7, 2026, six weeks before the Oct. 19 referendum. Results are weighted by region, age and gender to census data. A probability sample of this size would carry a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Emily is a reporter and producer with CBC's West of Centre podcast. Previously, she covered Edmonton city hall. She can be reached at emily.williams@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Brazil: Flavio Bolsonaro faces corruption probe weeks before election
articles.summary: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, Lula's top rival in next month's election, is under investigation for alleged corruption linked to financing a biopic about his father, former President Jair…

image.caption: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair BolsonaroImage: Edmar Barros/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the leading right-wing challenger to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, according to newly unsealed court documents.
What do we know about Bolsonaro's corruption probe?

The probe centers on funds Bolsonaro allegedly sought from Daniel Vorcaro, the disgraced banker behind the collapsed Banco Master, to help produce "Dark Horse," an unreleased film starring Jim Caviezel as the elder Bolsonaro.

Investigators are examining roughly $12 million that flowed from a Vorcaro-linked entity to a fund tied to Eduardo Bolsonaro, the senator's brother and campaign adviser, who lives in Texas. One document alleges Eduardo advised on how the money should be managed once in the United States.
Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro?

Supreme Court Justice Andre Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee, opened the investigation in July at the request of federal police, but the case remained sealed until Chief Justice Luiz Edson Fachin ordered it made public this week, Reuters reported.

Federal police raided the production company behind the film and the office of congressman Mario Frias, its executive producer, on Thursday. Both have been barred from leaving the country and deny wrongdoing.
How did the Bolsonaros respond?
Flavio Bolsonaro has denied any misconduct, telling reporters at a campaign stop, "It is very positive that the documents are unsealed," the Associated Press reported
"I want transparency in everything."

Eduardo Bolsonaro similarly rejected the allegations, telling Reuters the funds were routed through the US to avoid interference from Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw his father's coup conviction.
"They want to frame this as bribe money, which it isn't," he said.
On social media, he said investigators “are trying to repeat the mechanism that worked against Jair Bolsonaro.”
What did Lula say?

In a Thursday television interview, Lula said Banco Master "was created in the Bolsonaro administration" and shuttered during his own term. He has called for full transparency in the case regardless of political fallout.
The disclosures come three weeks before Brazil's October 4 election, in which polls show Bolsonaro and Lula roughly tied.

Political analysts say the timing leaves Bolsonaro less room to recover than when the scandal first surfaced in May, though the fallout could also cut against Lula given the case's ties to Vorcaro's dealings with multiple political and judicial figures.
A runoff, if needed, is set for October 25.

articles.title: BRICS leaders meet in India as wars and US tensions test the bloc
articles.summary: NEW DELHI — Leaders of the BRICS nations are meeting in New Delhi on Saturday for a summit focused on trade, investment and global conflicts, as the bloc seeks a bigger role in shaping the global…

blocks.text: NEW DELHI — Leaders of the BRICS nations are meeting in New Delhi on Saturday for a summit focused on trade, investment and global conflicts, as the bloc seeks a bigger role in shaping the global agenda for emerging and developing countries.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is hosting Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and counterparts from the other eight BRICS members. The summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising U.S.-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground among countries with competing geopolitical interests.
Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed around the summit venue and other parts of New Delhi, with traffic restrictions and diversions in place.

BRICS was founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2010. It has since expanded to 11 members, representing about half the world’s population and a significant share of global economic output. The group has increasingly called for greater representation for developing countries in global institutions.

The leaders are expected to discuss economic cooperation, energy, food security, technology, supply chains and reforms to global institutions. Reducing reliance on the U.S. dollar will also be a priority, with members promoting greater use of their own currencies in trade and payments, as well as pushing for alternatives to Western-dominated financial institutions.
Russia and China seek to expand influence
China and Russia see BRICS as a way to reduce Western dominance, particularly that of the United States, while strengthening cooperation among emerging and developing economies.
Putin, in a speech at the BRICS Business Forum in New Delhi on Friday, said the grouping was not against anyone and Moscow was open to cooperation with countries around the world
“We are in favor of our interests,” he said.

Iran has also pushed for mechanisms that could reduce the bloc’s reliance on Western financial systems and shield members from economic pressure, as Tehran faces sweeping sanctions and a U.S. blockade.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian backed expanding trade in national currencies among BRICS members.
“One of the most important steps is to expand the use of national currencies in trade among the members,” he told reporters on Friday.
China, meanwhile, is leveraging the grouping to deepen its influence within the bloc and position it as a counterweight to U.S. power.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Friday that Xi was expected to discuss major international issues and ways to deepen cooperation among BRICS members.
India balances strategic partnerships

For India, the summit highlights its effort to maintain strategic ties with Russia and Iran while deepening relations with the U.S. and Europe. New Delhi has sought to balance its longstanding partnerships with Moscow and Tehran with efforts to expand economic, defense and technology ties with Washington and other Western nations.

India has maintained close ties with both Moscow and Tehran despite the war in Ukraine and tensions between Iran and the U.S., while calling for dialogue and diplomacy to resolve conflicts. Modi met Putin and Pezeshkian separately in New Delhi on Friday ahead of the summit.

India is also hoping the forum will help ease its longstanding strained ties with China. Modi and Xi are expected to hold talks later Saturday, a meeting that could help consolidate a diplomatic thaw between the two countries after border tensions escalated in 2020.

A key test for India will be whether it can secure a joint statement from leaders at the summit. Those divisions were evident in May, when BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement over the Iran war, forcing India to issue a chair’s summary instead.

The summit convenes as fears grow that the Iran war, triggered by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28, may expand amid escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi rebels. The bloc’s unity under pressure is expected to be tested as its members navigate differing positions on the conflict and relations with the U.S.

articles.title: Russia's drone war comes to Moldova and Romania
articles.summary: Incursions by Russian drones into Moldovan and Romanian airspace are increasingly common. This week the Ukrainian president's plane was stopped from taking off from Chisinau. Observers suspect the…

image.caption: A Russian drone struck the border crossing of Starokozache between Ukraine and Moldova on the night of September 8 Image: OdeskaODA/Telegram

blocks.text: For Ukrainians, Russia's air war has been a bitter, bloody reality for years. People in Ukraine are being killed every day by missiles, bombs, and drones. But the country's central and southeastern European neighbors have also found themselves affected, albeit on a smaller scale: Missiles and drones sometimes invade their air space, and occasionally even crash on their territory.

Now the Russian drone war is coming dangerously close to two of Ukraine's neighbors: Romania and the Republic of Moldova, where drone incidents are now an almost daily occurrence. The drones often explode, leaving people injured, and there have also been recent attacks on Ukrainian checkpoints at the Moldovan and Romanian borders.

The attacks have now escalated to such a degree that many observers believe they can no longer be considered unintentional. They suspect the Kremlin is deliberately trying to bring the war to Ukraine's neighbors.

The latest drone incursion and crash on Tuesday caused a furore as it prevented a plane with the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on board from taking off in the Moldovan capital Chisinau. A Russian Geran drone, which can fly as fast as 500 kilometers per hour (311 mph), took off in Crimea, then flew through Ukrainian airspace and eventually crashed in a sunflower field near the Moldovan city of Riscani.

The drone also flew over Romania, where two fighter jets were scrambled from NATO's Kogalniceanu airbase near the Black Sea port of Constanta, though it remains unclear why they did not shoot down the drone, as they had on other occasions.

blocks.caption: Police investigate the debris from a drone that exploded on August 17, 2026, in the Moldovan village of TalmazaImage: Polizei Republik Moldau/DW

blocks.text: More and more incidents in Moldova and Romania

The most serious aspect of the incident was that it showed how limited Moldovan air defense is in its ability to protect the country's air space. The drones were detected and tracked by air traffic control, but it was not possible to shoot them down. According to publicly available information, the country possesses only a small number of Polish Piorun anti-aircraft missiles, and these are only able to protect certain specific targets.

There have been around three dozen drone incidents in Romania and Moldova since the beginning of August this year. The majority were airspace violations, but there have also been crashes and explosions, while debris has also been found. In Romania, several drones have also been shot down. According to official data, 17 drones crashed in August in Moldova alone – as many as in all of 2025.
Deaths at border crossings

There was also a drone strike on the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and southeastern Moldova on the night of September 8. The crossing, situated around a kilometer from Moldovan territory, and was damaged in the attack. Two people were killed and two others wounded, one of them a Moldovan citizen.
The Moldovan leadership has strongly condemned the drone attack. President Maia Sandu said on Wednesday that Russia's war had arrived at the Moldovan border.

"It is hard to understand, given this reality, that there are still voices who try to convince Moldovans that Russia is not the aggressor, or that the war in our part of the world has nothing to do with us," Sandu said.
Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down

The president of the Moldovan parliament, Igor Grosu, wrote on Facebook that these were incidents "we can no longer view as something remote." The threat from Russia, Grosu said, was not a "specter," and not propaganda: "It is a daily reality."
Moldova's Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatii said that the deaths of Moldovan citizens could no longer be ruled out in future.

Vladimir Bolea, the minister of infrastructure, warned that Giurgiulesti, Moldova's port on the Danube, could become a target after the Russian Foreign Ministry accused Romania and Moldova of using the port as a "transit hub" for arms shipments.
'Planned operation' by Russia?

Moldovan military and security expert Rosian Vasiloi, a former head of the Moldovan border police, wrote on Facebook in response to Tuesday's drone crash in Moldova: "This is a planned operation by the aggressor state."
He also referred to the drone's peculiar flight path: After flying from Ukraine over Moldova into Romania, it made an about-turn and flew back to Moldova.

Vasiloi concluded: "We can no longer view our airspace as separate from Ukraine's and Romania's. Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, and Romania already form an interconnected operational area as far as air threats and their impact on regional connectivity are concerned."

The Romanian leadership has not yet reacted to the latest incidents. But in July, the Romanian government made a political and military change of course: After a long period of restraint, it started to shoot down drones in Romanian airspace.

blocks.caption: The remains of a Russian Shahed drone shot down in Romania in July 2026. Russia's ambassador to Bucharest was summoned to receive a formal protestImage: Ministerul Afacerilor Externe

blocks.text: Former Romanian General Virgil Balaceanu, a regular analyst in the country's media, has urged Romania's leaders to accelerate the enhancement of Romanian air defenses. Balaceanu also believes that the drone incident on Tuesday was a deliberate maneuver.

Following this latest incident, the US Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a leading public think tank for analysis of Russia's war against Ukraine, wrote that while there was no evidence that the airspace violations were intentional, it could be said that Russia benefited from such actions.
In particular, it wrote, the incursions using Russia's latest, extremely fast Geran drone model "aim to further test NATO and Moldovan defenses and the response of the entire NATO alliance."
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: DW exclusive: Zelenskyy offers to meet Putin at G20 in Miami
articles.summary: In an interview with DW, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was in a strong position to negotiate and offered to meet Vladimir Putin in Miami.
articles.byline: Misha Komadovsky, Roshni Majumdar, Timothy Jones

image.caption: DW's Misha Komadovsky interviewed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on September 11 at Canadian Forces Base North BayImage: Misha Komadovsky/DW

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he would travel to Miami if his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, attended the Group of 20 (G20) leaders' summit scheduled for December.
Zelenskyy replied enthusiastically when DW's correspondent Misha Komadovsky posed the question on Friday.
"Yes, of course. We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions," he said.
Zelenskyy added that what he was going to say to Putin mattered less than results.
"It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That's it."
Zelenskyy and Putin have not met in person since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its smaller neighbor in February 2022.
The Kremlin has so far declined to say whether Putin would go to Miami for the meeting.
The Russian leader has not personally attended a G20 summit since 2019.
Last month, Russia's Finance Minister Anton Siluanov was however invited by the US to attend a meeting of G20 countries in North Carolina in a move that upset European officials.
Zelenskyy pushes for more Patriot missiles ahead of winter
Zelenskyy's interview with DW comes as summer is nearly over and Ukraine is gearing up for the cold months of winter.
The Ukrainian president has conceded that his country has been struggling to counter flying jet-propelled drones that Russia has been increasingly deploying.
"They [US] have political will to sell and to help, but the production is not too big. So it means that stocks is a variant," he said.
"Will Americans be ready to give us (Patriots)? I don’t know. We will see."
Patriot missiles are powerful weapons that are currently the most effective defense against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
What Zelenskyy needs from US and European allies
"Russia [currently] produces 140 ballistic missiles per month. So, according to the rules of NATO, if you want to destroy 140, you need a 1-to-2 [ratio], 280 missiles," Zelenskyy told DW.

"You will never have 280 missiles per month, and between us, it’s a huge challenge to have [even] 100 missiles per month. This is what I want. I want to have 100-120 for these difficult months, especially the cold months."
Germany earlier this week said it was going to send Patriot missiles from its national stock, without specifying how many missiles that would be.
Zelenskyy called on Kyiv's European allies to provide more support.
"They have to give as much as possible. With all respect to them, they have to give to Ukrainians to save their lives."
Zelenskyy also spoke of having secured agreements with several European companies to develop a Ukrainian-led anti-missile system called Freya.
He said he was hoping that the first test phase would begin by the end of December, stressing that time was short.
Ukraine faces Patriot missile shortage
Ukraine in 'good position for negotiations'
Zelenskyy said that it was a "good signal" that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv earlier this week, and not just Moscow.
He said he had made clear to them that his country was well-placed for negotiations on ending the conflict, with Russia estimated to be losing more than 30,000 soldiers a month.
Zelenskyy said this meant that Moscow was paying a "big price" for small gains on the battlefield.
"So that’s why we think that we have now good position for negotiations," he said, adding that his country was stronger than last year.

blocks.caption: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Zelenskyy in KyivImage: Ukrainian Presidential Press Office/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Grain and energy top priorities
The other concern that has been coming up steadily over this summer is the shipment of grains through the Black Sea, with Moscow and Kyiv currently targeting each other's ships and hindering exports.
Russia's de facto blockade of Ukraine's Black Sea ports in the Odesa region has led to a 76% fall in Ukraine's grain exports year-on-year so far in August.
Zelenskyy said he had spoken with the two envoys about an energy and grain ceasefire that could provide a starting point for peace.
"What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," he said.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia shuts down oil pipeline, blaming drones from Iraq
articles.summary:
Riyadh has increased its use of the East-West pipeline since the start of the Middle East war to bypass the closure of the strait of Hormuz

Saudi authorities said Friday drones launched from…

blocks.text: Saudi authorities said Friday drones launched from Iraq led to the temporary closure of a crucial oil export route used to bypass the lockdown of the strait of Hormuz.

Riyadh has increased its use of the East-West pipeline, which links Abqaiq, near the Gulf, to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, since the start of the Middle East war to bypass strait of Hormuz closed by Iran.
The Saudi foreign ministry condemned “the targeting of the East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions by several drones coming from Iraq, which caused human injuries and damage”.
“The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries,” an energy ministry official told the SPA news agency earlier.

Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline that carries Saudi oil to its Red Sea coast.

The news comes as Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.
The office of Iraqi prime minister Ali al-Zaidi confirmed the attack originated from Iraqi territory and said on X that the commander in charge of the southern province of Maysan had been dismissed.
The Iraqi government said it condemned “the attacks targeting our brethren in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia [that] originated from a location within the governorate”.

Riyadh said that, at the Iraqi prime minister’s request, it had chosen “not to respond at this stage and to support the efforts of the Iraqi government …to prevent attacks launched from Iraq against the Kingdom and neighbouring countries”.

Riyadh previously accused Iranian-backed Iraqi militias of targeting its oil infrastructure. But it stressed that the kingdom “reserves the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, its security, its facilities,” and its people.

Bahrain, Jordan and Qatar also condemned the attack on the Saudi pipeline, while the Gulf Cooperation Council denounced “a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the Kingdom”.

Oil prices have climbed past $100 a barrel this week, while average US diesel prices topped $6 for the first time on Friday – a potential headache for president Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections.
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced a maritime blockade in July against Saudi Arabia – which supports the Yemeni government – attacking its oil tankers in the Red Sea.
By taking control of the Yemeni Red Sea coast and the islands in the Bab al-Mandab Strait on Friday, the Houthis consolidated their grip on the strategic passage linking Europe and Asia.
Navigation through the Bab al-Mandab Strait was “safe” for all but Saudi Arabia after the latest advances, the Houthis said.

articles.title: Prosecution, victims: Duterte can’t seek charges refiling at trial stage
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution and the victims’ lawyers told a chamber of the International Criminal Court (ICC) that the lawyers of former President Rodrigo Duterte cannot challenge the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution and the victims’ lawyers told a chamber of the International Criminal Court (ICC) that the lawyers of former President Rodrigo Duterte cannot challenge the scope and form of the charges now that he is on his way to trial.

Both the prosecution and the common legal representative of victims (CLRVs) expressed their objections, in separate filings dated Sept. 10, to the motion of the defense calling for the amendment of the charges against Duterte, who is facing three counts of murder as a crime against humanity.

The camp of Duterte, in a filing on Aug. 31, specifically wants the Trial Chamber (TC) III to direct the prosecution to refile a set of charges that “properly informs the accused of the case he needs to meet,” including further defining the scope in terms of counts and coming up with an “exhaustive list underpinning acts” to represent the entirety of the charges.

The prosecution, which charged Duterte for the killing of 76 individuals in 49 incidents under his so-called war on drugs, opposed the motion because the questions on the “adequacy” posed by the defense had already been determined and affirmed by the pre-trial chamber (PTC).

“[T]he three counts each have a clear temporal, geographical and material scope, and this is consistent with the requirements of article 74(2) of the Statute. The Defence’s mere disagreement with the analysis of the Pre-Trial Chamber is insufficient to show any defect,” the prosecution said in its 10-page response to the motion.
The CLRVs, for its part, asked for the outright rejection of the motion of Duterte’s camp for being “procedurally misconceived.”
They said the defense cannot just ask the TC III to reopen the issue “under the guise of a motion concerning the ‘form’ of the charges.”

“[S]hould the Chamber consider that the defence genuinely seeks to challenge defects in the (document containing charges) itself, such objections belong to the pre-confirmation stage and cannot now be raised before the Trial Chamber,” they said in a 10-page response.
The defense merely reiterated its disagreement with the PTC’s earlier decision and “advance[d] no argument” to warrant a reversal, the CLRVs said.
The trial of Duterte, who is detained in The Hague, is slated to begin on Nov. 30 and is seen to continue until next year. /mr

articles.title: Death toll from Philippines ferry fire rises to 35, as officials warn toll will grow
articles.summary:
The deadly fire had begun in the ferry’s cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds

The bodies of passengers killed in a

blocks.text: The bodies of passengers killed in a ferry fire off the Philippines arrived at a port near the resort town of Coron, Palawan, on Saturday morning, as the country’s coast guard warned the death toll of 35 would grow.

Tents were being set up to receive 30 bodies brought from the M/V June Aster, which ran aground near the tourist hotspot after a fire erupted on Wednesday evening and tore through the vessel “in seconds”.

Coast guard spokesperson Noemie Cayabyab told a Saturday press conference the remains would be turned over to police forensic investigators for “proper disposition and identification” before allowing local authorities to inform family members.
“Currently, we are focused on the retrieval, and after that we will proceed with the investigation,” she said, confirming the bodies had been found in the ship’s economy accommodation area.
Police investigators were seen arriving at the port shortly after the press conference ended.
Asked how many bodies remained aboard the ship, she said authorities would provide an update later in the day.

Cayabyab told AFP on Friday evening that the first transfer had been capped at 30 bodies because of the capacity of the patrol vessel transporting them and that additional cadavers remained on the ferry.
Five others had been confirmed dead in the immediate wake of the fire.

Photos released by the coast guard showed rows of body bags being placed into a small ship alongside men in hazmat suits. Thirty passengers and 13 crew have so far been rescued, while 54 people remain unaccounted for.
On Friday, Cayabyab had told a radio station the fire had begun in the cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds.
“From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly,” she said of survivors’ accounts.
“Everything happened in seconds,” she said, adding that those who made it off the ship had not even had time to put on lifejackets.
Myra Cabilan said she had flown to Coron to find her missing brother, 40-year-old Rammel Gonzaga, who had taken the ferry from Manila on a business trip with his brother-in-law.
“His wife had just given birth a month ago. He was so happy he was given a daughter,” Cabilan said, fighting back tears.
“At dawn, I still believed he survived. But he’s still missing. I have lost hope.”
Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident have taken to leaving comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog.
The ferry’s manifest listed 134 crew and passengers, but two had not boarded, according to the coast guard. The ferry was also carrying goods, an electric vehicle, a pickup truck, and motorcycles.
The archipelago nation of 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas.
Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country’s more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.
On Thursday, the company that owns the M/V June Aster, Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc, said it was fully cooperating with the investigation.

blocks.text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is holding its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026, after being postponed at least four times: first in May 2022, then in May 2025, October 2025, and again in March 2026.

The historic polls are seen as a pivotal moment in the decades-long peace process in a region that was mired in conflict and socioeconomic and political challenges. The upcoming elections are also a test for the Bangsamoro transition and the institutions and systems established in the last seven years.
